title: Marāḥ al-arwāḥ
author: Aḥmad b. ʿAlī b. Masʿūd
subject: sarf
summary: Marāḥ al-arwāḥ (“the resting place of the spirits”) of Aḥmad b. ʿAlī b. Masʿūd is the last and fullest of the five books of ṣarf of the Ottoman madrasa, read after the Amthila, the Binā, the Maqṣūd and al-ʿIzzī. In seven chapters it takes the sound verb, with its thirty-five bābs, its past, future, command and prohibition, its participles and its nouns of time, place and instrument, and then the doubled, the hamzated, the mithāl, the hollow, the defective and the lafīf, ending the sixth chapter with the letters that are substituted for one another. It gives a reason for almost every form: why the past is built on fatḥa, why the hamza of joining has kasra, why qāla comes from qawala, and it reports the Baṣrans and the Kūfans, Sībawayh and al-Akhfash where they differ. The lessons follow its order, take each change (iʿlāl, idghām, the lightening of the hamza) step by step from its base form as the print gives it, and show the sound forms with The Nahwi's conjugation tool.

parts.title: Chapter one: the sound verb, its maṣdar and its bābs

lessons.title: The preface: ṣarf, the mother of the sciences
body: The book opens with the author's name, a prayer for him and his parents, and a saying the madrasa still repeats: “ṣarf is the mother of the sciences and naḥw their father”. Ṣarf shapes the word, naḥw sets it to work in a sentence, and every science that reads Arabic texts is born of the two. Those who know ṣarf “grow strong in understanding”, and those who lack it “go astray in transmission”: they misread what they hand on.

Then the author names and praises his book in rhymed prose: Marāḥ al-arwāḥ, “the resting place of the spirits”. A marāḥ is the place to which the herds come back in the evening to rest, and the rhymes play on the same sound: najāḥ, raḥrāḥ, rāḥ, tuffāḥ. The book is offered “for the boy”: it was written for young students, and it was read in the Ottoman madrasa as the last of its five books of ṣarf.

The second passage gives the plan. The ṣarrāf, the money-changer, here the student of ṣarf (both words come from ṣ-r-f, “to turn, to change”), needs two things. First, seven bābs “for knowing the patterns”: the sound, the doubled, the hamzated, the mithāl, the hollow, the defective and the lafīf. Second, “the derivation of nine things from every maṣdar”: the past, the future, the command, the prohibition, and the nouns of the doer, of the one done to, of time, of place and of the instrument.

So the book is cut into seven chapters, one for each kind of root. The first, on the sound verb, has its own sections for the nine things; each later chapter takes a root with a doubled letter, a hamza or a weak letter, runs it through the same nine things, and shows what changes and why.

Two words to fix now. Bāb here means a chapter by kind of root; in lesson 5 the same word means a class of conjugation, as ḍaraba yaḍribu. And “the future” (al-mustaqbal) is this book's usual name for the form other books call the muḍāriʿ; lesson 15 gives both names and their reasons.

the money-changer: the author's name for the student of ṣarf
the seven chapters, one for each kind of root
derivation: taking the nine things from the maṣdar

tasks.prompt: Name the seven bābs in the book's order.
tasks.answer: The sound (al-ṣaḥīḥ), the doubled (al-muḍāʿaf), the hamzated (al-mahmūz), the mithāl, the hollow (al-ajwaf), the defective (al-nāqiṣ) and the lafīf.

tasks.prompt: List the nine things that are derived from every maṣdar.
tasks.answer: The past, the future, the command, the prohibition, the active participle (noun of the doer), the passive participle (noun of the one done to), the noun of time, the noun of place and the noun of the instrument.

tasks.prompt: Why does the author call the student a ṣarrāf?
tasks.answer: Ṣarrāf is the money-changer, and the word has the same root, ṣ-r-f, as ṣarf. As the changer turns one coin into others, the student of ṣarf turns one maṣdar into the past, the future and the rest; the play on words names the student after his science.

quiz.prompt: “Ṣarf is the mother of the sciences, and naḥw…”
quiz.explanation: Al-naḥw abūhā: the two together give birth to the sciences of Arabic.

quiz.prompt: How many bābs does the ṣarrāf need for knowing the patterns?
quiz.explanation: Seven, one for each kind of root, and the book has seven chapters to match.

quiz.prompt: How many things does the book derive from every maṣdar?
quiz.explanation: The past, the future, the command, the prohibition, and the nouns of doer, object, time, place and instrument.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is NOT among the nine derived things?
quiz.explanation: The maṣdar is the source from which the nine are derived, not one of them.

quiz.prompt: Marāḥ al-arwāḥ means…
options: the resting place of the spirits
quiz.explanation: A marāḥ is where the herds come back to rest in the evening; the book is a resting place for the spirits.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is one of the seven bābs?
quiz.explanation: The lafīf, with two weak letters, is the seventh and last chapter.

quiz.explanation: Ṣarrāf and ṣarf share the root ṣ-r-f; the author plays on the money-changer.

text.original: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ. قَالَ الْمُفْتَقِرُ إِلَى اللَّهِ الْوَدُودِ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ، غَفَرَ اللَّهُ لَهُ وَلِوَالِدَيْهِ، وَأَحْسَنَ إِلَيْهِمَا وَإِلَيْهِ: اعْلَمْ أَنَّ الصَّرْفَ أُمُّ الْعُلُومِ، وَالنَّحْوُ أَبُوهَا، وَيَقْوَى فِي الدِّرَايَاتِ دَارُوهَا، وَيَطْغَى فِي الرِّوَايَاتِ عَارُوهَا. فَجَمَعْتُ فِيهِ كِتَابًا مَوْسُومًا بِمَرَاحِ الْأَرْوَاحِ، وَهُوَ لِلصَّبِيِّ جَنَاحُ النَّجَاحِ، وَرَاحُ رَحْرَاحٍ، وَفِي مَعِيَّتِهِ حِينَ رَاحَ مِثْلُ تُفَّاحٍ أَوْ رَاحٍ. وَبِاللَّهِ أَعْتَصِمُ عَمَّا يَصِمُ، وَأَسْتَعِينُ، وَهُوَ نِعْمَ الْمَوْلَى وَنِعْمَ الْمُعِينُ.
text.en: In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. The one in need of God, the Loving, Aḥmad b. ʿAlī b. Masʿūd — may God forgive him and his parents, and be good to them and to him — says: Know that ṣarf is the mother of the sciences and naḥw their father; those who know it grow strong in understanding, and those who lack it go astray in transmission. So I have gathered on it a book named Marāḥ al-arwāḥ (“the resting place of the spirits”): for the boy it is the wing of success and the wine of a broad cup, and in its company, when he goes off, it is like an apple or wine. In God I seek protection from what disgraces, and His help I seek; He is the best Master and the best Helper.

text.original: اعْلَمْ أَسْعَدَكَ اللَّهُ أَنَّ الصَّرَّافَ يَحْتَاجُ فِي مَعْرِفَةِ الْأَوْزَانِ إِلَى سَبْعَةِ أَبْوَابٍ: الصَّحِيحُ وَالْمُضَاعَفُ وَالْمَهْمُوزُ وَالْمِثَالُ وَالْأَجْوَفُ وَالنَّاقِصُ وَاللَّفِيفُ، وَاشْتِقَاقِ تِسْعَةِ أَشْيَاءَ مِنْ كُلِّ مَصْدَرٍ، وَهِيَ الْمَاضِي وَالْمُسْتَقْبَلُ وَالْأَمْرُ وَالنَّهْيُ وَاسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ وَالزَّمَانِ وَالْمَكَانِ وَالْآلَةِ؛ فَكَسَرْتُهُ عَلَى سَبْعَةِ أَبْوَابٍ.
text.en: Know — may God make you happy — that the ṣarrāf (the money-changer, here the student of ṣarf) needs, for knowing the patterns, seven chapters: the sound, the doubled, the verb with hamza, the mithāl, the hollow (ajwaf), the defective (nāqiṣ) and the lafīf; and the derivation of nine things from every maṣdar, which are the past, the future, the command, the prohibition, and the nouns of the doer, of the object, of time, of place and of the instrument. So I have divided it into seven chapters.

lessons.title: The sound verb, and the maṣdar as the origin
body: The first chapter begins with a definition. The sound verb is one in which, “in the place of the fāʾ, the ʿayn and the lām, there is no letter of weakness, no doubling and no hamza”: ḍaraba, “he hit”. This is narrower than the everyday word “sound”: madda, with its doubled dāl, and akhadha, with its hamza, have no weak letter, yet this book does not call them sound. Chapters two and three say why.

Why are the three root letters called by the letters of faʿala? “So that there would be in it something of the letters of the lips, of the middle and of the throat”: the fāʾ is made with the lips, the ʿayn deep in the throat, the lām in the middle of the mouth. The measure word takes in every region where letters are made.

Next, the maṣdar. Al-ḍarb, “hitting”, is the maṣdar “from which the nine things are born”, and it is the origin of derivation for the Baṣrans, for three reasons. Its meaning is one, the event alone, while the verb means two things, the event and its time; and the one comes before the many. It is a noun, and “the noun has no need of the verb”: a noun can stand without a verb, while a verb needs a noun for its doer, as the usual explanation runs. And its very name says so: a maṣdar is a “source”, the place from which these things issue (taṣduru).

Derivation (ishtiqāq) is defined as finding “a correspondence in wording and meaning” between two words, and it is of three kinds. The small: the same letters in the same order, ḍaraba from al-ḍarb. The great: the same letters in another order, jabadha, “he pulled”, from al-jadhb, “pulling”. The greatest: letters close in the place where they are made, naʿaqa, “he cried out”, from al-nahq, “braying”, where the ʿayn and the hāʾ are both letters of the throat.

“The derivation meant here is the small derivation.” Every one of the nine things keeps the letters of its maṣdar in their order: ḍaraba, yaḍribu, iḍrib, ḍārib, maḍrūb are all ḍ-r-b. A beginner who hears “derivation” should think of this kind only.

terms.en: the sound verb: no weak letter, doubling or hamza among its root letters
the verbal noun: the source of the nine derived things
small derivation: the same letters in the same order
great derivation: the same letters in another order
greatest derivation: letters near in their place of articulation
the grammarians of Basra

examples.en: ḍaraba min al-ḍarb: small derivation
jabadha min al-jadhb: great derivation, the letters reordered
naʿaqa min al-nahq: greatest derivation, ʿayn and hāʾ both of the throat

tasks.prompt: Why is ḍaraba sound in this book, while madda and akhadha are not?
tasks.answer: The sound verb has, among its fāʾ, ʿayn and lām, no weak letter, no doubling and no hamza. Ḍaraba has none of them; madda has a doubled letter (d-d) and akhadha a hamza, so they belong to the chapters on the doubled and the hamzated.

tasks.prompt: Give the Baṣrans' three reasons for making the maṣdar the origin of derivation.
tasks.answer: Its meaning is one (the event), while the verb's is many (event and time), and the one comes first; it is a noun, and the noun has no need of the verb; and its name, maṣdar, “source”, says that the things issue from it.

tasks.prompt: Say which kind of derivation each pair shows: jabadha / al-jadhb; ḍaraba / al-ḍarb; naʿaqa / al-nahq.
tasks.answer: Jabadha and al-jadhb: great (the same letters, another order). Ḍaraba and al-ḍarb: small (the same letters, the same order). Naʿaqa and al-nahq: greatest (ʿayn and hāʾ are near in the throat).

tasks.prompt: Why were the fāʾ, the ʿayn and the lām chosen for the measure?
tasks.answer: Because between them they come from the three regions where letters are made: the fāʾ from the lips, the lām from the middle of the mouth and the ʿayn from the throat.

quiz.prompt: Which verb is sound (ṣaḥīḥ) in this book?
quiz.explanation: Madda is doubled, akhadha hamzated and qāla hollow; ḍaraba has none of these.

quiz.prompt: For the Baṣrans, the origin of derivation is…
quiz.explanation: Al-ḍarb is the maṣdar from which the nine things are born.

quiz.prompt: Why does the verb come after the maṣdar, by the first reason?
options: The verb means event and time, the maṣdar the event alone
quiz.explanation: The one comes before the many: the maṣdar's meaning is one, the verb's two.

quiz.prompt: Jabadha from al-jadhb is…
quiz.explanation: The same letters, but the dhāl and the bāʾ have changed places.

quiz.prompt: Which derivation does ṣarf mean in this book?
quiz.explanation: “The derivation meant here is the small derivation.”

quiz.prompt: The fāʾ, ʿayn and lām of the measure come from…
options: the lips, the throat and the middle of the mouth
quiz.explanation: Fāʾ from the lips, ʿayn from the throat, lām from the middle.

quiz.prompt: The word maṣdar means…
options: a source, from which things issue
quiz.explanation: These things issue (taṣduru) from it.

text.original: الصَّحِيحُ هُوَ الَّذِي لَيْسَ فِي مُقَابَلَةِ الْفَاءِ وَالْعَيْنِ وَاللَّامِ حَرْفُ عِلَّةٍ وَالتَّضْعِيفُ وَالْهَمْزَةُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ. وَاخْتُصَّ الْفَاءُ وَالْعَيْنُ وَاللَّامُ لِلْوَزْنِ حَتَّى يَكُونَ فِيهِ مِنْ حُرُوفِ الشَّفَةِ وَالْوَسَطِ وَالْحَلْقِ شَيْءٌ.
text.en: The sound [verb] is that in which, in the place of the fāʾ, the ʿayn and the lām, there is no letter of weakness, no doubling and no hamza, as ḍaraba “he hit”. The fāʾ, the ʿayn and the lām were chosen for the pattern so that there would be in it something of the letters of the lips, of the middle and of the throat.

text.original: فَقَوْلُنَا: الضَّرْبُ مَصْدَرٌ يَتَوَلَّدُ مِنْهُ الْأَشْيَاءُ التِّسْعَةُ، وَهُوَ أَصْلٌ فِي الِاشْتِقَاقِ عِنْدَ الْبَصْرِيِّينَ؛ لِأَنَّ مَفْهُومَهُ وَاحِدٌ، وَمَفْهُومَ الْفِعْلِ مُتَعَدِّدٌ لِدَلَالَتِهِ عَلَى الْحَدَثِ وَالزَّمَانِ، وَالْوَاحِدُ قَبْلَ الْمُتَعَدِّدِ، وَإِذَا كَانَ أَصْلًا لِلْأَفْعَالِ يَكُونُ أَصْلًا لِمُتَعَلِّقَاتِهَا؛ وَلِأَنَّهُ اسْمٌ، وَالِاسْمُ مُسْتَغْنٍ عَنِ الْفِعْلِ. وَأَيْضًا يُقَالُ لَهُ: مَصْدَرٌ؛ لِأَنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَشْيَاءَ تَصْدُرُ عَنْهُ.
text.en: So we say: al-ḍarbu “hitting” is a maṣdar from which the nine things are born, and it is the origin in derivation according to the Baṣrans: because its concept is one, while the concept of the verb is multiple, since it indicates the event and the time, and the one comes before the multiple; and if it is the origin of the verbs, it is the origin of what is connected with them; and because it is a noun, and the noun has no need of the verb. It is also called maṣdar (“source”) because these things issue (taṣduru) from it.

text.original: الِاشْتِقَاقُ: أَنْ تَجِدَ بَيْنَ اللَّفْظَيْنِ تَنَاسُبًا فِي اللَّفْظِ وَالْمَعْنَى، وَهُوَ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَنْوَاعٍ: صَغِيرٌ، وَهُوَ أَنْ يَكُونَ بَيْنَهُمَا تَنَاسُبٌ فِي الْحُرُوفِ وَالتَّرْتِيبِ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ مِنَ الضَّرْبِ؛ وَكَبِيرٌ، وَهُوَ أَنْ يَكُونَ بَيْنَهُمَا تَنَاسُبٌ فِي اللَّفْظِ وَالْمَعْنَى دُونَ التَّرْتِيبِ، نَحْوُ: جَبَذَ مِنَ الْجَذْبِ؛ وَأَكْبَرُ، وَهُوَ أَنْ يَكُونَ بَيْنَهُمَا تَنَاسُبٌ فِي الْمَخْرَجِ، نَحْوُ: نَعَقَ مِنَ النَّهْقِ. وَالْمُرَادُ بِالِاشْتِقَاقِ الْمَذْكُورِ هُنَا الِاشْتِقَاقُ الصَّغِيرُ.
text.en: Derivation (ishtiqāq) is that you find between two words a correspondence in wording and meaning. It is of three kinds: the small, which is that there is a correspondence between them in the letters and their order, as ḍaraba “he hit” from al-ḍarbi “hitting”; the great, which is that there is a correspondence between them in wording and meaning without the order, as jabadha “he pulled” from al-jadhbi “pulling”; and the greatest, which is that there is a correspondence between them in the point of articulation, as naʿaqa “he cried out” from al-nahqi “braying”. The derivation meant here is the small derivation.

lessons.title: The Kūfans' case for the verb, and the answer
body: The Kūfans held the opposite: “the verb should be the origin”. Their first argument is the change of weak letters (iʿlāl). Where the verb changes, the maṣdar changes too: yaʿidu loses its wāw and so does ʿidatan; qāma turns its wāw into alif and qiyāman turns it into yāʾ. Where the verb keeps its letter, the maṣdar keeps it: wajila wajalan, qāwama qiwāman, not qiyāman. The maṣdar follows the verb, and what is followed is the origin.

Their second argument: the maṣdar emphasises the verb. Ḍarabtu ḍarban, “I hit a hitting”, is as if you said ḍarabtu ḍarabtu, “I hit, I hit”; and “what is emphasised is the origin, not what emphasises”. Their third: maṣdar does not mean “source” but “issued”, like a passive participle; the Arabs say mashrabun ʿadhbun, “a sweet drink”, using a pattern of place in the sense of mashrūb, “drunk”. So the maṣdar is what issues from the verb.

“We say in answer to them”: the author takes the Baṣran side. The change in the maṣdar comes from conformity (mushākala), not from the verb being its pivot. Conformity changes forms all the time without making one the origin of the other: taʿidu drops its wāw only to match yaʿidu, and tukrimu drops its hamza only to match ukrimu (lessons 16 and 19).

Being emphasised shows a priority in iʿrāb, not in derivation: in jāʾanī Zaydun Zaydun, “Zayd, Zayd came to me”, the second Zayd emphasises the first, yet nobody derives one Zayd from the other. And mashrabun ʿadhbun is a figure of speech, “of the kind of jarā al-nahru, ‘the river flowed’”: it is the water that flows, not the river, and it is the drink that is sweet, not the place of drinking.

Keep the result: the maṣdar is the origin of all nine. In practice, though, the book derives them in a chain, as the coming sections show: the past from the maṣdar, the future from the past, the command and the active participle from the future, the passive participle from the passive future.

tasks.prompt: Explain the Kūfans' argument from qāma qiyāman and qāwama qiwāman.
tasks.answer: In qāma the wāw of q-w-m changes, and the maṣdar qiyām changes it too (into yāʾ); in qāwama the wāw stays, and so it stays in qiwām. The maṣdar's change follows the verb's, so, they say, the verb is the origin.

tasks.prompt: How does the author answer that argument?
tasks.answer: The maṣdar changes for conformity with its verb, not because the verb is its origin; conformity changes forms in the same way in taʿidu, which drops its wāw to match yaʿidu, and in tukrimu, which drops its hamza to match ukrimu.

tasks.prompt: Why does ḍarabtu ḍarban not prove that the verb is the origin?
tasks.answer: Being emphasised gives a priority in iʿrāb, not in derivation: in jāʾanī Zaydun Zaydun the first Zayd is emphasised by the second, but neither is derived from the other.

quiz.prompt: For the Kūfans, the origin of derivation is…
quiz.explanation: “The verb should be the origin.”

quiz.prompt: Which pair shows verb and maṣdar both keeping the wāw?
quiz.explanation: Yawjalu keeps its wāw, and so does wajal.

quiz.prompt: The author's answer: the maṣdar changes because of…
quiz.explanation: It changes to match its verb, as taʿidu matches yaʿidu.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾanī Zaydun Zaydun the emphasis shows…
options: that the first Zayd is derived
that the second Zayd is the origin
a priority in iʿrāb, not in derivation
quiz.explanation: One Zayd is not derived from the other.

quiz.prompt: Mashrabun ʿadhbun is answered as…
quiz.explanation: It is the drink that is sweet, as it is the water that flows.

quiz.prompt: Whose side does the author take?
quiz.explanation: “We say in answer to them”: he answers the Kūfans.

quiz.prompt: Ḍarabtu ḍarban is said to stand as…
quiz.explanation: The maṣdar repeats the verb's meaning as an emphasis.

text.original: قَالَ الْكُوفِيُّونَ: يَنْبَغِي أَنْ يَكُونَ الْفِعْلُ أَصْلًا؛ لِأَنَّ إِعْلَالَهُ مَدَارٌ لِإِعْلَالِ الْمَصْدَرِ وُجُودًا وَعَدَمًا؛ أَمَّا وُجُودًا فَفِي: يَعِدُ عِدَةً، وَقَامَ قِيَامًا، وَأَمَّا عَدَمًا فَفِي نَحْوِ: وَجِلَ وَجَلًا، وَقَاوَمَ قِوَامًا، وَمَدَارِيَّتُهُ تَدُلُّ عَلَى أَصَالَتِهِ. وَأَيْضًا يُؤَكَّدُ الْفِعْلُ بِهِ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتُ ضَرْبًا، وَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ: ضَرَبْتُ ضَرَبْتُ، وَالْمُؤَكَّدُ أَصْلٌ دُونَ الْمُؤَكِّدِ. وَيُقَالُ لَهُ: مَصْدَرٌ؛ لِكَوْنِهِ مَصْدُورًا عَنِ الْفِعْلِ، كَمَا قَالُوا: مَشْرَبٌ عَذْبٌ، وَمَرْكَبٌ فَارِهٌ، أَيْ: مَشْرُوبٌ وَمَرْكُوبٌ.
text.en: The Kūfans said: the verb should be the origin, because its weakening (iʿlāl) is the pivot of the weakening of the maṣdar, in being and in not being: in being, in yaʿidu ʿidatan “he promises, a promise” and qāma qiyāman “he stood, a standing”; in not being, in the like of wajila wajalan “he feared, a fearing” and qāwama qiwāman “he resisted, a resisting”; and its being the pivot shows that it is the origin. Also, the verb is emphasised by it, as ḍarabtu ḍarban “I hit a hitting”, which stands as ḍarabtu ḍarabtu “I hit, I hit”, and what is emphasised is the origin, not what emphasises. It is called maṣdar because it is issued (maṣdūr) from the verb, as they said mashrabun ʿadhbun “a sweet drink” and markabun fārihun “a fine mount”, that is, mashrūbun “drunk” and markūbun “ridden”.

text.original: قُلْنَا فِي جَوَابِهِمْ: إِعْلَالُ الْمَصْدَرِ لِلْمُشَاكَلَةِ لَا لِلْمَدَارِيَّةِ، كَحَذْفِ الْوَاوِ فِي تَعِدُ وَالْهَمْزَةِ فِي تُكْرِمُ، وَالْمُؤَكَّدِيَّةُ لَا تَدُلُّ عَلَى الْأَصَالَةِ فِي الِاشْتِقَاقِ، بَلْ فِي الْإِعْرَابِ، كَمَا فِي: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ زَيْدٌ، وَقَوْلُهُمْ: مَشْرَبٌ عَذْبٌ وَمَرْكَبٌ فَارِهٌ، مِنْ بَابِ: جَرَى النَّهْرُ، وَسَالَ الْمِيزَابُ.
text.en: We say in answer to them: the weakening of the maṣdar is for conformity, not because [the verb] is its pivot, like the dropping of the wāw in taʿidu “you promise” and of the hamza in tukrimu “you honour”. Being the emphasised does not show being the origin in derivation, but in iʿrāb, as in jāʾanī Zaydun Zaydun “Zayd, Zayd came to me”. And their saying mashrabun ʿadhbun and markabun fārihun is of the kind of jarā al-nahru “the river flowed” and sāla al-mīzābu “the gutter ran”.

lessons.title: The maṣdars of the triliteral and of the longer verbs
body: “The maṣdar of the triliteral is plentiful”: a three-letter verb has no single maṣdar pattern, and “according to Sībawayh it rises to thirty-two”. The book lists them by example: qatl, fisq and shughl (faʿl, fiʿl, fuʿl); raḥma, nishda, kudra with the tāʾ; daʿwā, dhikrā, bushrā with the short alif; layyān, ḥirmān, ghufrān, nazawān with -ān; and so on to madkhal, marjiʿ, masʿāt and maḥmida with a mīm.
No rule tells which of these a given verb takes; the madrasa learns them by hearing and from the dictionary. What the list teaches is to recognise a maṣdar when you meet one in any of these shapes.

The maṣdar also comes on the patterns of the two participles: qumtu qāʾiman, “I stood a standing”, uses the pattern fāʿil; and in the verse bi-ayyikumu al-maftūnu (68:6), al-maftūn, on the pattern mafʿūl, is taken as a maṣdar, “which of you has the affliction”. It comes for intensity too: al-tahdār and al-talʿāb, “much prattling, much playing”, on tafʿāl, and al-ḥiththīthā and al-dillīlā on fiʿʿīlā.

“The maṣdar of the non-triliteral comes on one course”: each augmented pattern has its regular maṣdar, as the conjugation tool gives it: akrama, ikrām; qaṭṭaʿa, taqṭīʿ; istakhraja, istikhrāj. The exceptions named are rare forms: killām from kallama (whose usual maṣdar is taklīm), qittāl and qītāl from qātala, tiḥimmāl from taḥammala, and zilzāl from zalzala.

A trap: the qāʾiman of qumtu qāʾiman looks like an active participle, and in many sentences it is one (a ḥāl, “standing”). Here the book counts it as a maṣdar, because it stands where qiyāman would stand: “I stood a standing”.

terms.en: the maṣdar of the three-letter verb: many patterns, learnt by hearing
the maṣdar of the longer verbs: one regular pattern each
intensity, as in tahdār and ḥiththīthā
the great Baṣran grammarian, who counted thirty-two patterns

examples.en: qatl, fisq, shughl: faʿl, fiʿl, fuʿl
qumtu qāʾiman: a maṣdar on the pattern fāʿil
al-tahdār, al-talʿāb, al-ḥiththīthā, al-dillīlā: maṣdars of intensity
ikrām, taqṭīʿ, istikhrāj: the regular maṣdars of akrama, qaṭṭaʿa, istakhraja (conjugation tool)

tasks.prompt: Sort these maṣdars by their pattern: raḥma, ghufrān, dhikrā, dukhūl, madkhal.
tasks.answer: Raḥma: faʿla, with the tāʾ. Ghufrān: fuʿlān. Dhikrā: fiʿlā, with the short alif. Dukhūl: fuʿūl. Madkhal: mafʿal, with the mīm.

tasks.prompt: Give the regular maṣdar of akrama, qaṭṭaʿa and istakhraja (from the conjugation tool), and the rare forms the book names for qātala and kallama.
tasks.answer: Akrama: ikrām; qaṭṭaʿa: taqṭīʿ; istakhraja: istikhrāj. For qātala the book names qittāl and qītāl, for kallama killām: exceptions to the one regular course.

tasks.prompt: In qumtu qāʾiman, why is qāʾiman counted as a maṣdar?
tasks.answer: It stands where the maṣdar qiyāman would stand, “I stood a standing”: the maṣdar has here come on the pattern of the active participle, fāʿil.

quiz.prompt: How many maṣdar patterns of the triliteral did Sībawayh count, by the book?
quiz.explanation: “According to Sībawayh it rises to thirty-two.”

quiz.prompt: Which maṣdar has the pattern with mīm?
quiz.explanation: Madkhal, marjiʿ, masʿāt and maḥmida end the list: maṣdars with a mīm.

quiz.prompt: Al-tahdār, “much prattling”, is a maṣdar of…
quiz.explanation: Tafʿāl is given as a pattern of intensity (mubālagha).

quiz.prompt: The maṣdar of the non-triliteral comes…
options: on one course, with few exceptions
quiz.explanation: Each augmented pattern has its regular maṣdar.

quiz.prompt: Which is named as a rare maṣdar of qātala?
quiz.explanation: Qittāl and qītāl, beside the regular pattern.

quiz.prompt: In bi-ayyikumu al-maftūnu, al-maftūn is taken as…
options: a maṣdar on the pattern mafʿūl
quiz.explanation: “Which of you has the affliction”: the maṣdar on the pattern of the passive participle.

quiz.prompt: The regular maṣdar of istakhraja is…
quiz.explanation: Istafʿala gives istifʿāl: istikhrāj.

text.original: وَمَصْدَرُ الثُّلَاثِيِّ كَثِيرٌ، وَعِنْدَ سِيبَوَيْهِ يَرْتَقِي إِلَى اثْنَيْنِ وَثَلَاثِينَ بَابًا، نَحْوُ: قَتْلٍ، وَفِسْقٍ، وَشُغْلٍ، وَرَحْمَةٍ، وَنِشْدَةٍ، وَكُدْرَةٍ، وَدَعْوَى، وَذِكْرَى، وَبُشْرَى، وَلَيَّانٍ، وَحِرْمَانٍ، وَغُفْرَانٍ، وَنَزَوَانٍ، وَطَلَبٍ، وَخَنِقٍ، وَصِغَرٍ، وَهُدًى، وَغَلَبَةٍ، وَسَرِقَةٍ، وَذَهَابٍ، وَصِرَافٍ، وَسُؤَالٍ، وَزَهَادَةٍ، وَدِرَايَةٍ، وَدُخُولٍ، وَقَبُولٍ، وَوَجِيفٍ، وَصُهُوبَةٍ، وَمَدْخَلٍ، وَمَرْجِعٍ، وَمَسْعَاةٍ، وَمَحْمِدَةٍ.
text.en: The maṣdar of the triliteral is plentiful; according to Sībawayh it rises to thirty-two patterns, as qatlin “killing”, fisqin “sinfulness”, shughlin “being busy”, raḥmatin “mercy”, nishdatin “searching”, kudratin “turbidity”, daʿwā “claim”, dhikrā “remembrance”, bushrā “good news”, layyānin “putting off”, ḥirmānin “deprivation”, ghufrānin “forgiveness”, nazawānin “leaping”, ṭalabin “seeking”, khaniqin “strangling”, ṣigharin “smallness”, hudan “guidance”, ghalabatin “overcoming”, sariqatin “theft”, dhahābin “going”, ṣirāfin “being in heat”, suʾālin “asking”, zahādatin “abstinence”, dirāyatin “knowing”, dukhūlin “entering”, qabūlin “acceptance”, wajīfin “trotting”, ṣuhūbatin “reddishness”, madkhalin “entering”, marjiʿin “returning”, masʿātin “endeavour” and maḥmidatin “praise”.

text.original: وَيَجِيءُ عَلَى اسْمَيِ الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ، نَحْوُ: قُمْتُ قَائِمًا، وَنَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: ﴿بِأَيِّكُمُ الْمَفْتُونُ﴾، وَيَجِيءُ لِلْمُبَالَغَةِ، نَحْوُ: التَّهْدَارِ وَالتَّلْعَابِ وَالْحِثِّيثَى وَالدِّلِّيلَى. وَمَصْدَرُ غَيْرِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ يَجِيءُ عَلَى سَنَنٍ وَاحِدٍ، إِلَّا فِي كَلَّمَ يَجِيءُ كِلَّامًا، وَفِي قَاتَلَ قِتَّالًا وَقِيتَالًا، وَفِي تَحَمَّلَ تِحِمَّالًا، وَفِي زَلْزَلَ زِلْزَالًا.
text.en: It also comes on [the patterns of] the active and the passive participle, as qumtu qāʾiman “I stood, a standing”, and as His saying, Most High: biʾayyikumu al-maftūnu “which of you is the afflicted [one]” [68:6]; and it comes for intensiveness, as al-tahdāri “much prattling”, al-talʿābi “much playing”, al-ḥiththīthā “much urging” and al-dillīlā “much guiding”. The maṣdar of the non-triliteral comes on one course, except that from kallama “he spoke to” comes killāman, from qātala “he fought” qittālan and qītālan, from taḥammala “he bore” tiḥimmālan, and from zalzala “he shook” zilzālan.

lessons.title: The six bābs of the triliteral, and the three pillars
body: “The verbs that are derived from the maṣdar are thirty-five bābs”, and six of them belong to the bare triliteral. A bāb here is a pairing of vowels on the ʿayn in the past and the future: ḍaraba yaḍribu (a–i), qatala yaqtulu (a–u), ʿalima yaʿlamu (i–a), fataḥa yaftaḥu (a–a), karuma yakrumu (u–u) and ḥasiba yaḥsibu (i–i). The conjugation tool names the second bāb after naṣara yanṣuru; qatala yaqtulu is the same class.

“The first three are called the pillars of the bābs” (daʿāʾim al-abwāb), for two reasons: their vowels differ in the past and the future, and they are many. Fataḥa yaftaḥu is no pillar: its vowels do not differ, and it “does not come without a letter of the throat”: a hamza, hāʾ, ʿayn, ḥāʾ, ghayn or khāʾ as its ʿayn or lām, as the ḥāʾ of fataḥa.

What of verbs with a–a and no throat letter? Rakana yarkanu, “to lean”, and abā yaʾbā, “to refuse”, are “from mixed dialects and from the irregular”: as the term is usually explained, the past of one dialect has been joined to the future of another. Baqā yabqā, fanā yafnā and qalā yaqlā are the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ, “who fled from the kasra to the fatḥa”: they say baqā where others say baqiya, so these are really faʿila yafʿalu.

Karuma yakrumu is no pillar either, “because it comes only from natures and qualities”: being noble, being beautiful, never an act done to someone. Ḥasiba yaḥsibu is no pillar “because it is rare”. A seventh pairing, faʿila yafʿulu, is only an irregularity, as faḍila yafḍulu, “to be left over”.

The pillars matter because a learner who meets a new verb usually meets one of them. Hearing the past alone, you cannot tell the bāb: ḍaraba and qatala both have fatḥa. The future decides, which is why the madrasa always recites the two together: ḍaraba yaḍribu, qatala yaqtulu.

terms.en: a class of conjugation: the vowel of the ʿayn in past and future
the pillars of the bābs: ḍaraba, qatala, ʿalima
the letters of the throat: hamza, hāʾ, ʿayn, ḥāʾ, ghayn, khāʾ
mixed dialects: a past and a future from different dialects
the irregular: what breaks the rule

examples.en: rakana yarkanu, abā yaʾbā: a–a without a throat letter, from mixed dialects

examples.arabic: بَقَى يَبْقَى، وَفَنَى يَفْنَى، وَقَلَى يَقْلَى
examples.en: baqā yabqā, fanā yafnā, qalā yaqlā: the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ
faḍila yafḍulu: faʿila yafʿulu, irregular

examples.arabic: ضَرَبَ يَضْرِبُ اِضْرِبْ — قَتَلَ يَقْتُلُ اُقْتُلْ
examples.en: the past, future and command of two pillars (conjugation tool)

tasks.prompt: Give two reasons why fataḥa yaftaḥu is not one of the pillars.
tasks.answer: Its vowels do not differ between past and future (a–a), and it does not come without a letter of the throat as its ʿayn or lām.

tasks.prompt: Why does baqā yabqā not break the rule that a–a needs a throat letter?
tasks.answer: It is the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ, who turn the kasra into a fatḥa: in other dialects it is baqiya yabqā, faʿila yafʿalu, which needs no throat letter.

tasks.prompt: Give the past, future and command of ʿalima and qatala from the conjugation tool.
tasks.answer: ʿAlima yaʿlamu iʿlam (from the tool: عَلِمَ يَعْلَمُ اِعْلَمْ); qatala yaqtulu uqtul (قَتَلَ يَقْتُلُ اُقْتُلْ).

tasks.prompt: Why is karuma yakrumu not a pillar?
tasks.answer: It comes only for natures and qualities (being noble, being handsome), never for acts, so it is a narrow class and not one of the main ones.

quiz.prompt: How many bābs belong to the bare triliteral?
quiz.explanation: Ḍaraba, qatala, ʿalima, fataḥa, karuma and ḥasiba.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT one of the three pillars?
quiz.explanation: Its vowels do not differ, and it needs a throat letter.

quiz.prompt: Why are the pillars called pillars?
options: Their vowels differ in past and future, and they are many
quiz.explanation: Both reasons are given in the passage.

quiz.prompt: Baqā yabqā is explained as…
options: the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ, fleeing from kasra to fatḥa
quiz.explanation: Others say baqiya; Ṭayyiʾ turn the kasra into fatḥa.

quiz.prompt: Karuma yakrumu comes only for…
quiz.explanation: Being noble, being handsome: states, not acts done to others.

quiz.prompt: Ḥasiba yaḥsibu is not a pillar because it is…
quiz.explanation: “Because it is rare.”

quiz.prompt: Rakana yarkanu is…
options: from mixed dialects and the irregular
quiz.explanation: A–a without a throat letter: the book calls it mixed dialects and irregular.

text.original: وَالْأَفْعَالُ الَّتِي تُشْتَقُّ مِنَ الْمَصْدَرِ خَمْسَةٌ وَثَلَاثُونَ بَابًا: سِتَّةٌ لِلثُّلَاثِيِّ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ يَضْرِبُ، وَقَتَلَ يَقْتُلُ، وَعَلِمَ يَعْلَمُ، وَفَتَحَ يَفْتَحُ، وَكَرُمَ يَكْرُمُ، وَحَسِبَ يَحْسِبُ. وَتُسَمَّى الثَّلَاثَةُ الْأُوَلُ دَعَائِمَ الْأَبْوَابِ؛ لِاخْتِلَافِ حَرَكَاتِهِنَّ فِي الْمَاضِي وَالْمُسْتَقْبَلِ، وَكَثْرَتِهِنَّ. وَفَتَحَ يَفْتَحُ لَا يَدْخُلُ فِي الدَّعَائِمِ؛ لِانْعِدَامِ اخْتِلَافِ الْحَرَكَاتِ، وَانْعِدَامِ مَجِيئِهِ بِغَيْرِ حَرْفِ الْحَلْقِ.
text.en: The verbs that are derived from the maṣdar are thirty-five patterns. Six are for the triliteral, as ḍaraba yaḍribu “to hit”, qatala yaqtulu “to kill”, ʿalima yaʿlamu “to know”, fataḥa yaftaḥu “to open”, karuma yakrumu “to be noble” and ḥasiba yaḥsibu “to reckon”. The first three are called the pillars of the patterns (daʿāʾim al-abwāb), because their vowels differ in the past and the future, and because they are many. Fataḥa yaftaḥu does not enter among the pillars, because the difference of vowels is lacking, and because it does not come without a letter of the throat.

text.original: وَأَمَّا رَكَنَ يَرْكَنُ، وَأَبَى يَأْبَى، فَمِنَ اللُّغَاتِ الْمُتَدَاخِلَةِ وَالشَّوَاذِّ. وَأَمَّا بَقَى يَبْقَى، وَفَنَى يَفْنَى، وَقَلَى يَقْلَى، فَلُغَاتُ بَنِي طَيِّئٍ، وَقَدْ فَرُّوا مِنَ الْكَسْرَةِ إِلَى الْفَتْحَةِ. وَكَرُمَ يَكْرُمُ لَا يَدْخُلُ فِي الدَّعَائِمِ أَيْضًا؛ لِأَنَّهُ لَا يَجِيءُ إِلَّا مِنَ الطَّبَائِعِ وَالنُّعُوتِ، وَحَسِبَ يَحْسِبُ لَا يَدْخُلُ فِي الدَّعَائِمِ لِقِلَّتِهِ. وَقَدْ جَاءَ فَعِلَ يَفْعُلُ عَلَى لُغَةِ مَنْ قَالَ: كُدْتَ تَكَادُ، وَهِيَ شَاذَّةٌ، كَفَضِلَ يَفْضُلُ، وَدِمْتَ تَدُومُ.
text.en: As for rakana yarkanu “to lean” and abā yaʾbā “to refuse”, they are from mixed dialects and from the irregular. As for baqā yabqā “to remain”, fanā yafnā “to perish” and qalā yaqlā “to hate”, they are the dialect of the Banū Ṭayyiʾ, who fled from the kasra to the fatḥa. Karuma yakrumu does not enter among the pillars either, because it comes only from natures and qualities; and ḥasiba yaḥsibu does not enter among the pillars because it is rare. Faʿila yafʿulu has come in the dialect of those who say kudta takādu “you were about to, you are about to”, and it is irregular, as faḍila yafḍulu “to be left over” and dimta tadūmu “you lasted, you last”.

lessons.title: The thirty-five bābs: augmented, four-letter and attached verbs
body: The thirty-five bābs add up as the print counts them: six for the bare triliteral (lesson 5), twelve for its branches, one for the bare quadriliteral, three for its branches, and thirteen attached forms. The twelve “branches of the triliteral” (munshaʿibat al-thulāthī) are the augmented patterns: akrama, qaṭṭaʿa, qātala, tafaḍḍala, taḍāraba, inṣarafa, iḥtaqara, istakhraja, ikhshawshana, ijlawwadha, iḥmārra and iḥmarra.

The last two hide their pattern. Their origins are iḥmārara and iḥmarara; the two rāʾs “were assimilated because they are of one kind”. The proof is irʿawā, “he desisted”: a defective verb of the same pattern ifʿalla, whose last two letters, being of different kinds, are not assimilated. Irʿawā shows on its face the shape iḥmarra hides.

The quadriliteral has one bare bāb, daḥraja, “he rolled”, and three branches: iḥranjama, iqshaʿarra and tadaḥraja. Then come the attached forms (mulḥaq): triliteral roots given one added letter so that they take the shape of a quadriliteral and are conjugated like it. Six are attached to daḥraja (shamlala, ḥawqala, bayṭara, jahwara, qalnasa, qalsā), five to tadaḥraja (tajalbaba, tajawraba, tashayṭana, tarahwaka, tamaskana) and two to iḥranjama (iqʿansasa, islanqā).

“The proof of attachment is that the two maṣdars are one”: ḥawqala makes ḥawqala(tan) as daḥraja makes daḥraja(tan), so ḥawqala is attached. By the same test akrama, though it has four letters, is not attached to daḥraja: its maṣdar is ikrām, not a faʿlala. It is an augmented triliteral with a meaning of its own.

The conjugation tool gives the twelve branches where the root is sound: akrama yukrimu ikrām, istakhraja yastakhriju istikhrāj. The quadriliteral and the attached forms it does not give; for them the madrasa recites daḥraja, yudaḥriju, daḥrajatan, as the Maqṣūd does.

terms.en: the branches of the triliteral: its augmented patterns
the quadriliteral: a verb of four root letters, daḥraja
the attached: a triliteral given a letter to take a quadriliteral shape
assimilation because the two letters are of one kind
the proof of attachment: the same maṣdar pattern

examples.en: akrama, qaṭṭaʿa, qātala: the first three branches of the triliteral
iḥmārara, iḥmarara: the origins of iḥmārra and iḥmarra
shamlala, ḥawqala, bayṭara: attached to daḥraja

examples.arabic: أَكْرَمَ يُكْرِمُ إِكْرَامٌ — اِسْتَخْرَجَ يَسْتَخْرِجُ اِسْتِخْرَاجٌ
examples.en: two branches with past, future and maṣdar (conjugation tool)

diagram.caption: How the thirty-five bābs add up (Marāḥ, pp. 8–10)

tasks.prompt: Add up the thirty-five bābs as the book counts them.
tasks.answer: Six for the bare triliteral, twelve for its branches, one for the bare quadriliteral, three for its branches, six attached to daḥraja, five attached to tadaḥraja and two attached to iḥranjama: 6 + 12 + 1 + 3 + 6 + 5 + 2 = 35.

tasks.prompt: What is the origin of iḥmarra, and what proves it?
tasks.answer: Iḥmarara: the two rāʾs, being of one kind, were assimilated. The proof is irʿawā, a defective verb of the same pattern, whose last letters are not of one kind and so stay apart, showing the full shape of the pattern.

tasks.prompt: Is ḥawqala attached to daḥraja? Is akrama? Use the book's test.
tasks.answer: The test is that the two maṣdars be one. Ḥawqala has a maṣdar of the pattern of daḥraja, so it is attached. Akrama's maṣdar is ikrām, not of that pattern, so it is not attached: it is an augmented triliteral.

quiz.prompt: How many branches of the triliteral does the book count?
quiz.explanation: From akrama to iḥmarra.

quiz.prompt: The origin of iḥmarra is…
quiz.explanation: The two rāʾs of iḥmarara were assimilated.

quiz.prompt: What does irʿawā prove?
options: the unassimilated shape of the pattern ifʿalla
quiz.explanation: Its last letters are not of one kind, so they stay apart.

quiz.prompt: The proof of attachment (ilḥāq) is…
options: that the verb has four letters
that the two maṣdars are one
quiz.explanation: “The proof of attachment is that the two maṣdars are one.”

quiz.prompt: Ḥawqala is attached to…
quiz.explanation: It is among the six attached to daḥraja.

quiz.prompt: Which is a branch of the quadriliteral?
quiz.explanation: Iḥranjama, iqshaʿarra and tadaḥraja are the three.

quiz.prompt: Tajalbaba, “she put on a jilbāb”, is attached to…
quiz.explanation: It is among the five attached to tadaḥraja.

text.original: وَاثْنَا عَشَرَ لِمُنْشَعِبَةِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ، نَحْوُ: أَكْرَمَ، وَقَطَّعَ، وَقَاتَلَ، وَتَفَضَّلَ، وَتَضَارَبَ، وَانْصَرَفَ، وَاحْتَقَرَ، وَاسْتَخْرَجَ، وَاخْشَوْشَنَ، وَاجْلَوَّذَ، وَاحْمَارَّ، وَاحْمَرَّ، أَصْلُهُمَا: احْمَارَرَ وَاحْمَرَرَ، فَأُدْغِمَا لِلْجِنْسِيَّةِ، وَتَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ ارْعَوَى، وَهُوَ نَاقِصٌ مِنْ بَابِ افْعَلَّ، وَلَا يُدْغَمُ لِانْعِدَامِ الْجِنْسِيَّةِ.
text.en: Twelve are for the branches of the triliteral (munshaʿibat al-thulāthī), as akrama “he honoured”, qaṭṭaʿa “he cut to pieces”, qātala “he fought”, tafaḍḍala “he did a favour”, taḍāraba “they hit one another”, inṣarafa “he went away”, iḥtaqara “he despised”, istakhraja “he drew out”, ikhshawshana “it became very rough”, ijlawwadha “he went on quickly”, and iḥmārra and iḥmarra “it became red”, whose origins are iḥmārara and iḥmarara; they were assimilated because [the two letters] are of one kind. This is shown by irʿawā “he desisted”, which is defective, of the pattern ifʿalla, and is not assimilated because [the two letters] are not of one kind.

text.original: وَوَاحِدٌ لِلرُّبَاعِيِّ، نَحْوُ: دَحْرَجَ، وَثَلَاثَةٌ لِمُنْشَعِبَةِ الرُّبَاعِيِّ، نَحْوُ: احْرَنْجَمَ، وَاقْشَعَرَّ، وَتَدَحْرَجَ، وَسِتَّةٌ لِلْمُلْحَقِ بِدَحْرَجَ، نَحْوُ: شَمْلَلَ، وَحَوْقَلَ، وَبَيْطَرَ، وَجَهْوَرَ، وَقَلْنَسَ، وَقَلْسَى، وَخَمْسَةٌ لِلْمُلْحَقِ بِتَدَحْرَجَ، نَحْوُ: تَجَلْبَبَ، وَتَجَوْرَبَ، وَتَشَيْطَنَ، وَتَرَهْوَكَ، وَتَمَسْكَنَ، وَاثْنَانِ لِلْمُلْحَقِ بِاحْرَنْجَمَ، نَحْوُ: اقْعَنْسَسَ، وَاسْلَنْقَى. وَمِصْدَاقُ الْإِلْحَاقِ اتِّحَادُ الْمَصْدَرَيْنِ.
text.en: One is for the quadriliteral, as daḥraja “he rolled”; three for the branches of the quadriliteral, as iḥranjama “they crowded together”, iqshaʿarra “it shuddered” and tadaḥraja “it rolled”; six for what is attached (mulḥaq) to daḥraja, as shamlala “he hurried”, ḥawqala “he grew weak”, bayṭara “he treated animals”, jahwara “he spoke aloud”, qalnasa and qalsā “he put a cap on [him]”; five for what is attached to tadaḥraja, as tajalbaba “she put on a jilbāb”, tajawraba “he put on socks”, tashayṭana “he became a devil”, tarahwaka “he swaggered” and tamaskana “he became humble”; and two for what is attached to iḥranjama, as iqʿansasa “he drew back” and islanqā “he lay on his back”. The proof of attachment is that the two maṣdars are one [in pattern].

lessons.title: Why the past is built on fatḥa
body: The past “comes in fourteen forms, as ḍaraba to ḍarabnā”, and the book asks three questions about its ending. Why is it built (mabnī), its last vowel never changing? Why on a vowel and not on a sukūn? And why on the fatḥa? The answers turn on one idea: how far a verb resembles a noun, above all the active participle.

It is mabnī “because what requires iʿrāb is missing”: the active participle did not take its power of governing from the past, as it did from the future, so the past was not given iʿrāb in return. Or, put the other way, the muḍāriʿ is given iʿrāb because it resembles the participle much, and the past resembles it little. Yet it resembles the noun a little, in that it can describe an indefinite noun: marartu bi-rajulin ḍaraba wa-ḍāribin, “I passed by a man who hit, and by one hitting”. That little resemblance earns it a vowel rather than a sukūn.

Why fatḥa? “Because it is the brother of the sukūn: the fatḥa is a part of the alif, and the alif is the brother of the sukūn.” Of the vowels, fatḥa is the lightest and the nearest to having no vowel at all, so it suits a verb that stands only one step away from the sukūn.

“The command was made mabnī on the sukūn because it does not resemble it” at all. So there are three degrees: the muḍāriʿ, much like the noun, takes iʿrāb; the past, a little like it, is built on fatḥa; the command, not like it, is built on sukūn.

Then the endings of the past. An alif, a wāw and a nūn were added to show humā, hum and hunna: ḍarabā, ḍarabū, ḍarabna. The bāʾ of ḍarabū takes a ḍamma for the sake of the wāw. Not so in ramaw: the letter that stood before the wāw was the yāʾ of ramayū, which has dropped, so the mīm keeps its fatḥa. In raḍū, from raḍiyū, the ḍād takes a ḍamma all the same, “so that going from a kasra to a ḍamma is not required”.

terms.en: built: a word whose ending does not change
inflected: a word whose ending changes with its governor
resemblance, here of a verb to the noun
the brother of the sukūn: the fatḥa, the lightest vowel

examples.en: marartu bi-rajulin ḍaraba wa-ḍāribin: the past describing an indefinite, like the participle
ḍarabū: the bāʾ takes ḍamma before the wāw
ramaw: the mīm keeps its fatḥa, for the yāʾ stood between
raḍū: ḍamma after all, to avoid going from kasra to ḍamma

tasks.prompt: Why is the past built on a vowel and not on a sukūn?
tasks.answer: Because it resembles the noun a little: like the active participle it can describe an indefinite noun (marartu bi-rajulin ḍaraba wa-ḍāribin). That little resemblance gives it a vowel, though not iʿrāb.

tasks.prompt: Why the fatḥa, of all the vowels?
tasks.answer: Because the fatḥa is “the brother of the sukūn”: it is a part of the alif, and the alif is the brother of the sukūn. It is the lightest vowel, nearest to having none.

tasks.prompt: Explain the vowel before the wāw in ḍarabū, ramaw and raḍū.
tasks.answer: Ḍarabū: the bāʾ stands before the wāw and takes a ḍamma for it. Ramaw: the mīm was not the letter before the wāw (the yāʾ of ramayū was, and it dropped), so it keeps its fatḥa. Raḍū: the ḍād was not before the wāw either, but it takes a ḍamma so that the word does not go from a kasra to a ḍamma.

tasks.prompt: Arrange the muḍāriʿ, the past and the command by how much they resemble the noun, and give the ending each has.
tasks.answer: The muḍāriʿ resembles it much and is muʿrab; the past resembles it a little and is built on the fatḥa; the command does not resemble it and is built on the sukūn.

quiz.prompt: How many forms does the past come in?
quiz.explanation: Ḍaraba to ḍarabnā: fourteen forms.

quiz.prompt: The past is mabnī on…
quiz.explanation: On a vowel, and on the fatḥa, the brother of the sukūn.

quiz.prompt: Why does the past have a vowel at all?
options: It resembles the noun a little, describing an indefinite
quiz.explanation: Marartu bi-rajulin ḍaraba wa-ḍāribin.

quiz.prompt: The command is mabnī on the sukūn because…
options: it does not resemble the noun
quiz.explanation: No resemblance, so no vowel.

quiz.prompt: Which form is muʿrab, by the book?
quiz.explanation: It resembles the active participle much.

quiz.prompt: In ramaw, why does the mīm keep its fatḥa?
options: The yāʾ, now dropped, stood before the wāw
quiz.explanation: The origin is ramayū.

quiz.prompt: The added alif, wāw and nūn of the past point to…
quiz.explanation: Ḍarabā, ḍarabū, ḍarabna.

text.original: وَهُوَ يَجِيءُ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةَ عَشَرَ وَجْهًا، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ إِلَى ضَرَبْنَا. وَإِنَّمَا بُنِيَ الْمَاضِي لِفَوَاتِ مُوجِبِ الْإِعْرَابِ، وَعَلَى الْحَرَكَةِ لِمُشَابَهَتِهِ بِالِاسْمِ فِي وُقُوعِهِ صِفَةً لِلنَّكِرَةِ، نَحْوُ: مَرَرْتُ بِرَجُلٍ ضَرَبَ وَضَارِبٍ، وَعَلَى الْفَتْحِ لِأَنَّهُ أَخُو السُّكُونِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْفَتْحَةَ جُزْءُ الْأَلِفِ، وَالْأَلِفُ أَخُو السُّكُونِ.
text.en: It comes in fourteen forms, as ḍaraba “he hit” to ḍarabnā “we hit”. The past was made mabnī only because what requires iʿrāb is missing; [it was made mabnī] on a vowel because it resembles the noun in coming as an adjective of an indefinite, as marartu bi-rajulin ḍaraba wa-ḍāribin “I passed by a man who hit, and [by one] hitting”; and on the fatḥa because it is the brother of the sukūn: for the fatḥa is a part of the alif, and the alif is the brother of the sukūn.

text.original: وَلَمْ يُعْرَبْ؛ لِأَنَّ اسْمَ الْفَاعِلِ لَمْ يَأْخُذْ مِنْهُ الْعَمَلَ، بِخِلَافِ الْمُسْتَقْبَلِ؛ لِأَنَّ اسْمَ الْفَاعِلِ أَخَذَ مِنْهُ الْعَمَلَ، فَأُعْطِيَ الْإِعْرَابُ لَهُ عِوَضًا، أَوْ لِكَثْرَةِ مُشَابَهَتِهِ لَهُ، يَعْنِي: يُعْرَبُ الْمُضَارِعُ لِكَثْرَةِ مُشَابَهَتِهِ بِاسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ، وَبُنِيَ الْمَاضِي عَلَى الْحَرَكَةِ لِقِلَّةِ مُشَابَهَتِهِ لَهُ.
text.en: It was not given iʿrāb because the active participle did not take the governing from it, unlike the future: the active participle took the governing from it, so iʿrāb was given to it in compensation; or because it resembles it much. That is, the muḍāriʿ is given iʿrāb because it resembles the active participle much, and the past was made mabnī on a vowel because it resembles it little.

text.original: وَبُنِيَ الْأَمْرُ عَلَى السُّكُونِ لِعَدَمِ مُشَابَهَتِهِ لَهُ. وَزِيدَتِ الْأَلِفُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالنُّونُ فِي آخِرِهِ حَتَّى يَدْلُلْنَ عَلَى: هُمَا وَهُمْ وَهُنَّ. وَضُمَّ الْبَاءُ فِي ضَرَبُوا لِأَجْلِ الْوَاوِ، بِخِلَافِ رَمَوْا؛ لِأَنَّ الْمِيمَ لَيْسَتْ بِمَا قَبْلَهَا، وَضُمَّ فِي رَضُوا وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنِ الضَّادُ بِمَا قَبْلَهَا حَتَّى لَا يَلْزَمَ الْخُرُوجُ مِنَ الْكَسْرَةِ إِلَى الضَّمَّةِ.
text.en: The command was made mabnī on the sukūn because it does not resemble it. The alif, the wāw and the nūn were added at its end so that they indicate humā “they two”, hum “they (m.)” and hunna “they (f.)”. The bāʾ in ḍarabū “they hit” was given a ḍamma for the sake of the wāw, unlike ramaw “they threw”, because the mīm was not what stood before it; and in raḍū “they were pleased” it was given a ḍamma, though the ḍād was not what stood before it, so that going from a kasra to a ḍamma is not required.

lessons.title: The tāʾ of the feminine, and the sukūn before the pronoun
lessons.arabic: تَاءُ التَّأْنِيثِ وَسُكُونُ مَا قَبْلَ الضَّمِيرِ
lessons.transliteration: tāʾ al-taʾnīth wa-sukūn mā qabl al-ḍamīr
body: Four passages walk through the fourteen forms. First, spelling: an alif is written after the wāw of ḍarabū to mark where the word ends, so that the plural wāw is not taken for the wāw “and” in a phrase like ḥaḍarū wa-takallama Zaydun; or, as others say, to tell it from the wāw that belongs to the root, as in lan yadʿuwa, which is written without it.

The tāʾ of ḍarabat marks the feminine “because the tāʾ is from the second point of articulation, and the feminine too is second in creation”: Eve was made after Adam. This tāʾ “is not a pronoun”; lesson 14 shows why. Then a rule of rhythm: in ḍarabna and ḍarabta the bāʾ is made quiescent “so that four successive vowels do not come together in what is like a single word”. The doer's pronoun is so bound to the verb that ḍa-ra-ba-ta would be four vowels in one word.

From this the book draws a rule of syntax: you cannot join a noun to that pronoun without an emphasis; not ḍarabtu wa-Zaydun but ḍarabtu anā wa-Zaydun, “I and Zayd hit”. Three cases do not break the rule. In ḍarabatā the tāʾ “counts as unvowelled”: its fatḥa is only lent by the alif, which is why ramatā drops the alif of ramā (ramātā is “a poor dialect”). In ḍarabaka the pronoun is an object, not part of the verb. And hudabid and ʿulabiṭ are shortened from hudābid and ʿulābiṭ, as mikhyaṭ from mikhyāṭ.

The tāʾ is dropped in ḍarabna, “so that two signs of the feminine do not come together”. In muslimāt the tāʾ of muslima drops before -āt because the two are of one kind; in ḥublayāt the alif of ḥublā stays, for alif and tāʾ are not of one kind. The tāʾ and nūn of ḍarabna are not of one kind either, but the tāʾ goes “because of the heaviness of the verb”.

Last, the shared forms: the dual of “you” is ḍarabtumā for men and women alike, and the speaker has ḍarabtu and ḍarabnā for both, because the dual is little used, pronouns are made for brevity, and the speaker, seen or heard, is never in doubt.

terms.en: the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine: ḍarabat
a run of vowels, which the language avoids beyond three
like one word: the verb with its doer's pronoun
the two signs of the feminine, which do not meet

examples.en: ḍarabtu anā wa-Zaydun: joining onto the pronoun after an emphasis
ramatā, and the poor dialect's ramātā
hudābid and ʿulābiṭ: the origins of hudabid and ʿulabiṭ

tasks.prompt: Why is the bāʾ quiescent in ḍarabna and ḍarabta, but not in ḍarabaka?
tasks.answer: The pronoun of the doer is like a part of the verb, so ḍa-ra-ba-na would be four vowels in a row in one word; the bāʾ is made quiescent to avoid it. In ḍarabaka the pronoun is an object (manṣūb), not like a part of the word, so the four vowels are allowed.

tasks.prompt: Why does ramatā have no alif after the mīm?
tasks.answer: The tāʾ counts as unvowelled, its fatḥa being lent by the dual alif; the alif of ramā meets it as if before a quiescent letter and drops. Only a poor dialect says ramātā.

tasks.prompt: Why can one not say ḍarabtu wa-Zaydun?
tasks.answer: The pronoun -tu is like a part of the verb, so a noun cannot be joined to it by “and” directly; it needs the emphasis first: ḍarabtu anā wa-Zaydun.

tasks.prompt: Which persons share one form in the past, and why?
tasks.answer: The dual of “you” (ḍarabtumā, men and women) and the speaker (ḍarabtu, ḍarabnā, men and women). The dual is little used, pronouns are made short, and there is no doubt about a speaker, who is seen or heard.

quiz.prompt: Why is an alif written after the wāw of ḍarabū?
options: To mark the plural wāw off from the wāw “and”
quiz.explanation: As in ḥaḍarū wa-takallama Zaydun; others say: to tell it from the wāw of lan yadʿuwa.

quiz.prompt: The tāʾ of ḍarabat is…
options: a sign of the feminine, not a pronoun
quiz.explanation: The book says so here and proves it on p. 25.

quiz.prompt: Why is the bāʾ of ḍarabta quiescent?
options: To avoid four vowels in what is like one word
quiz.explanation: The doer's pronoun counts as part of the word.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct Arabic, by the book?
quiz.explanation: Joining onto the attached pronoun needs the emphasis anā.

quiz.prompt: Why does the tāʾ drop in ḍarabna?
options: So that two signs of the feminine do not meet
So that four vowels do not meet
Because the nūn is a root letter
quiz.explanation: The verb is heavy, so the tāʾ goes, though it and the nūn are not of one kind.

quiz.prompt: Ramātā is…
quiz.explanation: The standard form is ramatā, without the alif.

quiz.prompt: Ḍarabtumā is used for…
options: two men and two women addressed
quiz.explanation: The duals of the man and the woman addressed were made the same.

text.original: وَكُتِبَ الْأَلِفُ فِي ضَرَبُوا لِلْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ وَاوِ الْجَمْعِ وَوَاوِ الْعَطْفِ فِي مِثْلِ: حَضَرَ وَتَكَلَّمَ زَيْدٌ، وَقِيلَ: لِلْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ وَاوِ الْجَمْعِ وَوَاوِ الْوَاحِدِ فِي مِثْلِ: لَنْ يَدْعُوَ.
text.en: The alif was written in ḍarabū to distinguish the wāw of the plural from the wāw of joining, in the like of ḥaḍara wa-takallama Zaydun “Zayd came and spoke”; and it is said: to distinguish the wāw of the plural from the wāw of the singular, in the like of lan yadʿuwa “he will not call”.

text.original: وَجُعِلَتِ التَّاءُ عَلَامَةً لِلْمُؤَنَّثِ فِي ضَرَبَتْ؛ لِأَنَّ التَّاءَ مِنَ الْمَخْرَجِ الثَّانِي، وَالْمُؤَنَّثَ أَيْضًا ثَانٍ فِي التَّخْلِيقِ، وَهَذِهِ التَّاءُ لَيْسَتْ بِضَمِيرٍ كَمَا يَجِيءُ. وَأُسْكِنَتِ الْبَاءُ فِي مِثْلِ: ضَرَبْنَ وَضَرَبْتَ حَتَّى لَا يَجْتَمِعَ أَرْبَعُ حَرَكَاتٍ مُتَوَالِيَاتٍ فِيمَا هُوَ كَالْكَلِمَةِ الْوَاحِدَةِ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ لَا يَجُوزُ الْعَطْفُ عَلَى ضَمِيرِهِ بِغَيْرِ التَّأْكِيدِ، لَا يُقَالُ: ضَرَبْتُ وَزَيْدٌ، بَلْ يُقَالُ: ضَرَبْتُ أَنَا وَزَيْدٌ.
text.en: The tāʾ was made the sign of the feminine in ḍarabat “she hit” because the tāʾ is from the second point of articulation, and the feminine too is second in creation; this tāʾ is not a pronoun, as will come. The bāʾ was made unvowelled in the like of ḍarabna “they (f.) hit” and ḍarabta “you hit” so that four successive vowels do not come together in what is like a single word; for this reason joining onto its pronoun without an emphasis is not allowed: one does not say ḍarabtu wa-Zaydun, but one says ḍarabtu anā wa-Zaydun “I and Zayd hit”.

text.original: بِخِلَافِ ضَرَبَتَا؛ لِأَنَّ التَّاءَ فِيهِ فِي حُكْمِ السَّاكِنِ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ يَسْقُطُ الْأَلِفُ فِي مِثْلِ: رَمَتَا؛ لِكَوْنِ الْحَرَكَةِ عَارِضَةً، إِلَّا فِي لُغَةٍ رَدِيئَةٍ يَقُولُ أَهْلُهَا: رَمَاتَا، وَبِخِلَافِ ضَرَبَكَ؛ لِأَنَّهُ لَيْسَ كَالْكَلِمَةِ الْوَاحِدَةِ؛ لِأَنَّ ضَمِيرَهُ مَنْصُوبٌ، وَبِخِلَافِ هُدَبِدٍ وَعُلَبِطٍ؛ لِأَنَّ أَصْلَهُمَا هُدَابِدٌ وَعُلَابِطٌ، ثُمَّ قُصِرَ الْأَلِفُ لِلتَّخْفِيفِ، كَمَا فِي مِخْيَطٍ، أَصْلُهُ مِخْيَاطٌ.
text.en: Unlike ḍarabatā “they two (f.) hit”, because the tāʾ in it counts as unvowelled; for this reason the alif falls away in the like of ramatā “they two (f.) threw”, since the vowel is accidental — except in a poor dialect whose people say ramātā. And unlike ḍarabaka “he hit you”, because it is not like a single word, since its pronoun is manṣūb. And unlike hudabidin “thick milk” and ʿulabiṭin “a large flock”, because their origins are hudābidun and ʿulābiṭun; then the alif was shortened for lightness, as in mikhyaṭin “needle”, whose origin is mikhyāṭun.

text.original: وَحُذِفَ التَّاءُ فِي ضَرَبْنَ حَتَّى لَا يَجْتَمِعَ عَلَامَتَا التَّأْنِيثِ، كَمَا فِي مُسْلِمَاتٍ، وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُونَا مِنْ جِنْسٍ وَاحِدٍ؛ لِثِقَلِ الْفِعْلِ، بِخِلَافِ حُبْلَيَاتٍ؛ لِعَدَمِ الْجِنْسِيَّةِ. وَسُوِّيَ بَيْنَ تَثْنِيَتَيِ الْمُخَاطَبِ وَالْمُخَاطَبَةِ، وَبَيْنَ الْإِخْبَارَاتِ؛ لِقِلَّةِ الِاسْتِعْمَالِ فِي التَّثْنِيَةِ، وَوَضْعِ الضَّمَائِرِ لِلْإِيجَازِ، وَعَدَمِ الِالْتِبَاسِ فِي الْإِخْبَارِ.
text.en: The tāʾ was dropped in ḍarabna so that two signs of the feminine do not come together, as in muslimātin “Muslim women”, even though they are not of one kind, because of the heaviness of the verb; unlike ḥublayātin “pregnant women”, because [the signs] are not of one kind. The duals of the man addressed and of the woman addressed were made the same, and so were the forms of the speaker (al-ikhbārāt), because the dual is little used, because pronouns are made for brevity, and because there is no confusion in the speaker's forms.

lessons.title: The forms of “you” and “I” in the past
body: Why ḍarabtumā and not ḍarabtā? Without the mīm the alif could be taken for “the alif of lengthening”, the long vowel a poet adds at the end of a line, as in fa-kayfa antā, “so how are you?”, where antā is only anta drawn out. The mīm was chosen “because beneath it antumā is implied”: each ending mirrors its separate pronoun. Its tāʾ has a ḍamma “because it is the pronoun of the doer”; the singular ḍarabta has a fatḥa only to keep it apart from ḍarabtu, a danger the dual does not have.

In ḍarabtum the mīm keeps step with the dual, and the plural's own pronoun, the wāw, has dropped: the origin is ḍarabtumū. The mīm “stands as a noun”, and no noun ends in a wāw after a ḍamma except huwa; so adluwun, the plural of dalw, “bucket”, becomes adlin. The wāw stays in ḍarabū, whose bāʾ is not like a noun, and it comes back in ḍarabtumūhu, “you hit him”, where the attached object keeps it from the end.

Ḍarabtunna has a doubled nūn, unlike ḍarabna, because its origin is ḍarabtumna: the mīm was assimilated into the nūn, the two being close; the same closeness lets ʿambar be said for ʿanbar, “ambergris”. Another view: the origin was ḍarabtuna; every nūn of the women wants a quiescent letter before it, the tāʾ could not be made quiescent or dropped, so a nūn was put in and assimilated.

Ḍarabtu has a tāʾ “because beneath it anā is implied”: a letter of anā itself would cause confusion (an alif would look like the dual, a nūn like the women's plural), so the tāʾ was taken from its sisters ḍarabta and ḍarabti. Ḍarabnā has the nūn of naḥnu, and an alif after it “so that it is not confused with ḍarabna”.

None of these reasons is needed to conjugate; the forms are learnt from the table. The madrasa reads them to train the habit the whole book teaches: every letter of a form is there for a cause, and the cause can be named.

standing as a noun: said of the mīm of -tum

tasks.prompt: Why does ḍarabtumā have a mīm?
tasks.answer: Without it, ḍarabtā could be mistaken for ḍarabta with the alif of lengthening that poets add at the end of a line (fa-kayfa antā). The mīm was chosen because antumā is implied beneath it.

tasks.prompt: Give the origin of ḍarabtum and say why its wāw dropped.
tasks.answer: Ḍarabtumū. The mīm stands as a noun, and no noun ends in a wāw after a ḍamma except huwa, so the wāw was dropped, as adluwun became adlin.

tasks.prompt: Why does the wāw come back in ḍarabtumūhu?
tasks.answer: Because the object pronoun -hu is attached after it, so the wāw is no longer at the end of the word, and only a final wāw after a ḍamma is avoided.

tasks.prompt: State both views of the origin of ḍarabtunna.
tasks.answer: First: ḍarabtumna, with the mīm assimilated into the nūn because the two are close. Second: ḍarabtuna; since every nūn of the women needs a quiescent letter before it and the tāʾ could neither be made quiescent nor dropped, a nūn was added and assimilated.

quiz.prompt: The mīm of ḍarabtumā keeps it apart from…
quiz.explanation: As in the verse ending fa-kayfa antā.

quiz.prompt: Why does the tāʾ of ḍarabtumā have a ḍamma?
options: It is a sign of the feminine
It is the pronoun of the doer
quiz.explanation: The singular ḍarabta takes fatḥa only to differ from ḍarabtu.

quiz.prompt: The origin of ḍarabtum is…
quiz.explanation: The final wāw dropped after the mīm, which stands as a noun.

quiz.prompt: Adlin, the plural of dalw, shows that…
options: no noun ends in a wāw after a ḍamma
the mīm stands as a verb
quiz.explanation: Adluwun became adlin.

quiz.prompt: The first view gives the origin of ḍarabtunna as…
quiz.explanation: The mīm was assimilated into the nūn.

quiz.prompt: Why was the tāʾ chosen for ḍarabtu?
options: It is a letter of anā
A letter of anā would confuse, and the tāʾ is in its sisters
quiz.explanation: Ḍarabta and ḍarabti have the tāʾ too.

quiz.prompt: The alif of ḍarabnā keeps it apart from…
quiz.explanation: “So that it is not confused with ḍarabna.”

text.original: وَزِيدَتِ الْمِيمُ فِي ضَرَبْتُمَا حَتَّى لَا يَلْتَبِسَ بِأَلِفِ الْإِشْبَاعِ فِي مِثْلِ قَوْلِ الشَّاعِرِ: أَخُوكَ أَخُو مُكَاشَرَةٍ وَضِحْكٍ * وَحَيَّاكَ الْإِلَهُ فَكَيْفَ أَنْتَا. وَخُصَّتِ الْمِيمُ فِي ضَرَبْتُمَا؛ لِأَنَّ تَحْتَهُ أَنْتُمَا مُضْمَرٌ، وَأُدْخِلَتِ الْمِيمُ فِي أَنْتُمَا لِقُرْبِ الْمِيمِ إِلَى التَّاءِ فِي الْمَخْرَجِ، وَقِيلَ: تَبَعًا لِهُمَا.
text.en: The mīm was added in ḍarabtumā “you two hit” so that it is not confused with the alif of lengthening (ishbāʿ), in the like of the poet's saying: akhūka akhū mukāsharatin wa-ḍiḥkin / wa-ḥayyāka al-ilāhu fa-kayfa antā “your brother is a man of grinning and laughter, and God has greeted you — so how are you?”. The mīm was chosen in ḍarabtumā because beneath it antumā “you two” is implied; and the mīm was put into antumā because the mīm is near the tāʾ in point of articulation; and it is said: following humā “they two”.

text.original: وَضُمَّتِ التَّاءُ فِي ضَرَبْتُمَا؛ لِأَنَّهَا ضَمِيرُ الْفَاعِلِ، وَفُتِحَتِ التَّاءُ فِي الْوَاحِدِ الْمُخَاطَبِ خَوْفًا مِنَ الِالْتِبَاسِ بِالْمُتَكَلِّمِ، وَلَا الْتِبَاسَ فِي التَّثْنِيَةِ، وَقِيلَ: اتِّبَاعًا لِلْمِيمِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْمِيمَ شَفَوِيَّةٌ، فَجَعَلُوا حَرَكَةَ التَّاءِ مِنْ جِنْسِهَا، وَهُوَ الضَّمُّ الشَّفَوِيُّ.
text.en: The tāʾ in ḍarabtumā was given a ḍamma because it is the pronoun of the fāʿil; the tāʾ of the singular man addressed was given a fatḥa for fear of confusion with the speaker, and there is no confusion in the dual. It is also said: following the mīm, because the mīm is a letter of the lips, so they made the vowel of the tāʾ of its kind, which is the ḍamma of the lips.

text.original: وَزِيدَتِ الْمِيمُ فِي ضَرَبْتُمْ حَتَّى يَطَّرِدَ بِالتَّثْنِيَةِ، وَضَمِيرُ الْجَمْعِ فِيهِ مَحْذُوفٌ، وَهُوَ الْوَاوُ؛ لِأَنَّ أَصْلَهُ ضَرَبْتُمُوا، فَحُذِفَتِ الْوَاوُ؛ لِأَنَّ الْمِيمَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الِاسْمِ، وَلَا يُوجَدُ فِي آخِرِ الِاسْمِ وَاوٌ وَمَا قَبْلَهَا مَضْمُومٌ إِلَّا هُوَ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ يُقَالُ فِي جَمْعِ دَلْوٍ: أَدْلٍ، أَصْلُهُ أَدْلُوٌ، بِخِلَافِ ضَرَبُوا؛ لِأَنَّ بَاءَهُ لَيْسَتْ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الِاسْمِ، وَبِخِلَافِ ضَرَبْتُمُوهُ؛ لِأَنَّ الْوَاوَ خَرَجَ مِنَ الطَّرَفِ بِسَبَبِ الضَّمِيرِ، كَمَا فِي الْعَظَايَةِ.
text.en: The mīm was added in ḍarabtum “you (pl.) hit” so that it goes on a par with the dual. The pronoun of the plural in it, which is the wāw, is dropped, because its origin is ḍarabtumū; the wāw was dropped because the mīm stands as a noun, and at the end of a noun there is no wāw with a ḍamma before it except huwa. For this reason one says, in the plural of dalwin “bucket”, adlin, whose origin is adluwun. Unlike ḍarabū, because its bāʾ does not stand as a noun; and unlike ḍarabtumūhu “you hit him”, because the wāw has left the end because of the pronoun, as in al-ʿaẓāyati “the lizard”.

text.original: وَشُدِّدَ نُونُ ضَرَبْتُنَّ دُونَ ضَرَبْنَ؛ لِأَنَّ أَصْلَهُ ضَرَبْتُمْنَ، فَأُدْغِمَ الْمِيمُ فِي النُّونِ لِقُرْبِ الْمِيمِ مِنَ النُّونِ فِي الْمَخْرَجِ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ تُبْدَلُ الْمِيمُ مِنَ النُّونِ فِي مِثْلِ: عَمْبَرٍ؛ لِأَنَّ أَصْلَهُ عَنْبَرٌ. وَقِيلَ: أَصْلُهُ ضَرَبْتُنَ، فَأُرِيدَ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَا قَبْلَ النُّونِ سَاكِنًا لِيَطَّرِدَ بِجَمِيعِ نُونَاتِ النِّسَاءِ، وَلَا يُمْكِنُ إِسْكَانُ تَاءِ الْمُخَاطَبَةِ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، وَلَا يُمْكِنُ حَذْفُهَا؛ لِأَنَّهَا عَلَامَةٌ، وَالْعَلَامَةُ لَا تُحْذَفُ، فَأُدْخِلَ النُّونُ لِقُرْبِ النُّونِ مِنَ النُّونِ، ثُمَّ أُدْغِمَ.
text.en: The nūn of ḍarabtunna “you (f. pl.) hit” was doubled, unlike ḍarabna, because its origin is ḍarabtumna; the mīm was assimilated into the nūn because the mīm is near the nūn in point of articulation. For this reason the mīm replaces the nūn in the like of ʿambarin, because its origin is ʿanbarun “ambergris”. It is also said: its origin is ḍarabtuna; it was wanted that what is before the nūn be unvowelled, to go on a par with all the nūns of women; making the tāʾ of the woman addressed unvowelled is not possible, because two unvowelled letters would meet, nor is dropping it possible, because it is a sign, and a sign is not dropped; so a nūn was put in, because the nūn is near the nūn, and then it was assimilated.

text.original: زِيدَتِ التَّاءُ فِي ضَرَبْتُ؛ لِأَنَّ تَحْتَهُ أَنَا مُضْمَرٌ، وَلَا يُمْكِنُ الزِّيَادَةُ مِنْ حُرُوفِ أَنَا لِلِالْتِبَاسِ، فَاخْتِيرَ التَّاءُ لِوُجُودِهِ فِي أَخَوَاتِهِ. زِيدَتِ النُّونُ فِي ضَرَبْنَا؛ لِأَنَّ تَحْتَهُ نَحْنُ مُضْمَرٌ، ثُمَّ زِيدَتِ الْأَلِفُ حَتَّى لَا يَلْتَبِسَ بِضَرَبْنَ، وَقِيلَ: لِأَنَّ تَحْتَهُ إِنَّا مُضْمَرٌ.
text.en: The tāʾ was added in ḍarabtu “I hit” because beneath it anā “I” is implied; adding one of the letters of anā is not possible because of confusion, so the tāʾ was chosen because it is found in its sisters. The nūn was added in ḍarabnā “we hit” because beneath it naḥnu “we” is implied; then the alif was added so that it is not confused with ḍarabna; and it is said: because beneath it innā is implied.

lessons.title: The sixty pronouns
body: “The pronouns enter the past and its sisters, and they rise to sixty kinds.” The book reaches the number by a calculation, the way the madrasa likes to see a division built up step by step. In origin there are three: marfūʿ, manṣūb and majrūr, the pronouns of the three cases. Each is either attached (muttaṣil) to a word or separate (munfaṣil): three times two makes six.

One of the six is impossible: the separate majrūr. A word in jarr always comes after the preposition or noun that puts it in jarr, joined to it; a separate one would have to stand on its own, as if before its governor, “so putting the majrūr before what puts it in jarr” would be required. Five classes remain: the marfūʿ attached and separate, the manṣūb attached and separate, and the majrūr attached.

Next, how many in one class? “In reason” eighteen: six for the absent (he, she; the two; they, men and women), six for the person addressed, six for the speaker. But the absent man and woman share one dual, and so do the man and woman addressed: five each. The speaker needs only two, I and we, “because the speaker is seen in most cases, or it is known by the voice” whether a man or a woman speaks. Five and five and two make twelve.

Twelve in each of five classes: sixty. The twelve attached marfūʿ are the endings of ḍaraba to ḍarabnā; the twelve separate marfūʿ are huwa, humā, hum, hiya, hunna, anta, antumā, antum, anti, antunna, anā and naḥnu, set before the verb: huwa ḍaraba to naḥnu ḍarabnā. The next lessons take the rest.

Do not confuse the twelve with the fourteen forms of the past (lesson 8). The verb has fourteen because the dual of the absent has two forms, ḍarabā and ḍarabatā, and the dual of “you” is counted twice; the pronoun of the dual, the alif, is one.

terms.en: the attached pronoun, joined to a word
the separate pronoun, a word of its own
the absent person: he, she, they
the speaking person: I, we

examples.en: ḍaraba to ḍarabnā: the twelve attached marfūʿ
huwa ḍaraba to naḥnu ḍarabnā: the twelve separate marfūʿ

diagram.caption: Five classes of twelve: the sixty pronouns (Marāḥ, pp. 17–19)

tasks.prompt: Show how the book reaches sixty pronouns.
tasks.answer: Three cases (marfūʿ, manṣūb, majrūr) times attached and separate gives six; the separate majrūr is impossible, leaving five classes. Each class has twelve (five for the absent, five for the addressed, two for the speaker). Five times twelve is sixty.

tasks.prompt: Why is there no separate majrūr pronoun?
tasks.answer: A word in jarr must come after, and joined to, what puts it in jarr; a separate majrūr would mean putting it before (or apart from) its governor, which is not allowed.

tasks.prompt: Why does the speaker have only two forms, and the absent five?
tasks.answer: The absent man and woman share one dual, so they have five; the speaker is seen, or known by the voice, so no form is needed for a male or female speaker: only I and we.

quiz.prompt: How many pronoun classes are there after the calculation?
quiz.explanation: Six, less the separate majrūr.

quiz.prompt: Which class does not exist?
quiz.explanation: The majrūr cannot stand apart from what puts it in jarr.

quiz.prompt: In reason, one class admits how many forms?
quiz.explanation: Six absent, six addressed, six speaking, before the reduction to twelve.

quiz.prompt: Why does the speaker need only two forms?
options: The speaker is seen or known by the voice
quiz.explanation: So there is no need to mark the speaker as male or female.

quiz.prompt: How many pronouns are there in all?
quiz.explanation: Five classes of twelve.

quiz.prompt: Huwa ḍaraba to naḥnu ḍarabnā shows…
quiz.explanation: Separate pronouns in the case of the doer.

quiz.prompt: Al-ḥikāya, in this passage, is…
quiz.explanation: Six in reason for the speaker, two in use.

text.original: وَتَدْخُلُ الْمُضْمَرَاتُ فِي الْمَاضِي وَأَخَوَاتِهِ، وَهِيَ تَرْتَقِي إِلَى سِتِّينَ نَوْعًا؛ لِأَنَّهَا فِي الْأَصْلِ ثَلَاثَةٌ: مَرْفُوعٌ وَمَنْصُوبٌ وَمَجْرُورٌ، ثُمَّ يَصِيرُ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهَا اثْنَيْنِ نَظَرًا إِلَى اتِّصَالِهِ وَانْفِصَالِهِ، فَاضْرِبِ الِاثْنَيْنِ فِي الثَّلَاثَةِ حَتَّى يَصِيرَ سِتَّةً، ثُمَّ أَخْرِجِ الْمَجْرُورَ الْمُنْفَصِلَ حَتَّى لَا يَلْزَمَ تَقْدِيمُ الْمَجْرُورِ عَلَى الْجَارِّ، فَبَقِيَ لَكَ خَمْسَةٌ: مَرْفُوعٌ مُتَّصِلٌ وَمُنْفَصِلٌ، وَمَنْصُوبٌ مُتَّصِلٌ وَمُنْفَصِلٌ، وَمَجْرُورٌ مُتَّصِلٌ.
text.en: The pronouns enter the past and its sisters, and they rise to sixty kinds, because in origin they are three: marfūʿ, manṣūb and majrūr; then each of them becomes two in view of its being attached and separate. Multiply the two by the three, so that it becomes six; then take out the separate majrūr, so that putting the majrūr before what puts it in jarr is not required. There remain for you five: marfūʿ attached and separate, manṣūb attached and separate, and majrūr attached.

text.original: ثُمَّ انْظُرْ إِلَى الْمَرْفُوعِ الْمُتَّصِلِ، وَهُوَ يَحْتَمِلُ ثَمَانِيَةَ عَشَرَ وَجْهًا فِي الْعَقْلِ: سِتَّةٌ فِي الْغَيْبَةِ، وَسِتَّةٌ فِي الْمُخَاطَبِ وَالْمُخَاطَبَةِ، وَسِتَّةٌ فِي الْحِكَايَةِ، وَاكْتُفِيَ بِخَمْسَةٍ فِي الْغَائِبِ وَالْغَائِبَةِ بِاشْتِرَاكِ التَّثْنِيَةِ لِقِلَّةِ اسْتِعْمَالِهَا، وَكَذَلِكَ فِي الْمُخَاطَبِ وَالْمُخَاطَبَةِ، وَفِي الْحِكَايَةِ بِلَفْظَيْنِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْمُتَكَلِّمَ يُرَى فِي أَكْثَرِ الْأَحْوَالِ، أَوْ يُعْلَمُ بِالصَّوْتِ أَنَّهُ مُذَكَّرٌ أَوْ مُؤَنَّثٌ، فَبَقِيَ لَكَ اثْنَا عَشَرَ نَوْعًا.
text.en: Then look at the attached marfūʿ: in reason it admits eighteen forms: six in the absent (ghayba), six in the man and the woman addressed, and six in the speaking (ḥikāya). Five were deemed enough in the absent man and the absent woman, by sharing the dual, because it is little used; and likewise in the man and the woman addressed; and in the speaking two words, because the speaker is seen in most cases, or it is known by the voice whether he is masculine or feminine. So there remain for you twelve kinds.

text.original: وَإِذَا صَارَ قِسْمٌ وَاحِدٌ مِنْ تِلْكَ الْقِسْمَةِ اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ نَوْعًا فَيَصِيرُ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهَا مِثْلَ ذَلِكَ، فَيَحْصُلُ لَكَ بِضَرْبِ الْخَمْسَةِ فِي اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ سِتُّونَ نَوْعًا: اثْنَا عَشَرَ لِلْمَرْفُوعِ الْمُتَّصِلِ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ إِلَى ضَرَبْنَا، وَاثْنَا عَشَرَ لِلْمَرْفُوعِ الْمُنْفَصِلِ، نَحْوُ: هُوَ ضَرَبَ إِلَى نَحْنُ ضَرَبْنَا.
text.en: If one division of that division becomes twelve kinds, each of them becomes the like of that; so by multiplying the five by twelve you obtain sixty kinds: twelve for the attached marfūʿ, as ḍaraba “he hit” to ḍarabnā “we hit”, and twelve for the separate marfūʿ, as huwa ḍaraba “he hit” to naḥnu ḍarabnā “we hit”.

lessons.title: Huwa and hiya: the separate pronouns explained
body: If huwa made its dual and plural the plain way, they would be huwā and huwū. Instead, the wāw “was made a mīm in the plural, because their point of articulation is one and two wāws come together”: wāw and mīm are both made with the lips. That gave humū; then the final wāw dropped, as in ḍarabtumū (lesson 9), and the result is hum. The dual humā “was treated like it”; or the mīm was put there “so that the fatḥa falls on the strong mīm” rather than on a weak wāw. Antumā has its mīm as ḍarabtumā has, and antum follows it.

Why does huwa itself keep its wāw? A word of two letters, h and w, has fewer than “the proper measure”: drop the wāw and almost nothing is left. But when it is “embraced” by another word it does drop: lahu, “to him”, is la + hu, the letters of the two together being enough. The hāʾ keeps its ḍamma, lahu, unless a kasra or a quiescent yāʾ comes before it: then it takes a kasra, ghulāmihi, fīhi, “so that going from a kasra to a ḍamma is not required”.

Hiya is treated like huwa. Its yāʾ can be made an alif, as the Arabs say yā ghulāmā for yā ghulāmī, “O my servant”, and yā bādātu for yā bādiyatu. In the dual the yāʾ becomes a mīm, humā, “so that the fatḥa does not fall on the weak yāʾ”. And hunna has a doubled nūn for the same reason as ḍarabtunna.

Two rules here reach far beyond pronouns. The language avoids going from a kasra straight to a ḍamma: it changed ḍarabū's neighbours in lesson 7 and changes the hāʾ of ghulāmihi here. And a weak letter, wāw or yāʾ, is a poor bearer of a vowel, so the language prefers to put the vowel on a strong letter. Both will come back in every chapter on the weak verbs.

terms.en: the separate pronoun: huwa, hiya, humā, hum, hunna
the proper measure: the fewest letters a word may have
embracing: a pronoun joined to another word, as lahu
going from a kasra to a ḍamma, which the language avoids

examples.en: huwā, huwū: the plain duals and plurals that the language did not use
humū: the step between huwū and hum
lahu: the wāw of huwa dropped when embraced
ghulāmihi, fīhi: the hāʾ with kasra after kasra or yāʾ
yā ghulāmī, yā ghulāmā: a yāʾ made an alif
