tasks.prompt: Why does the wāw of qawl stay, while that of miwzān changes?
tasks.answer: A quiescent weak letter takes the kind of the vowel before it, so the wāw of miwzān becomes a yāʾ after the kasra: mīzān. After a fatḥa it stays, because fatḥa and sukūn are both light: qawl.

tasks.prompt: Explain aghzaytu.
tasks.answer: Its origin is aghzawtu, with a quiescent wāw after a fatḥa, which by rule would stay. It became a yāʾ to follow its future yughzī, where the wāw after a kasra must be a yāʾ.

tasks.prompt: Give al-Khalīl's account of kaynūna.
tasks.answer: The origin is kaywanūna; the wāw and the yāʾ were merged into a doubled yāʾ, as maywit became mayyit; then the doubled yāʾ was lightened, as mayyit becomes mayt: kaynūna.

quiz.prompt: A quiescent weak letter usually becomes…
options: the letter of the vowel before it
quiz.explanation: Mīzān, yūsiru.

quiz.prompt: Why does the wāw of qawl stay?
options: Fatḥa and sukūn are both light
quiz.explanation: Some allow qāl.

quiz.prompt: The origin of mīzān is…
quiz.explanation: From w-z-n.

quiz.prompt: Aghzaytu became a yāʾ…
quiz.explanation: Its future has a yāʾ after kasra.

quiz.prompt: Al-Khalīl's origin of kaynūna is…
quiz.explanation: Merged as in mayyit, then lightened.

quiz.prompt: Mayt is…
quiz.explanation: The model for lightening kaynūna.

quiz.explanation: The other three are yāʾ verbs.

text.original: الْأَرْبَعَةُ إِذَا كَانَ مَا قَبْلَهَا مَفْتُوحًا، نَحْوُ: قَوْلٍ وَبَيْعٍ وَخَوِفٍ وَطَوُلٍ، وَلَا يُعَلُّ الْأَوَّلُ؛ لِأَنَّ حَرْفَ الْعِلَّةِ إِذَا سَكَنَتْ جُعِلَتْ مِنْ جِنْسِ حَرَكَةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا لِلِينِ عَرِيكَةِ السَّاكِنِ وَاسْتِدْعَاءِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، نَحْوُ: مِيزَانٍ، أَصْلُهُ مِوْزَانٌ، وَيُوسِرُ، أَصْلُهُ يُيْسِرُ، إِلَّا إِذَا انْفَتَحَ مَا قَبْلَهَا لِخِفَّةِ الْفَتْحَةِ وَالسُّكُونِ، وَعِنْدَ بَعْضِهِمْ يَجُوزُ الْقَلْبُ، نَحْوُ: قَالٍ.
text.en: The four when what is before it has a fatḥa, as qawlin “saying”, bayʿin “selling”, khawifin and ṭawulin. The first is not changed: because a letter of weakness, when it is unvowelled, is made of the kind of the vowel before it, since the nature of the unvowelled letter is soft and what is before it calls for it, as mīzānin “scales”, whose origin is miwzānun, and yūsiru “he becomes rich”, whose origin is yuysiru; except when what is before it has a fatḥa, because of the lightness of the fatḥa and the sukūn. With some of them the change is allowed, as qālin.

text.original: وَيُعَلُّ نَحْوُ: أَغْزَيْتُ، أَصْلُهُ أَغْزَوْتُ، وَاوٌ سَاكِنٌ، تَبَعًا لِيُغْزِي، وَيُعَلُّ نَحْوُ: كَيْنُونَةٍ مِنَ الْكَوْنِ مَعَ سُكُونِ الْوَاوِ وَانْفِتَاحِ مَا قَبْلَهَا؛ لِأَنَّ أَصْلَهُ كَيْوَنُونَةٌ عِنْدَ الْخَلِيلِ، فَأُدْغِمَتْ كَمَا فِي مَيِّتٍ، أَصْلُهُ مَيْوِتٌ، ثُمَّ خُفِّفَتْ فَصَارَتْ كَيْنُونَةً، كَمَا خُفِّفَتْ فِي مَيْتٍ.
text.en: The like of aghzaytu “I sent on a raid” is changed — its origin is aghzawtu, with an unvowelled wāw — following yughzī; and the like of kaynūnatin “being”, from al-kawni “being”, is changed, though the wāw is unvowelled and what is before it has a fatḥa, because its origin is kaywanūnatun according to al-Khalīl: it was assimilated, as in mayyitin “dead”, whose origin is maywitun, then lightened, and it became kaynūnatan, as it was lightened in maytin.

text.original: وَقِيلَ: أَصْلُهَا كُونُونَةٌ بِضَمِّ الْكَافِ، ثُمَّ فُتِحَ حَتَّى لَا يَصِيرَ الْيَاءُ وَاوًا فِي نَحْوِ: الصَّيْرُورَةِ وَالْغَيْبُوبَةِ وَالْقَيْلُولَةِ، ثُمَّ جُعِلَتِ الْوَاوُ يَاءً تَبَعًا لِلْيَائِيَّاتِ لِكَثْرَتِهَا، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ قِيلَ: لَا يَجِيءُ مِنَ الْوَاوِيَّاتِ غَيْرُ الْكَيْنُونَةِ، وَالدَّيْمُومَةِ، وَالسَّيْدُودَةِ، وَالْهَيْعُوعَةِ.
text.en: And it is said: its origin is kūnūnatun, with a ḍamma on the kāf; then [the kāf] was given a fatḥa, so that the yāʾ does not become a wāw in the like of al-ṣayrūrati “becoming”, al-ghaybūbati “absence” and al-qaylūlati “the midday rest”; then the wāw was made a yāʾ, following the verbs with yāʾ, because they are many. For that reason it is said: of the verbs with wāw nothing [of this pattern] comes but al-kaynūnati “being”, al-daymūmati “lasting”, al-saydūdati “lordship” and al-hayʿūʿati “vomiting”.

lessons.title: Ibn Jinnī's conditions: when wāw and yāʾ become alif
body: The other three cases after a fatḥa have a vowelled weak letter, as qawala, khawifa, ṭawula. Here comes the central rule of the hollow verb, which the book gives from Ibn Jinnī: the weak letter “is made unvowelled for lightness, then changed into an alif, because the fatḥa calls for it and the nature of the unvowelled letter is soft”. Qawala becomes qāla; dawar becomes dār, “house”.

But only on seven conditions: that it be in a verb, or in a noun on a verb's measure; that its vowel be not accidental; that the fatḥa before it not count as a sukūn; that the word's meaning have no sense of commotion; that two changes not meet in the word; that the change would not bring a ḍamma onto the weak letter in the future; and that the letter not be kept to show the origin.

Some nouns are changed though they are not on a verb's measure, by following: diyār, “houses”, after its singular dār; qiyām, “standing”, after its verb qāma; siyāṭ, “whips”, after the wāw of its singular sawṭ, which is quiescent, “dead” like the alif of dīnār. And each condition has its examples of words left unchanged. Ḥawaka, “weavers”, and khawana, “traitors”, leave the verb's measure by their tāʾ. Daʿawu al-qawma keeps its wāw, because the ḍamma is only lent by the next word. ʿAwira, “to be one-eyed”, and ijtawarū, “to be neighbours”, are treated as if their vowel were a sukūn, as the wāw of aʿwar, “one-eyed”, and the alif of tajāwara are quiescent.

Ḥayawān, “living being”, keeps its letters so that its many vowels show the restlessness of life; mawatān, “death”, its opposite, follows it. Ṭawā, “he folded”, changes its lām but not its wāw, so that two changes do not meet; and ṭawayā follows it. Ḥayiya is left so: if it became ḥāya, its future would need yaḥāyu, a ḍamma on the yāʾ. And qawad, “retaliation”, keeps its wāw to show the origin.

Learn the rule with its main condition, and the exceptions as a list: a vowelled wāw or yāʾ after a fatḥa becomes alif in verbs and verb-like nouns. Almost every form of qāla, bāʿa and khāfa in the next lessons starts from this step.

terms.en: turning a vowelled wāw or yāʾ after a fatḥa into alif
the grammarian whose seven conditions the book reports
an accidental vowel, lent from outside the word
commotion in the meaning, as in ḥayawān
following: diyār changed after dār

examples.arabic: قَالَ، أَصْلُهُ قَوَلَ، وَدَارٌ، أَصْلُهُ دَوَرٌ
examples.en: qāla from qawala, dār from dawar: the conditions met
diyār, qiyām, siyāṭ: changed by following
ḥayawān, mawatān: kept for the sense
ṭawā, ṭawayā: the wāw kept so that two changes do not meet

grid.caption: Ibn Jinnī's conditions, and the words that fail them (Marāḥ, pp. 87–90)

Kept unchanged because it fails
rows: a verb, or a noun on its measure

tasks.prompt: Derive qāla from qawala in Ibn Jinnī's two steps.
tasks.answer: The wāw is made quiescent for lightness (qawla); then, quiescent after a fatḥa, it is changed into an alif, since the fatḥa calls for it and a quiescent letter is soft: qāla.

tasks.prompt: Why is siyāṭ changed, though it is not on a verb's measure?
tasks.answer: By following: its singular sawṭ has a quiescent, “dead” wāw, like the alif of dīnār, so in the plural the wāw after the kasra is changed into a yāʾ. Diyār (after dār) and qiyām (after qāma) are changed by following too.

tasks.prompt: Why is the wāw of ʿawira kept?
tasks.answer: Because its vowel counts as a sukūn: the wāw of ʿawira is treated as the quiescent wāw of aʿwar, “one-eyed”, so the condition that the vowel not count as a sukūn fails.

tasks.prompt: Why is the wāw of ṭawā not changed into an alif?
tasks.answer: Its lām (yāʾ) is already changed into an alif; changing the wāw too would bring two changes into one word. Ṭawayā follows ṭawā, though it would not have two changes.

quiz.prompt: A vowelled wāw after a fatḥa in a verb becomes…
quiz.explanation: Qawala becomes qāla.

quiz.prompt: Whose conditions does the book report?
quiz.explanation: Seven conditions for the change.

quiz.prompt: Ḥawaka, “weavers”, is not changed because…
options: its tāʾ takes it out of the verb's measure
quiz.explanation: The sign of the feminine.

quiz.prompt: Daʿawu al-qawma keeps its wāw because its vowel is…
quiz.explanation: The ḍamma is lent by the meeting with the next word.

quiz.prompt: Ḥayawān keeps its letters to show…
quiz.explanation: Mawatān, its opposite, follows it.

quiz.prompt: Why is ḥayiya not changed to ḥāya?
options: The future would need a ḍamma on the yāʾ
quiz.explanation: Yaḥāyu would be required.

quiz.prompt: Diyār is changed…
quiz.explanation: Changed for following, though not on a verb's measure.

text.original: قَالَ ابْنُ جِنِّي: فِي الثَّلَاثَةِ الْأَخِيرَةِ تُسَكَّنُ حَرْفُ الْعِلَّةِ لِلْخِفَّةِ، ثُمَّ تُقْلَبُ أَلِفًا لِاسْتِدْعَاءِ الْفَتْحَةِ وَلِينِ عَرِيكَةِ السَّاكِنِ، إِذَا كُنَّ فِي فِعْلٍ، أَوْ فِي اسْمٍ عَلَى وَزْنِ فِعْلٍ، إِذَا كَانَتْ حَرَكَتُهُنَّ غَيْرَ عَارِضَةٍ، وَلَا يَكُونُ فَتْحَةُ مَا قَبْلَهَا فِي حُكْمِ السُّكُونِ، وَلَا يَكُونُ فِي مَعْنَى الْكَلِمَةِ اضْطِرَابٌ، وَلَا يَجْتَمِعُ فِيهَا إِعْلَالَانِ، وَلَا يَلْزَمُ ضَمُّ حَرْفِ الْعِلَّةِ فِي مُضَارِعِهِ، وَلَا يُتْرَكُ لِلدَّلَالَةِ عَلَى الْأَصْلِ.
text.en: Ibn Jinnī said: in the last three the letter of weakness is made unvowelled for lightness, then changed into an alif, because the fatḥa calls for it and the nature of the unvowelled letter is soft: when they are in a verb, or in a noun on the measure of a verb; when their vowel is not accidental; when the fatḥa before it does not count as a sukūn; when there is no [sense of] commotion (iḍṭirāb) in the meaning of the word; when two changes do not come together in it; when a ḍamma on the letter of weakness is not required in its muḍāriʿ; and when it is not left [unchanged] to point to the origin.

text.original: وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ يُعَلُّ قَالَ، أَصْلُهُ قَوَلَ، وَدَارٌ، أَصْلُهُ دَوَرٌ؛ لِوُجُودِ الشَّرَائِطِ الْمَذْكُورَةِ. وَيُعَلُّ مِثْلُ: دِيَارٍ تَبَعًا لِوَاحِدِهِ، وَمِثْلُ: قِيَامٍ تَبَعًا لِفِعْلِهِ.
text.en: For that reason qāla “he said” is changed, whose origin is qawala, and dārun “a house”, whose origin is dawarun, because the conditions mentioned are present. The like of diyārin “houses” is changed following its singular, and the like of qiyāmin “standing” following its verb.

text.original: وَمِثْلُ: سِيَاطٍ تَبَعًا لِوَاوِ وَاحِدِهِ، وَهِيَ مُشَابِهَةٌ بِأَلِفِ دِينَارٍ فِي كَوْنِهَا مَيِّتَةً، أَعْنِي: يُعَلُّ هَذِهِ الْأَشْيَاءُ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ أَفْعَالًا وَلَا عَلَى وَزْنِ أَفْعَالٍ لِلْمُتَابَعَةِ. وَلَا يُعَلُّ نَحْوُ: الْحَوَكَةِ، وَالْخَوَنَةِ، وَحَيَدَى، وَصَوَرَى؛ لِخُرُوجِهِنَّ عَنْ وَزْنِ الْفِعْلِ بِعَلَامَةِ التَّأْنِيثِ، وَقِيلَ: حَتَّى يَدْلُلْنَ عَلَى الْأَصْلِ.
text.en: And the like of siyāṭin “whips”, following the wāw of its singular, which resembles the alif of dīnārin “dinar” in being dead; I mean, these things are changed, though they are neither verbs nor on the measure of verbs, for the following. The like of al-ḥawakati “the weavers”, al-khawanati “the traitors”, ḥayadā “shying” and ṣawarā [the name of a place] is not changed, because they leave the measure of the verb by the sign of the feminine; and it is said: so that they point to the origin.

text.original: وَنَحْوُ: دَعَوُا الْقَوْمَ لِطُرُوِّ حَرَكَتِهِ، وَنَحْوُ: عَوِرَ وَاجْتَوَرُوا؛ لِأَنَّ حَرَكَةَ الْعَيْنِ وَالتَّاءِ فِي حُكْمِ السُّكُونِ، أَيْ: فِي حُكْمِ عَيْنِ أَعْوَرَ وَأَلِفِ تَجَاوَرَ. وَنَحْوُ: الْحَيَوَانِ حَتَّى يَدُلَّ بِحَرَكَتِهِ عَلَى اضْطِرَابِ مَعْنَاهُ، وَالْمَوَتَانُ مَحْمُولٌ عَلَيْهِ؛ لِأَنَّهُ نَقِيضُهُ.
text.en: And the like of daʿawu al-qawma “they called the people”, because its vowel is accidental; and the like of ʿawira “he was one-eyed” and ijtawarū “they were neighbours”, because the vowel of the ʿayn and of the tāʾ counts as a sukūn, that is, as the ʿayn of aʿwara and the alif of tajāwara. And the like of al-ḥayawāni “the living being”, so that by its vowels it points to the commotion of its meaning; and al-mawatānu “death” is treated like it, because it is its opposite.

text.original: وَنَحْوُ: طَوَى حَتَّى لَا يَجْتَمِعَ فِيهِ إِعْلَالَانِ، وَطَوَيَا مَحْمُولٌ عَلَيْهِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَجْتَمِعْ فِيهِ إِعْلَالَانِ، وَنَحْوُ: حَيِيَ حَتَّى لَا يَلْزَمَ ضَمُّ الْيَاءِ فِي الْمُضَارِعِ، يَعْنِي: إِذَا قُلْتَ: حَايَ، يَجِيءُ مُسْتَقْبَلُهُ يَحَايُ، وَنَحْوُ: الْقَوَدِ حَتَّى يَدُلَّ عَلَى الْأَصْلِ.
text.en: And the like of ṭawā “he folded”, so that two changes do not come together in it; and ṭawayā “they two folded” is treated like it, though two changes do not come together in it. And the like of ḥayiya “he lived”, so that a ḍamma on the yāʾ is not required in the muḍāriʿ; that is, if you said ḥāya, its future would come as yaḥāyu. And the like of al-qawadi “retaliation”, so that it points to the origin.

lessons.title: After a ḍamma, and after a kasra
body: Four cases after a ḍamma, named by muysir, buyiʿa, yaghzuwu and lan yadʿuwa. A quiescent yāʾ after a ḍamma becomes a wāw: muysir, mūsir, “rich”. A yāʾ with kasra after a ḍamma (buyiʿa, the passive of bāʿa) is first made quiescent for lightness and then a wāw, būʿa; or else the vowel before it is made of its kind, and it becomes bīʿa, “it was sold” (lesson 53 has the three dialects). A wāw with ḍamma after a ḍamma is made quiescent: yaghzuwu, yaghzū, “he raids”. A wāw with fatḥa after a ḍamma stays, “because of the lightness of the fatḥa”: lan yadʿuwa, “he will not call”; so too ʿuyaba, “great fault-finder”, and nuwama, “great sleeper”.

Four cases after a kasra, named by miwzān, dāʿiwa, raḍiyū and tarmiyīna. A quiescent wāw after a kasra becomes a yāʾ: mīzān. A wāw with fatḥa after a kasra becomes a yāʾ too, “because what is before it calls for it and the nature of the fatḥa is soft”: dāʿiwa, dāʿiya, “one who calls (f.)”.

But diwal, “turns of fortune”, keeps its wāw: nouns not derived from a verb “are not changed, because of their lightness, except when they are on the measure of the verb”, and diwal is neither. The weak letters are changed above all in verbs and in what is like them.

A yāʾ with ḍamma after a kasra, as raḍiyū, is made quiescent for lightness and then dropped, two quiescent letters meeting: raḍū, “they were pleased” (with the ḍād's ḍamma of lesson 7). A yāʾ with kasra after a kasra, as tarmiyīna, goes the same way: tarmīna, “you (a woman) throw”.

Notice how few outcomes there are: the weak letter becomes the long letter of the vowel before it (mūsir, mīzān, dāʿiya), loses its vowel (yaghzū), drops (raḍū, tarmīna), or stays under a fatḥa (lan yadʿuwa).

terms.en: making a weak letter quiescent for lightness
changing a weak letter to match the vowel before it
the lightness of the fatḥa, which keeps lan yadʿuwa unchanged
nouns not derived from a verb, which are not changed

examples.en: mūsir, from muysir: the quiescent yāʾ after ḍamma made wāw
bīʿa, from buyiʿa: “it was sold”
dāʿiya, from dāʿiwa: the wāw with fatḥa after kasra made yāʾ
diwal: not changed, a noun not on a verb's measure

tasks.prompt: Say what happens to the weak letter in yaghzuwu and in lan yadʿuwa, and why they differ.
tasks.answer: In yaghzuwu the wāw has a heavy ḍamma after a ḍamma, so it is made quiescent: yaghzū. In lan yadʿuwa its vowel is the light fatḥa, so it stays.

tasks.prompt: Derive dāʿiya and raḍū.
tasks.answer: Dāʿiwa: the wāw with fatḥa after a kasra becomes a yāʾ, the kasra calling for it and the fatḥa being soft: dāʿiya. Raḍiyū: the yāʾ with ḍamma after a kasra is made quiescent, then drops as two quiescent letters meet: raḍū.

tasks.prompt: Why is diwal not changed into diyal?
tasks.answer: Nouns not derived from a verb are light and not changed unless they are on a verb's measure; diwal is neither derived from a verb nor on its measure.

quiz.prompt: Muysir becomes…
quiz.explanation: A quiescent yāʾ after ḍamma becomes wāw.

quiz.prompt: Yaghzuwu becomes yaghzū by…
quiz.explanation: The ḍamma is heavy on the wāw.

quiz.prompt: Lan yadʿuwa is not changed because…
quiz.explanation: So too ʿuyaba and nuwama.

quiz.prompt: Dāʿiwa becomes…
quiz.explanation: A wāw with fatḥa after kasra becomes yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Diwal keeps its wāw because it is…
options: a noun neither derived from a verb nor on its measure
quiz.explanation: Such nouns are light.

quiz.prompt: Raḍiyū becomes raḍū by…
options: making the yāʾ quiescent, then dropping it
quiz.explanation: Two quiescent letters meet.

quiz.prompt: Tarmiyīna becomes…
quiz.explanation: Like raḍiyū in the change.

text.original: الْأَرْبَعَةُ إِذَا كَانَ مَا قَبْلَهَا مَضْمُومًا، نَحْوُ: مُيْسِرٍ، وَبُيِعَ، وَيَغْزُوُ، وَلَنْ يَدْعُوَ، يُجْعَلُ فِي الْأُولَى وَاوًا لِضَمَّةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا وَلِينِ عَرِيكَةِ السَّاكِنِ، فَصَارَ مُوسِرٌ، وَفِي الثَّانِيَةِ تُسَكَّنُ لِلْخِفَّةِ، ثُمَّ يُجْعَلُ وَاوًا لِضَمَّةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا وَلِينِ عَرِيكَةِ السَّاكِنِ، فَصَارَ بُوعَ، وَإِذَا جُعِلَتْ حَرَكَةُ مَا قَبْلَ حَرْفِ الْعِلَّةِ مِنْ جِنْسِهِ فَصَارَ حِينَئِذٍ بِيعَ، وَتُسَكَّنُ فِي الثَّالِثَةِ لِلْخِفَّةِ فَصَارَ يَغْزُو، وَلَا يُعَلُّ الرَّابِعَةُ لِخِفَّةِ الْفَتْحَةِ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ لَا يُعَلُّ عُيَبَةٌ وَلَا نُوَمَةٌ.
text.en: The four when what is before them has a ḍamma, as muysirin, buyiʿa, yaghzuwu and lan yadʿuwa “he will not call”. In the first it is made a wāw, because of the ḍamma before it and the softness of the nature of the unvowelled letter, and it became mūsirun “rich”. In the second it is made unvowelled for lightness, then made a wāw, because of the ḍamma before it and the softness of the nature of the unvowelled letter, and it became būʿa; and when the vowel before the letter of weakness is made of its kind, it then became bīʿa “it was sold”. In the third it is made unvowelled for lightness, and it became yaghzū “he raids”. The fourth is not changed, because of the lightness of the fatḥa; for that reason ʿuyabatun “a great fault-finder” and nuwamatun “a great sleeper” are not changed.

text.original: الْأَرْبَعَةُ إِذَا كَانَ مَا قَبْلَهَا مَكْسُورًا، نَحْوُ: مِوْزَانٍ، وَدَاعِوَةٍ، وَرَضِيُوا، وَتَرْمِيِينَ، فَفِي الْأُولَى يُجْعَلُ يَاءً لِمَا مَرَّ، وَفِي الثَّانِيَةِ تُجْعَلُ يَاءً لِاسْتِدْعَاءِ مَا قَبْلَهَا وَلِينِ عَرِيكَةِ الْفَتْحَةِ، فَصَارَ دَاعِيَةً. وَلَا يُعَلُّ مِثْلُ: دِوَلٍ؛ لِأَنَّ الْأَسْمَاءَ لَيْسَتْ بِمُشْتَقَّةٍ مِنَ الْفِعْلِ، لَا تُعَلُّ لِخِفَّتِهَا إِلَّا إِذَا كَانَ عَلَى وَزْنِ الْفِعْلِ، وَهُوَ لَيْسَ بِمُشْتَقٍّ مِنَ الْفِعْلِ وَلَا عَلَى وَزْنِ الْفِعْلِ. وَفِي الثَّالِثَةِ تُسَكَّنُ لِلْخِفَّةِ، ثُمَّ تُحْذَفُ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، فَصَارَ رَضُوا، وَالرَّابِعَةُ مِثْلُهَا فِي الْإِعْلَالِ.
text.en: The four when what is before them has a kasra, as miwzānin, dāʿiwatin, raḍiyū and tarmiyīna. In the first it is made a yāʾ, for the reason that has passed. In the second it is made a yāʾ, because what is before it calls for it and the nature of the fatḥa is soft, and it became dāʿiyatan “one who calls (f.)”. The like of diwalin “turns [of fortune]” is not changed, because nouns that are not derived from the verb are not changed, because of their lightness, except when they are on the measure of the verb; and it is neither derived from the verb nor on the measure of the verb. In the third it is made unvowelled for lightness, then dropped because two unvowelled letters come together, and it became raḍū “they were pleased”; and the fourth is like it in the change.

lessons.title: After a quiescent letter: yaqūlu, yabīʿu, yakhāfu
body: The last three cases: a vowelled weak letter after a quiescent sound letter, as in the bases yakhwafu, yabyiʿu and yaqwulu. “Their vowels are given to what is before them, because of the weakness of the letters of weakness and the strength of the sound letter”: the vowel moves to the letter that can carry it. Yabyiʿu becomes yabīʿu, yaqwulu becomes yaqūlu.

In yakhwafu one more step follows: after the vowel moves, yakhawfu has a quiescent wāw after a fatḥa, and here it becomes an alif, “because of the fatḥa before it and the softness of the nature of the accidental unvowelled letter”: yakhāfu. Not so al-khawf, “fear”, whose wāw has always been quiescent. A sukūn that comes by change yields; an original sukūn stands.

The same move is refused in many words, each for a reason. Aʿyun, “eyes”, and adwur, “houses”, keep their letters, “so that they are not confused with the verbs”. Jadwal, “stream”, so as not to undo the attachment. Qawwama, “he set straight”, so that “a change within a change” is not required. Al-ramy, “throwing”, so that an inflected word does not end in a quiescent letter. Taqwīm, tibyān, miqwāl and mikhyāṭ, so that two quiescent letters do not meet. Mikhyaṭ, “needle”, is short for mikhyāṭ, and follows it.

Then two objections. Why is iqāma, “setting up”, changed, when changing it brings two quiescent letters together, as in its sisters? Because it follows qāma. Then why is taqwīm not changed to follow qāma too? Because qawwama, its own verb, is closer to it and blocks the pull of qāma; aqāma, being augmented, cannot help qāma pull. (The print's wording of this answer is uncertain; this is our reading.)
For practice the rule is short: in the bases yaqwulu, yabyiʿu, yakhwafu, move the vowel of the weak letter back to the quiescent letter before it, and let the weak letter follow that vowel: ū, ī, ā.

terms.en: moving the weak letter's vowel to the sound quiescent letter before it
accidental sukūn, which lets the wāw of yakhawfu become alif
a change within a change, which the language avoids
the pull of a verb on its derived forms

examples.en: yakhwafu, yabyiʿu, yaqwulu: the bases
yakhāfu, yabīʿu, yaqūlu: the forms
aʿyun, adwur: kept, so as not to look like verbs
kept, so that two quiescent letters do not meet

tasks.prompt: Derive yakhāfu from yakhwafu, and say why al-khawf is not changed the same way.
tasks.answer: The wāw's fatḥa moves back to the khāʾ (yakhawfu); the wāw, now quiescent after a fatḥa, with a sukūn that is accidental, becomes an alif: yakhāfu. In al-khawf the sukūn of the wāw is original, so it stays.

tasks.prompt: Why is aʿyun not changed to aʿīn?
tasks.answer: So that the noun does not look like a verb: moving the vowel back would give a form like the future of a verb.

tasks.prompt: Why is iqāma changed, though its change brings two quiescent letters together?
tasks.answer: Because it follows qāma, the triliteral that is original in the change.

quiz.explanation: The sound letter is strong, the weak letter weak.

quiz.explanation: After a fatḥa, it yields to an alif.

quiz.explanation: Only an accidental sukūn yields.

text.original: وَالثَّلَاثَةُ إِذَا كَانَ مَا قَبْلَهَا سَاكِنًا، نَحْوُ: يَخْوَفُ وَيَبْيِعُ وَيَقْوُلُ، يُعْطَى حَرَكَاتُهُنَّ إِلَى مَا قَبْلَهُنَّ لِضَعْفِ حُرُوفِ الْعِلَّةِ وَقُوَّةِ الْحَرْفِ الصَّحِيحِ، وَلَكِنْ يُجْعَلُ فِي يَخَوْفُ أَلِفًا لِفَتْحَةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا وَلِينِ عَرِيكَةِ السَّاكِنِ الْعَارِضِيِّ، بِخِلَافِ الْخَوْفِ، فَصَارَ يَخَافُ وَيَبِيعُ وَيَقُولُ.
text.en: The three when what is before them is unvowelled, as yakhwafu, yabyiʿu and yaqwulu: their vowels are given to what is before them, because of the weakness of the letters of weakness and the strength of the sound letter; but in yakhawfu it is made an alif, because of the fatḥa before it and the softness of the nature of the accidental unvowelled letter — unlike al-khawfi “fear” — and they became yakhāfu “he fears”, yabīʿu “he sells” and yaqūlu “he says”.

text.original: وَلَا يُعَلُّ نَحْوُ: أَعْيُنٍ وَأَدْوُرٍ حَتَّى لَا يَلْتَبِسَ بِالْأَفْعَالِ، وَنَحْوُ: جَدْوَلٍ حَتَّى لَا يَبْطُلَ الْإِلْحَاقُ، وَنَحْوُ: قَوَّمَ حَتَّى لَا يَلْزَمَ الْإِعْلَالُ فِي الْإِعْلَالِ، وَنَحْوُ: الرَّمْيِ حَتَّى لَا يَلْزَمَ السَّاكِنُ فِي آخِرِ الْمُعْرَبِ، وَنَحْوُ: تَقْوِيمٍ وَتِبْيَانٍ وَمِقْوَالٍ وَمِخْيَاطٍ حَتَّى لَا يَجْتَمِعَ السَّاكِنَانِ بِتَقْدِيرِ الْإِعْلَالِ، وَمِخْيَطٌ مَنْقُوصٌ مِنَ الْمِخْيَاطِ، فَلَا يُعَلُّ تَبَعًا لَهُ.
text.en: The like of aʿyunin “eyes” and adwurin “houses” is not changed, so that they are not confused with the verbs; the like of jadwalin “stream”, so that the attachment is not undone; the like of qawwama “he set straight”, so that a change within a change is not required; the like of al-ramyi “throwing”, so that an unvowelled letter is not required at the end of an inflected word; and the like of taqwīmin “setting straight”, tibyānin “making clear”, miqwālin “eloquent” and mikhyāṭin “needle”, so that two unvowelled letters do not come together on the supposition of the change. mikhyaṭun is shortened from al-mikhyāṭi, so it is not changed, following it.

text.original: فَإِنْ قِيلَ: لِمَ يُعَلُّ الْإِقَامَةُ مَعَ حُصُولِ اجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ إِذَا أُعِلَّتْ كَإِعْلَالِ أَخَوَاتِهَا؟ قُلْنَا: تَبَعًا لِقَامَ. فَإِنْ قِيلَ: لِمَ لَا يُعَلُّ التَّقْوِيمُ تَبَعًا لِقَامَ وَهُوَ ثُلَاثِيٌّ أَصِيلٌ فِي الْإِعْلَالِ؟ قُلْنَا: أَبْطَلَ قَوْلُهُ «قَوَّمَ» اسْتِتْبَاعَ قَامَ، وَإِنْ كَانَ أَصِيلًا فِي الْإِعْلَالِ؛ لِقُوَّةِ قَوَّمَ فِي الْأُخُوَّةِ مَعَ التَّقْوِيمِ، وَلَا يَصْلُحُ أَقَامَ أَنْ يَكُونَ مُقَوِّيًا لِقَامَ؛ لِأَنَّهُ لَيْسَ مِنْ ثُلَاثِيٍّ أَصِيلٍ.
text.en: If it is said: why is al-iqāmatu “setting up” changed, though two unvowelled letters do come together when it is changed like the change of its sisters? We say: following qāma. If it is said: why is al-taqwīmu not changed following qāma, which is an original triliteral in the change? We say: the word qawwama cancelled the pull of qāma, even though that is original in the change, because qawwama is stronger in its brotherhood with taqwīm; and aqāma is not fit to strengthen qāma, because it is not from an original triliteral.

lessons.title: The past of qāla: qulna, khifna, biʿna
body: Three more words keep their wāw or yāʾ “so that they point to the origin”: mā aqwalahu, “how eloquent he is!”, aghyalati al-marʾatu, “the woman suckled while with child”, and istaḥwadha, “he gained mastery”. Then the past of qāla in full: qāla, qālā, qālū, qālat, qālatā, qulna, qulta, qultumā, qultum, qulti, qultumā, qultunna, qultu, qulnā.

Look at the two halves. Where the ending begins with a vowel (-ā, -ū, -at), the alif stays: qālā, qālū. Where it begins with a consonant (-na, -tu, -nā), the alif meets a quiescent lām and drops. So qulna comes from qawalna: the wāw became an alif (qālna), the alif dropped between two quiescent letters (qalna), “then the qāf was given a ḍamma so that it points to the dropped wāw”. The vowel left behind remembers the letter that went, as the Maqṣūd taught.

Khifna, “they (women) feared”, from khawifna, has a kasra instead, “because the rule in moving is to move the vowel of the wāw”: the wāw's own kasra goes to the khāʾ. That cannot work in qulna, whose wāw has a fatḥa, for the qāf already has one: so there a ḍamma, the wāw's kin, is put in instead.

Qulna, “they (women) said”, is the same as qulna, “say! (women)”. No difference is made, because the Arabs “are content with the implied difference”, as in biʿna, which is both “they sold” and “they were sold”; or it came about “through an oversight of the one who laid down the language”, as the past and the command of tafaʿʿala are the same in the dual and plural: tafaḍḍalā is “they two did a favour” and “do a favour, you two!”.

Nor is ṭulna, “they (women) were long”, told apart from qulna by its vowel. You know from ṭawīl, “long”, that ṭulna is ṭawulna (faʿīl comes mostly from faʿula); and from the futures you know the rest: yakhāfu shows that khifna is khawifna (faʿala yafʿalu would need a throat letter), and yabīʿu shows that biʿna is bayaʿna (no hollow yāʾ verb comes from faʿula).

terms.en: the hollow verb with wāw (qāla) and with yāʾ (bāʿa)
pointing to the dropped letter: the ḍamma of qulna
the implied difference: forms alike in sound, apart in origin
an oversight of the one who laid down the language

examples.en: kept unchanged to point to the origin
qawalna, qalna, qulna: the steps
khifna: the wāw's own kasra moved to the khāʾ
tafaḍḍalā: past and command alike (conjugation tool)

tasks.prompt: Derive qulna from qawalna, step by step.
tasks.answer: The wāw, vowelled after a fatḥa, becomes an alif (qālna); the alif meets the quiescent lām and drops (qalna); the qāf takes a ḍamma to point to the dropped wāw: qulna.

tasks.prompt: Why khifna with a kasra, but qulna with a ḍamma?
tasks.answer: The rule is to move the weak letter's own vowel. Khawifna's wāw has a kasra, which moves to the khāʾ: khifna. Qawalna's wāw has a fatḥa, and the qāf already has a fatḥa, so a ḍamma, the vowel that belongs with the wāw, is given instead.

tasks.prompt: How do we know that ṭulna is ṭawulna and biʿna is bayaʿna?
tasks.answer: Ṭawīl, “long”, is faʿīl, which comes mostly from faʿula, so ṭulna is ṭawulna. Yabīʿu shows a yāʾ verb with kasra in the future, and the hollow yāʾ verb does not come from faʿula, so biʿna is bayaʿna.

tasks.prompt: Which persons of qāla keep the alif, and which lose it? Give the reason.
tasks.answer: Qāla, qālā, qālū, qālat, qālatā keep it, because their endings begin with a vowel. Qulna, qulta and the rest lose it, because the ending makes the lām quiescent and the alif drops between two quiescent letters.

quiz.explanation: So too aghyalat and istaḥwadha.

quiz.explanation: Yakhāfu, with fatḥa and no throat letter, must be faʿila yafʿalu.

text.original: وَلَا يُعَلُّ مِثْلُ: مَا أَقْوَلَهُ، وَأَغْيَلَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ، وَاسْتَحْوَذَ، حَتَّى يَدْلُلْنَ عَلَى الْأَصْلِ. وَتَقُولُ فِي إِلْحَاقِ الضَّمَائِرِ: قَالَ قَالَا قَالُوا قَالَتْ قَالَتَا قُلْنَ قُلْتَ قُلْتُمَا قُلْتُمْ قُلْتِ قُلْتُمَا قُلْتُنَّ قُلْتُ قُلْنَا.
text.en: The like of mā aqwalahu “how eloquent he is!”, aghyalati al-marʾatu “the woman suckled while with child” and istaḥwadha “he gained mastery” is not changed, so that they point to the origin. In joining the pronouns you say: qāla qālā qālū qālat qālatā qulna qulta qultumā qultum qulti qultumā qultunna qultu qulnā “he said” … “we said”.

text.original: أَصْلُ قَالَ قَوَلَ، فَجُعِلَ الْوَاوُ أَلِفًا كَمَا مَرَّ، وَأَصْلُ قُلْنَ قَوَلْنَ، فَقُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ أَلِفًا، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتْ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، فَصَارَ قَلْنَ، ثُمَّ ضُمَّ الْقَافُ حَتَّى يَدُلَّ عَلَى الْوَاوِ الْمَحْذُوفَةِ، وَلَا يُضَمُّ فِي خِفْنَ؛ لِأَنَّ الْأَصْلَ فِي النَّقْلِ نَقْلُ حَرَكَةِ الْوَاوِ لِسُهُولَتِهَا، وَلَا يُمْكِنُ هَذَا فِي قُلْنَ؛ لِأَنَّهُ يَلْزَمُ فَتْحُ الْمَفْتُوحَةِ.
text.en: The origin of qāla is qawala; the wāw was made an alif, as has passed. The origin of qulna “they (f.) said” is qawalna: the wāw was changed into an alif, then dropped because two unvowelled letters came together, and it became qalna; then the qāf was given a ḍamma so that it points to the dropped wāw. It is not given a ḍamma in khifna “they (f.) feared”, because the rule in moving [a vowel] is to move the vowel of the wāw, for its ease; and this is not possible in qulna, because it would require giving a fatḥa to what already has a fatḥa.

text.original: وَلَا يُفْرَقُ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ فِي الْأَمْرِ؛ لِأَنَّهُمْ لَا يَعْتَبِرُونَ الِاشْتِرَاكَ الضِّمْنِيَّ، وَيَكْتَفُونَ بِالْفَرْقِ التَّقْدِيرِيِّ، كَمَا فِي بِعْنَ، وَهُوَ مُشْتَرَكٌ بَيْنَ الْمَعْلُومِ وَالْمَجْهُولِ أَيْضًا، أَوْ وَقَعَ مِنْ غِرَّةِ الْوَاضِعِ، كَمَا فِي الِاثْنَيْنِ وَالْجَمَاعَةِ مِنَ الْأَمْرِ وَالْمَاضِي فِي تَفَعَّلَ وَتَفَاعَلَ وَتَفَعْلَلَ.
text.en: No difference is made between it and the feminine plural in the command, because they do not take account of a sharing that is implicit, and they are content with the implied difference, as in biʿna, which is shared between the active and the passive too; or it came about through an oversight of the one who laid down [the language], as in the dual and the plural of the command and the past in tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala and tafaʿlala.

text.original: وَلَا يُفْرَقُ بَيْنَ فَعُلْنَ وَفَعَلْنَ، نَحْوُ: طُلْنَ وَقُلْنَ؛ لِأَنَّهُ يُعْلَمُ مِنَ الطَّوِيلِ أَنَّ أَصْلَ طُلْنَ طَوُلْنَ؛ لِأَنَّ الْفَعِيلَ يَجِيءُ مِنْ فَعُلَ يَفْعُلُ غَالِبًا، كَمَا يُعْلَمُ الْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ خِفْنَ وَبِعْنَ مِنْ مُسْتَقْبَلِهِمَا، أَعْنِي: يُعْلَمُ مِنْ يَخَافُ أَنَّ أَصْلَ خِفْنَ خَوِفْنَ؛ لِأَنَّ بَابَ فَعَلَ يَفْعَلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ فِيهِمَا لَا يَجِيءُ إِلَّا مِنْ حُرُوفِ الْحَلْقِ، وَيُعْلَمُ مِنْ يَبِيعُ أَنَّ أَصْلَ بِعْنَ بَيَعْنَ؛ لِأَنَّ الْأَجْوَفَ الْيَائِيَّ لَا يَجِيءُ مِنْ بَابِ فَعُلَ يَفْعُلُ.
text.en: No difference is made between faʿulna and faʿalna, as ṭulna “they (f.) were long” and qulna “they (f.) said”, because it is known from al-ṭawīli “the long” that the origin of ṭulna is ṭawulna, since faʿīl mostly comes from faʿula yafʿulu; as the difference between khifna and biʿna is known from their future: I mean, it is known from yakhāfu that the origin of khifna is khawifna, because the bāb of faʿala yafʿalu, with a fatḥa on the ʿayn in both, comes only from the letters of the throat; and it is known from yabīʿu that the origin of biʿna is bayaʿna, because the hollow verb with yāʾ does not come from the bāb of faʿula yafʿulu.

lessons.title: The future and the command of qāla
body: The future yaqūlu comes from yaqwulu by the rule of lesson 48: the wāw's ḍamma moves back to the qāf. In yaqulna, “they (women) say”, the long ū shortens, the wāw dropping between two quiescent letters (ū and the quiescent lām).

The command qul comes from uqwul in three steps: the vowel of the wāw moves to the qāf (uqūl); the wāw drops, two quiescent letters meeting (the ū and the lām, quiescent for the command); and the hamza of joining drops, “because it was no longer needed”, the qāf having a vowel. Hence qul, “say!”, two letters, like ʿid in the mithāl.

Then a fine point. In quli al-ḥaqqa, “say the truth!”, the lām has a kasra, yet the wāw does not come back. That vowel “came about through something from outside”, the meeting with the next word, “so it counts as a sukūn by implication”. In qūlā, “say! (two)”, and qūlanna, “do say!”, the wāw does come back, because their vowel comes “through two things from inside”: the alif of the doer and the nūn of emphasis, which counts as part of the word. That is also why the muḍāriʿ before that nūn becomes built, hal yafʿalanna.

And daʿatā, “they two (women) called”: here the alif of daʿā stays dropped though the alif of the doer gives the tāʾ a vowel, “because the tāʾ is not of the word itself”: the tāʾ is a sign added to the verb, unlike the lām of qūlā, which is a root letter.

With the heavy nūn: qūlanna, qūlānni, qūlunna, qūlinna, qūlānni, qulnānni; with the light: qūlan, qūlun, qūlin. Compare the sound verb's iḍribanna (lesson 21): the same endings, with the wāw back in every form except the women's.

terms.en: a vowel from outside the word, which counts as a sukūn
a vowel from inside the word: from the alif of the doer or the nūn of emphasis
counting as a sukūn
the nūn of emphasis, which counts as part of the word

examples.en: yaqulna: the wāw dropped between two quiescent letters
uqwul: the origin of qul
quli al-ḥaqqa: the wāw stays dropped, the kasra being from outside
daʿatā: the alif stays dropped, the tāʾ not being of the word

tasks.prompt: Derive qul from uqwul.
tasks.answer: The wāw's ḍamma moves to the qāf (uqūl); the wāw drops, since it meets the quiescent lām; the hamza of joining is no longer needed before the vowelled qāf, and drops: qul.

tasks.prompt: Why does the wāw stay dropped in quli al-ḥaqqa but come back in qūlā?
tasks.answer: In quli al-ḥaqqa the lām's kasra comes from outside, the meeting with the next word, so the lām still counts as quiescent. In qūlā the vowel comes from inside, the alif of the doer, so the lām is truly vowelled and the wāw returns.

tasks.prompt: Give qāla's command with the heavy nūn, and explain why qulnānni alone has no wāw.
tasks.answer: Qūlanna, qūlānni, qūlunna, qūlinna, qūlānni, qulnānni. In the women's form the lām stays quiescent before -na (constant sukūn), so the wāw still meets two quiescent letters and stays dropped.

text.original: الْمُسْتَقْبَلُ: يَقُولُ إِلَخْ، أَصْلُهُ يَقْوُلُ، وَإِعْلَالُهُ مَرَّ، فَحُذِفَ الْوَاوُ فِي يَقُلْنَ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ. الْأَمْرُ: قُلْ إِلَخْ، أَصْلُهُ اقْوُلْ، فَنُقِلَتْ حَرَكَةُ الْوَاوِ إِلَى الْقَافِ، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتِ الْوَاوُ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتِ الْأَلِفُ لِانْعِدَامِ الِاحْتِيَاجِ إِلَيْهَا.
text.en: The future: yaqūlu “he says” and so on, whose origin is yaqwulu; its change has passed; and the wāw was dropped in yaqulna “they (f.) say” because two unvowelled letters came together. The command: qul “say!” and so on, whose origin is uqwul: the vowel of the wāw was moved to the qāf, then the wāw was dropped because two unvowelled letters came together, then the alif was dropped because it was no longer needed.

text.original: وَيُحْذَفُ الْوَاوُ فِي قُلِ الْحَقَّ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَجْتَمِعْ فِيهِ السَّاكِنَانِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْحَرَكَةَ فِيهِ حَصَلَتْ بِالْخَارِجِيِّ، فَيَكُونُ فِي حُكْمِ السُّكُونِ تَقْدِيرًا، بِخِلَافِ قُولَا وَقُولَنَّ؛ لِأَنَّ الْحَرَكَةَ فِيهِمَا حَصَلَتْ بِالدَّاخِلِيَّيْنِ، وَهُمَا أَلِفُ الْفَاعِلِ وَنُونُ التَّأْكِيدِ، وَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الدَّاخِلِ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ جَعَلُوا مَعَهُ آخِرَ الْمُضَارِعِ مَبْنِيًّا، نَحْوُ: هَلْ يَفْعَلَنَّ، وَيُحْذَفُ الْأَلِفُ فِي دَعَتَا وَإِنْ حَصَلَتِ الْحَرَكَةُ بِأَلِفِ الْفَاعِلِ؛ لِأَنَّ التَّاءَ لَيْسَتْ مِنْ نَفْسِ الْكَلِمَةِ، بِخِلَافِ اللَّامِ فِي قُولَا.
text.en: The wāw is dropped in quli al-ḥaqqa “say the truth!”, though two unvowelled letters do not come together in it, because the vowel in it came about through something from outside, so it counts as a sukūn by implication; unlike qūlā “say! (du.)” and qūlanna “do say!”, because the vowel in them came about through two things from inside, which are the alif of the doer and the nūn of emphasis — and [the nūn] stands as what is inside; for that reason they made the end of the muḍāriʿ mabnī with it, as hal yafʿalanna “will he indeed do?”. The alif is dropped in daʿatā “they two (f.) called”, though the vowel came about through the alif of the doer, because the tāʾ is not of the word itself, unlike the lām in qūlā.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ بِنُونِ التَّأْكِيدِ الْمُشَدَّدَةِ: قُولَنَّ قُولَانِّ قُولُنَّ قُولِنَّ قُولَانِّ قُلْنَانِّ، وَبِالْخَفِيفَةِ: قُولَنْ قُولُنْ قُولِنْ.
text.en: With the doubled nūn of emphasis you say: qūlanna qūlānni qūlunna qūlinna qūlānni qulnānni “do say!” (to one man, two, men; to one woman, two, women), and with the light: qūlan qūlun qūlin.

lessons.title: The active participle qāʾil; dropping and transposition
body: The active participle qāʾil, “saying”, comes from qāwil. Its wāw is vowelled after a fatḥa, so it becomes an alif: the alif of fāʿil between them “is not a strong barrier”, and the qāf's fatḥa reaches across it. So also kisāʾ, “garment”, from kisāw, whose final wāw became an alif and then a hamza.

Now two alifs stand together, and something must give. Not the first: dropping it would leave qāla, “he said”, the past. Not the second either, the root's own letter. So “the last was given a vowel, and it became a hamza”: qāʾil. The hamza is the alif made able to carry a vowel.

Some words drop the hamza instead: hāʿ and lāʿ, “impatient, anxious”, from hāʾiʿ and lāʾiʿ; and the Qurʾān's ʿalā shafā jurufin hārin, “on the brink of a crumbling bank” (9:109), where hār is hāʾir. Others change the order of the letters (qalb, transposition): shāk, “armed”, from shāʾik, and ḥād, “one”, from wāḥid.

Transposition is a recognised device of the language. Qisiyy, “bows”, the plural of qaws, comes from quwūs: the sīn was put forward, qusuww, “like ʿuṣuww”; the two final wāws became yāʾs, qusiyy; and the qāf took a kasra to follow the next letter, qisiyy, as in ʿiṣiyy, “sticks”. Aynuq, “she-camels”, on the measure aʿful, comes from anwuq: the wāw was put before the nūn, awnuq, and then turned into a yāʾ, “against analogy”.
For a reader the point is practical: when a word seems to break the rules, try moving its letters back into their root order.

terms.en: a weak barrier: the alif of fāʿil between the fatḥa and the wāw
transposition: changing the order of the root letters
dropping the hamza of the participle, as in hār
against analogy

examples.en: qāʾil from qāwil: the wāw made alif, then hamza
kisāʾ from kisāw: the final wāw made alif, then hamza
ʿalā shafā jurufin hārin: hār for hāʾir
ḥād from wāḥid: transposition

tasks.prompt: Derive qāʾil from qāwil.
tasks.answer: The wāw is vowelled, and the fatḥa of the qāf reaches it across the alif of fāʿil, which is no strong barrier; so it becomes an alif. Two alifs meet: dropping the first would give the past qāla, and the second cannot go; so the second is given a vowel and becomes a hamza: qāʾil.

tasks.prompt: Trace qisiyy back to quwūs.
tasks.answer: The sīn is put forward: qusuww (like ʿuṣuww). The two wāws at the end become yāʾs: qusiyy. The qāf takes a kasra to follow the next letter: qisiyy, as ʿiṣiyy.

tasks.prompt: Explain hārin in 9:109.
tasks.answer: It is the active participle hāʾir, “crumbling”, with its hamza dropped, as hāʿ for hāʾiʿ.

quiz.prompt: The origin of qāʾil is…
quiz.explanation: Fāʿil of q-w-l.

quiz.explanation: So the second becomes a hamza.

quiz.explanation: The fatḥa reaches the wāw across it.

quiz.explanation: The hamza dropped.

quiz.explanation: Its letters were moved.

quiz.explanation: Anwuq, awnuq, aynuq.

text.original: الْفَاعِلُ: قَائِلٌ إِلَخْ، أَصْلُهُ قَاوِلٌ، فَقُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ أَلِفًا لِتَحَرُّكِهَا وَانْفِتَاحِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، كَمَا فِي كِسَاءٍ، أَصْلُهُ كِسَاوٌ، وَجُعِلَ وَاوُهُ أَلِفًا لِوُقُوعِهِ فِي الطَّرَفِ، ثُمَّ جُعِلَ هَمْزَةً، وَلَا اعْتِبَارَ بِأَلِفِ الْفَاعِلِ؛ لِأَنَّهَا لَيْسَتْ بِحَاجِزَةٍ حَصِينَةٍ، فَاجْتَمَعَ الْأَلِفَانِ، وَلَا يُمْكِنُ إِسْقَاطُ الْأُولَى؛ لِأَنَّهُ يَلْتَبِسُ بِالْمَاضِي، وَكَذَلِكَ الثَّانِيَةُ، فَحُرِّكَتِ الْأَخِيرَةُ، فَصَارَتْ هَمْزَةً.
text.en: The fāʿil: qāʾilun “saying” and so on, whose origin is qāwilun: the wāw was changed into an alif because it is vowelled and what is before it has a fatḥa, as in kisāʾin “a garment”, whose origin is kisāwun: its wāw was made an alif because it stands at the end, then made a hamza; and the alif of the fāʿil is not taken into account, because it is not a strong barrier. So two alifs came together; dropping the first is not possible, because it would be confused with the past, and likewise the second; so the last was given a vowel, and it became a hamza.

text.original: وَيَجِيءُ فِي الْبَعْضِ بِالْحَذْفِ، نَحْوُ: هَاعٍ وَلَاعٍ، الْأَصْلُ هَائِعٌ وَلَائِعٌ، وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿عَلَى شَفَا جُرُفٍ هَارٍ﴾، أَيْ: هَائِرٍ. وَيَجِيءُ بِالْقَلْبِ، نَحْوُ: شَاكٍ، أَصْلُهُ شَائِكٌ، وَحَادٍ، أَصْلُهُ وَاحِدٌ.
text.en: In some it comes with dropping, as hāʿin “impatient” and lāʿin “anxious”, the origin being hāʾiʿun and lāʾiʿun; and from it is His saying, Most High: ʿalā shafā jurufin hārin “on the brink of a crumbling bank” [9:109], that is, hāʾirin. It comes with transposition (qalb), as shākin “armed”, whose origin is shāʾikun, and ḥādin “one”, whose origin is wāḥidun.

text.original: وَيَجُوزُ الْقَلْبُ فِي كَلَامِهِمْ، نَحْوُ: الْقِسِيِّ، أَصْلُهُ قُوُوسٌ، فَقُدِّمَ السِّينُ، فَصَارَ قُسُوٌّ، مِثْلُ: عُصُوٍّ، ثُمَّ جُعِلَ قُسِيٌّ لِوُقُوعِ الْوَاوَيْنِ فِي الطَّرَفِ، ثُمَّ كُسِرَ الْقَافُ إِتْبَاعًا لِمَا بَعْدَهَا، فَقَالُوا: قِسِيٌّ، كَمَا فِي عِصِيٍّ. وَمِنْهُ: أَيْنُقٌ عَلَى وَزْنِ أَعْفُلٍ، أَصْلُهُ أَنْوُقٌ، ثُمَّ قُدِّمَ الْوَاوُ عَلَى النُّونِ، فَصَارَ أَوْنُقٌ، ثُمَّ جُعِلَ الْوَاوُ يَاءً عَلَى غَيْرِ قِيَاسٍ.
text.en: Transposition is allowed in their speech, as al-qisiyyi “the bows”, whose origin is quwūsun: the sīn was put forward and it became qusuwwun, like ʿuṣuwwin; then it was made qusiyyun, because the two wāws stood at the end; then the qāf was given a kasra, following what comes after it, and they said qisiyyun, as in ʿiṣiyyin “sticks”. From it too is aynuqun “she-camels”, on the measure aʿful, whose origin is anwuqun: the wāw was put before the nūn and it became awnuqun; then the wāw was made a yāʾ, against analogy.

lessons.title: Maqūl and mabīʿ: Sībawayh and al-Akhfash
body: The passive participle maqūl, “said”, comes from maqwūl. It is changed as yaqūlu is: the wāw's ḍamma moves back to the qāf, maqūwl, and now two quiescent letters meet, the root wāw and the added wāw of mafʿūl. One of them must go, and here the two great Baṣrans part.

Sībawayh drops the added wāw, “because dropping the added letter is more fitting”. Al-Akhfash drops the root wāw, “because the added one is a sign, and a sign is not dropped”. Sībawayh answers: “a sign is not dropped when no other sign is found”, and here there is one, the mīm. So the word's measure is mafuʿl for Sībawayh, mafūl for al-Akhfash; the sound is the same.

Mabīʿ, “sold”, goes the same way. Changed as yabīʿu, it becomes mabuyūʿ, with the yāʾ and the wāw both quiescent. Sībawayh drops the wāw and gives the bāʾ a kasra “so that the yāʾ stays sound”: mabīʿ, on mafiʿl. Al-Akhfash drops the yāʾ, gives its kasra to the bāʾ as in biʿtu, “I sold”, which gives mabūʿ, and then turns the wāw after the kasra into a yāʾ, as in mīzān: mabīʿ, on mafīl.

The noun of place is maqāl from maqwal, changed as yakhāfu, and mabīʿ from mabyiʿ, changed as yabīʿu: so mabīʿ is both “sold” and “place of selling”. The book accepts it: “the implied difference” between them is taken into account. Al-fulk, “ship”, shows such a difference: read like usd, “lions”, it is a plural, idhā kuntum fī al-fulki wa-jarayna bihim (10:22), “when you are in the ships and they sail with them”; read like qurb, it is a singular, fī al-fulki al-mashḥūni (26:119), “in the laden ship”.
Know the dispute, but do not lose the form: whatever the analysis, the participles are maqūl and mabīʿ, and the noun of place maqāl.

the added letter: the wāw of mafʿūl

tasks.prompt: Give both analyses of maqūl, with their reasons.
tasks.answer: After the wāw's ḍamma moves back, two quiescent wāws meet. Sībawayh drops the added wāw (dropping the added is more fitting), so the measure is mafuʿl. Al-Akhfash drops the root wāw (the added wāw is a sign, not to be dropped), so the measure is mafūl. Sībawayh replies that the mīm is another sign.

tasks.prompt: Show al-Akhfash's steps for mabīʿ.
tasks.answer: Mabuyūʿ has a quiescent yāʾ and wāw; he drops the yāʾ and gives its kasra to the bāʾ (as in biʿtu): mabūʿ; then the wāw after the kasra becomes a yāʾ, as in mīzān: mabīʿ, on the measure mafīl.

tasks.prompt: Why can mabīʿ be both the participle and the place of selling?
tasks.answer: The place, from mabyiʿ, changed as yabīʿu, comes out the same as the participle; the implied difference between them is accepted, as al-fulk is singular or plural by an implied difference.

text.original: الْمَفْعُولُ: مَقُولٌ، أَصْلُهُ مَقْوُولٌ، فَأُعِلَّ كَإِعْلَالِ يَقُولُ، فَاجْتَمَعَ السَّاكِنَانِ، فَحُذِفَتِ الْوَاوُ الزَّائِدَةُ عِنْدَ سِيبَوَيْهِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْحَذْفَ بِالزَّائِدِ أَوْلَى، وَالْوَاوُ الْأَصْلِيُّ عِنْدَ الْأَخْفَشِ؛ لِأَنَّ الزَّائِدَةَ عَلَامَةٌ، وَالْعَلَامَةُ لَا تُحْذَفُ. وَقَالَ سِيبَوَيْهِ: لَا تُحْذَفُ الْعَلَامَةُ إِذَا لَمْ تُوجَدْ عَلَامَةٌ أُخْرَى، وَفِيهِ تُوجَدُ عَلَامَةٌ أُخْرَى، وَهِيَ الْمِيمُ.
text.en: The mafʿūl: maqūlun “said”, whose origin is maqwūlun: it was changed like the change of yaqūlu, so two unvowelled letters came together, and the added wāw was dropped according to Sībawayh, because dropping the added [letter] is more fitting; and the root wāw according to al-Akhfash, because the added one is a sign, and a sign is not dropped. Sībawayh said: a sign is not dropped when no other sign is found, and in it another sign is found, namely the mīm.

text.original: فَيَكُونُ وَزْنُهُ عِنْدَهُ مَفُعْلًا، وَعِنْدَ الْأَخْفَشِ مَفُولًا. وَكَذَلِكَ مَبِيعٌ، يَعْنِي: أُعِلَّ كَإِعْلَالِ يَبِيعُ، فَصَارَ مَبُيُوعٌ، فَاجْتَمَعَ سَاكِنَانِ: الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ، فَحُذِفَتِ الْوَاوُ عِنْدَ سِيبَوَيْهِ، ثُمَّ كُسِرَ الْبَاءُ حَتَّى تَسْلَمَ الْيَاءُ. وَعِنْدَ الْأَخْفَشِ حُذِفَ الْيَاءُ، فَأُعْطِيَ الْكَسْرَةُ لِمَا قَبْلَهَا كَمَا فِي بِعْتُ، فَصَارَ مَبُوعٌ، ثُمَّ جُعِلَ الْوَاوُ يَاءً كَمَا فِي مِيزَانٍ، فَيَكُونُ وَزْنُهُ عِنْدَ سِيبَوَيْهِ مَفِعْلًا، وَعِنْدَ الْأَخْفَشِ مَفِيلًا.
text.en: So its measure according to him is mafuʿl, and according to al-Akhfash mafūl. Likewise mabīʿun “sold”: that is, it was changed like the change of yabīʿu and became mabuyūʿun, and two unvowelled letters came together, the wāw and the yāʾ; the wāw was dropped according to Sībawayh, then the bāʾ was given a kasra so that the yāʾ stays sound. According to al-Akhfash the yāʾ was dropped and the kasra given to what is before it, as in biʿtu “I sold”, and it became mabūʿun; then the wāw was made a yāʾ, as in mīzānin; so its measure according to Sībawayh is mafiʿl, and according to al-Akhfash mafīl.

text.original: الْمَوْضِعُ: مَقَالٌ، أَصْلُهُ مَقْوَلٌ، فَأُعِلَّ كَمَا فِي يَخَافُ، وَكَذَلِكَ مَبِيعٌ، أَصْلُهُ مَبْيِعٌ، فَأُعِلَّ كَمَا فِي يَبِيعُ، وَاكْتُفِيَ بِالْفَرْقِ التَّقْدِيرِيِّ بَيْنَ الْمَوْضِعِ وَبَيْنَ اسْمِ الْمَفْعُولِ، وَهُوَ مُعْتَبَرٌ عِنْدَهُمْ، كَمَا فِي الْفُلْكِ: إِذَا قَدَّرْتَ سُكُونَهُ كَسُكُونِ أُسْدٍ يَكُونُ جَمْعًا، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: ﴿إِذَا كُنْتُمْ فِي الْفُلْكِ وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِمْ بِرِيحٍ﴾، وَإِذَا قَدَّرْتَ سُكُونَهُ كَسُكُونِ قُرْبٍ يَكُونُ وَاحِدًا، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: ﴿فِي الْفُلْكِ الْمَشْحُونِ﴾.
text.en: The place: maqālun, whose origin is maqwalun; it was changed as in yakhāfu. Likewise mabīʿun, whose origin is mabyiʿun; it was changed as in yabīʿu; and the implied difference between the place and the passive participle was thought enough. It is taken into account by them, as in al-fulki “the ship”: if you suppose its sukūn to be like the sukūn of usdin “lions”, it is a plural, as in His saying, Most High: idhā kuntum fī al-fulki wa-jarayna bihim bi-rīḥin “when you are in the ships, and they sail with them in a wind” [10:22]; and if you suppose its sukūn to be like the sukūn of qurbin “nearness”, it is a singular, as in His saying, Most High: fī al-fulki al-mashḥūni “in the laden ship” [26:119].

lessons.title: The passive: qīla and its three dialects
body: The passive past qīla, “it was said”, comes from quwila, the regular fuʿila. Three dialects deal with it. In the first, the wāw is made quiescent for lightness: qūla, “a weak dialect, because of the heaviness of the ḍamma and the wāw”. In the second, “the kasra of the wāw was given to what is before it”, qiwla, and the wāw, quiescent after a kasra, became a yāʾ: qīla, the form one usually hears.

In the third, the first letter is said with a touch of the ḍamma, ishmām, “so that it is known that what is before it had a ḍamma in the origin”: the qāf is said between qi and qu. The same three dialects hold in bīʿa, “it was sold”, inqīda, “he was led”, ikhtīra, “he was chosen”, and in qilna and biʿna.

Ishmām “is not allowed in the like of uqīma”, “it was set up”, because the letter before the yāʾ (the qāf) has no ḍamma in the origin; only the hamza of the pattern has one. Nor a wāw there (uqūma), for the wāw was allowed only after a ḍamma on the letter before the weak letter.

The passive future yuqālu comes from yuqwalu, “changed like yakhāfu”: the wāw's fatḥa moves to the qāf and the wāw becomes an alif. And “in the like of qulna and biʿna the active and the passive were made the same”, the implied difference being thought enough: biʿna is “they sold” and “they were sold”.
Ishmām is also a term of Qurʾān recitation: some readers say qīla and ghīḍa with this touch of ḍamma. When you hear it, recognise the old ḍamma of fuʿila surfacing in the hollow verb.

a weak dialect: qūla for qīla
the passive
the implied difference between biʿna active and passive

tasks.prompt: Give the three dialects of the passive of qāla, and how each is reached from quwila.
tasks.answer: Qūla: the wāw made quiescent (a weak dialect). Qīla: the wāw's kasra moved to the qāf, and the quiescent wāw after the kasra became a yāʾ. Qīla with ishmām: said with a touch of ḍamma on the qāf to show its original ḍamma.

tasks.prompt: Why is there no ishmām in uqīma?
tasks.answer: Ishmām shows an original ḍamma on the letter before the weak letter. In uqīma that letter, the qāf, had no ḍamma (the ḍamma is on the hamza), so there is nothing to show; for the same reason a wāw (uqūma) is not allowed.

tasks.prompt: Derive yuqālu.
tasks.answer: From yuqwalu: the wāw's fatḥa moves back to the qāf (yuqawlu), and the wāw, quiescent after a fatḥa by accident, becomes an alif, as in yakhāfu: yuqālu.

text.original: الْمَجْهُولُ: قِيلَ إِلَخْ، أَصْلُهُ قُوِلَ، فَأُسْكِنَ الْوَاوُ لِلْخِفَّةِ، فَصَارَ قُوْلَ، وَهُوَ لُغَةٌ ضَعِيفَةٌ لِثِقَلِ الضَّمَّةِ وَالْوَاوِ، وَفِي لُغَةٍ أُخْرَى أُعْطِيَ كَسْرَةُ الْوَاوِ إِلَى مَا قَبْلَهَا، فَصَارَ قِوْلَ، ثُمَّ صَارَ الْوَاوُ يَاءً لِكَسْرَةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، فَصَارَ قِيلَ. وَفِي لُغَةٍ تُشَمُّ حَتَّى يُعْلَمَ أَنَّ أَصْلَ مَا قَبْلَهَا مَضْمُومٌ، وَكَذَلِكَ بِيعَ وَانْقِيدَ وَاخْتِيرَ وَقِلْنَ وَبِعْنَ، يَعْنِي: يَجُوزُ فِيهِنَّ ثَلَاثُ لُغَاتٍ.
text.en: The passive: qīla “it was said” and so on, whose origin is quwila: the wāw was made unvowelled for lightness, and it became qūla, which is a weak dialect, because of the heaviness of the ḍamma and the wāw. In another dialect the kasra of the wāw was given to what is before it, and it became qiwla; then the wāw became a yāʾ because of the kasra before it, and it became qīla. In [yet another] dialect it is given a touch [of the ḍamma] (ishmām), so that it is known that what is before it had a ḍamma in the origin. Likewise bīʿa “it was sold”, inqīda “he was led”, ikhtīra “he was chosen”, qilna and biʿna; that is, three dialects are allowed in them.

text.original: وَلَا يَجُوزُ الْإِشْمَامُ فِي مِثْلِ: أُقِيمَ؛ لِانْعِدَامِ ضَمِّ مَا قَبْلَ الْيَاءِ، وَلَا يَجُوزُ بِالْوَاوِ أَيْضًا؛ لِأَنَّ جَوَازَ الْوَاوِ كَانَ لِانْضِمَامِ مَا قَبْلَ حَرْفِ الْعِلَّةِ، وَهُوَ لَيْسَ بِمَوْجُودٍ. وَسُوِّيَ فِي مِثْلِ: قُلْنَ وَبِعْنَ بَيْنَ الْمَعْلُومِ وَالْمَجْهُولِ اكْتِفَاءً بِالْفَرْقِ التَّقْدِيرِيِّ. وَأَصْلُ يُقَالُ يُقْوَلُ، فَأُعِلَّ كَإِعْلَالِ يَخَافُ.
text.en: Ishmām is not allowed in the like of uqīma “it was set up”, because there is no ḍamma before the yāʾ; nor is [it allowed] with the wāw, because the wāw was allowed because of the ḍamma before the letter of weakness, and that is not present. In the like of qulna and biʿna the active and the passive were made the same, the implied difference being thought enough. The origin of yuqālu “it is said” is yuqwalu; it was changed like the change of yakhāfu.

parts.title: Chapter six: the defective verb, and the substituted letters

lessons.title: The defective verb, and its past
body: The sixth chapter takes the verb weak in its lām. It is called nāqiṣ, “defective”, “because it falls short at the end”: its last letter disappears in many forms. And dhū al-arbaʿa, “the one of four”, because with the speaker's ending it has four letters: ramaytu, “I threw”, ghazawtu, “I raided”. It never comes from the bāb of faʿila yafʿilu (ḥasiba).

The past ramā is from ramaya: “the yāʾ was changed into an alif, as in qāla”, a vowelled weak letter after a fatḥa (lesson 46). Ramaw, “they threw”, is from ramayū: the yāʾ became an alif, the alif met the quiescent wāw and dropped. Raḍū, “they were pleased”, is the same, “except that the ḍād was given a ḍamma after the dropping”, so as not to pass from a kasra to the wāw.

Ramat, “she threw”, from ramayat, drops its letter in the same way, the alif meeting the quiescent tāʾ. And ramatā, “they two (women) threw”, drops it too, “though two unvowelled letters do not come together in it”: the tāʾ's fatḥa is lent by the dual alif, so “two unvowelled letters come together by implication” (lesson 50 gave the same reason for daʿatā).

Ramayna, “they (women) threw”, ramaytu and ramaynā keep the yāʾ: before -na and -tu it is quiescent after a fatḥa, and a quiescent weak letter after a fatḥa is not changed, “for the reason that has passed in al-qawl”. So the past of the defective has two faces, like the hollow's: with vowel endings the weak letter is an alif or gone; with consonant endings it shows itself.
Ghazā, “to raid”, from g-z-w, is conjugated the same way with its wāw: ghazā, ghazaw, ghazat, ghazawtu. The lessons that follow use ramā as the model, as the book does.

tasks.prompt: Derive ramā and ramaw from their bases.
tasks.answer: Ramā, from ramaya: the vowelled yāʾ after a fatḥa becomes an alif. Ramaw, from ramayū: the yāʾ becomes an alif, which then meets the quiescent wāw and drops.

tasks.prompt: Why does ramatā drop the weak letter, though its tāʾ has a vowel?
tasks.answer: The tāʾ's fatḥa is lent by the dual alif and the tāʾ is not part of the word itself, so the tāʾ counts as quiescent; the two quiescent letters meet by implication and the alif drops, as in ramat.

tasks.prompt: Why does raḍū have a ḍamma on the ḍād?
tasks.answer: From raḍiyū the yāʾ drops; the ḍād, which had a kasra, then takes a ḍamma so as not to pass from a kasra to the wāw.

tasks.prompt: Which persons of ramā show the yāʾ, and why?
tasks.answer: Ramayā, ramayna, ramayta and the rest with consonant endings: before -na, -tu and the like the yāʾ is quiescent after a fatḥa (or vowelled by the dual alif), and such a yāʾ is not changed.

text.original: يُقَالُ لَهُ: نَاقِصٌ؛ لِنُقْصَانِهِ فِي الْآخِرِ، وَذُو الْأَرْبَعَةِ؛ لِأَنَّهُ يَصِيرُ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَحْرُفٍ فِي الْإِخْبَارِ عَنْ نَفْسِكَ، نَحْوُ: رَمَيْتُ وَغَزَوْتُ. وَهُوَ لَا يَجِيءُ مِنْ بَابِ فَعِلَ يَفْعِلُ بِالْكَسْرِ فِيهِمَا.
text.en: It is called nāqiṣ “defective”, because it falls short at the end; and dhū al-arbaʿa “the one of four”, because it becomes four letters when you tell about yourself, as ramaytu “I threw” and ghazawtu “I raided”. It does not come from the bāb of faʿila yafʿilu, with the kasra in both.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي إِلْحَاقِ الضَّمَائِرِ: رَمَى إِلَخْ، أَصْلُهُ رَمَيَ، فَقُلِبَتِ الْيَاءُ أَلِفًا كَمَا فِي قَالَ. وَأَصْلُ رَمَوْا رَمَيُوا، فَقُلِبَتِ الْيَاءُ أَلِفًا، فَاجْتَمَعَ سَاكِنَانِ، فَحُذِفَتِ الْأَلِفُ، فَصَارَ رَمَوْا. وَكَذَلِكَ رَضُوا، إِلَّا أَنَّهُ ضُمَّ الضَّادُ فِيهِ بَعْدَ الْحَذْفِ حَتَّى لَا يَلْزَمَ الْخُرُوجُ مِنَ الْكَسْرَةِ إِلَى الْوَاوِ. وَأَصْلُ رَمَتْ رَمَيَتْ، فَحُذِفَتِ الْيَاءُ كَمَا فِي رَمَوْا، وَيُحْذَفُ فِي رَمَتَا وَإِنْ لَمْ يَجْتَمِعْ فِيهِ السَّاكِنَانِ؛ لِأَنَّهُ يَجْتَمِعُ السَّاكِنَانِ تَقْدِيرًا، وَتَمَامُهُ مَرَّ فِي قُولَا. وَلَا يُعَلُّ فِي رَمَيْنَ لِمَا مَرَّ فِي الْقَوْلِ.
text.en: In joining the pronouns you say: ramā “he threw” and so on, whose origin is ramaya: the yāʾ was changed into an alif, as in qāla. The origin of ramaw “they threw” is ramayū: the yāʾ was changed into an alif, two unvowelled letters came together, the alif was dropped, and it became ramaw. Likewise raḍū “they were pleased”, except that the ḍād was given a ḍamma in it after the dropping, so that going from a kasra to a wāw is not required. The origin of ramat “she threw” is ramayat: the yāʾ was dropped as in ramaw; and it is dropped in ramatā “they two (f.) threw”, though two unvowelled letters do not come together in it, because two unvowelled letters come together by implication; the rest of it has passed in qūlā. It is not changed in ramayna “they (f.) threw”, for the reason that has passed in al-qawli “saying”.

lessons.title: The future yarmī, and its jussive and subjunctive
body: The future yarmī is from yarmiyu: “the yāʾ was made unvowelled because of the heaviness of the ḍamma on it”. The dual yarmiyāni keeps its vowel, “because its vowel is a fatḥa, and that is light”. Yarmūna, “they throw”, is from yarmiyūna: the yāʾ was made quiescent and then dropped, two quiescent letters meeting.

Yaʿfūna, from ʿ-f-w, “to pardon”, is the same for men and for women, “the implied difference being thought enough”. For the men it is yaʿfuwūna shortened, and its wāw is the pronoun; for the women it is yaʿfu-w-na, its wāw is the root letter and its nūn the sign of the feminine. That is why the nūn stays in illā an yaʿfūna, “unless they (the wives) pardon” (2:237), after an, which would drop a nūn of rafʿ. Tarmīna, “you (a woman) throw”, from tarmiyīna, likewise sounds like tarmīna, “you (women) throw”.

“When you bring in the governor of jazm, the yāʾ falls away as the sign of jazm”: lam yarmi. That is why it can fall away in rafʿ “as a sign of the pause” at a verse end: wa-l-layli idhā yasri, “by the night when it passes” (89:4), as the print writes it. The governor of naṣb gives the yāʾ a fatḥa, “because of the lightness of naṣb”: lan yarmiya. But lan yakhshā, “he will not fear”, shows nothing, “because the alif does not bear a vowel”.

So the defective future has three endings to watch: -ī, -ū, -ā in rafʿ (yarmī, yaghzū, yakhshā); the weak letter dropped in jazm; a fatḥa on the wāw and the yāʾ, but not on the alif, in naṣb. Al-ʿIzzī, in the same print, gives the full tables; the grid below is his.

The trap is tarmīna: one form, two analyses. In “you (a woman) throw” it is taf-ʿīna, the root yāʾ gone and the ī the pronoun; in “you (women) throw” it is taf-ʿil-na, the ī the root yāʾ and the nūn the women's.

terms.en: the implied difference: yaʿfūna, tarmīna
the sign of jazm: the dropping of the weak letter
the sign of the pause: the yāʾ dropped at a verse end
the lightness of naṣb, which the yāʾ and wāw can carry

examples.en: yarmī, from yarmiyu: the ḍamma heavy on the yāʾ
illā an yaʿfūna: the women's nūn, kept after an
wa-l-layli idhā yasri: the yāʾ dropped in pause

tasks.prompt: Derive yarmī and yarmūna, and say why yarmiyāni is unchanged.
tasks.answer: Yarmiyu: the ḍamma is heavy on the yāʾ, so it is made quiescent: yarmī. Yarmiyūna: the yāʾ made quiescent, then dropped before the quiescent wāw: yarmūna. In yarmiyāni the yāʾ has the light fatḥa, so it stays.

tasks.prompt: Why does the nūn of yaʿfūna stay after an in 2:237?
tasks.answer: Here yaʿfūna is the women's plural: its wāw is the root letter and its nūn is the sign of the feminine, not the nūn of rafʿ, so an does not drop it.

tasks.prompt: Put yarmī, yaghzū and yakhshā after lam and after lan, using al-ʿIzzī's forms.
tasks.answer: Lam yarmi, lam yaghzu, lam yakhsha: the weak letter drops for jazm. Lan yarmiya, lan yaghzuwa: the yāʾ and the wāw take a fatḥa; lan yakhshā: the alif cannot take a vowel and stays as it is.

text.original: الْمُسْتَقْبَلُ: يَرْمِي إِلَخْ، أَصْلُهُ يَرْمِيُ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْيَاءُ لِثِقَلِ الضَّمَّةِ عَلَيْهَا، وَلَا يُعَلُّ فِي مِثْلِ: يَرْمِيَانِ؛ لِأَنَّ حَرَكَتَهُ فَتْحَةٌ، وَهِيَ خَفِيفَةٌ. وَأَصْلُ يَرْمُونَ يَرْمِيُونَ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْيَاءُ، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتْ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ.
text.en: The future: yarmī “he throws” and so on, whose origin is yarmiyu: the yāʾ was made unvowelled because of the heaviness of the ḍamma on it; and it is not changed in the like of yarmiyāni “they two throw”, because its vowel is a fatḥa, and that is light. The origin of yarmūna “they throw” is yarmiyūna: the yāʾ was made unvowelled, then dropped because two unvowelled letters came together.

text.original: وَسُوِّيَ بَيْنَ الرِّجَالِ وَالنِّسَاءِ فِي مِثْلِ: يَعْفُونَ اكْتِفَاءً بِالْفَرْقِ التَّقْدِيرِيِّ؛ الْوَاوُ ضَمِيرٌ فِي الرِّجَالِ، وَفِي النِّسَاءِ أَصْلِيَّةٌ، وَالنُّونُ عَلَامَةُ التَّأْنِيثِ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ لَا تَسْقُطُ فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: ﴿إِلَّا أَنْ يَعْفُونَ﴾. وَأَصْلُ تَرْمِينَ تَرْمِيِينَ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْيَاءُ، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتْ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، وَهُوَ مُشْتَرَكٌ فِي اللَّفْظِ مَعَ جَمَاعَةِ النِّسَاءِ.
text.en: Men and women were made the same in the like of yaʿfūna “they pardon”, the implied difference being thought enough: with the men the wāw is a pronoun, and with the women it is a root letter and the nūn is the sign of the feminine; for that reason it does not fall away in His saying, Most High: illā an yaʿfūna “unless they (f.) pardon” [2:237]. The origin of tarmīna “you (f.) throw” is tarmiyīna: the yāʾ was made unvowelled, then dropped because two unvowelled letters came together; and it is shared in its sound with the plural of women.

text.original: وَإِذَا أَدْخَلْتَ الْجَازِمَ تَسْقُطُ الْيَاءُ عَلَامَةً لِلْجَزْمِ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ تَسْقُطُ فِي حَالَةِ الرَّفْعِ عَلَامَةً لِلْوَقْفِ فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَسْرِ﴾. وَتُنْصَبُ إِذَا أَدْخَلْتَ النَّاصِبَ عَلَيْهِ لِخِفَّةِ النَّصْبِ، وَلَمْ تُنْصَبْ فِي مِثْلِ: لَنْ يَخْشَى؛ لِأَنَّ الْأَلِفَ لَا تَحْتَمِلُ الْحَرَكَةَ.
text.en: When you bring in the governor of jazm, the yāʾ falls away as the sign of jazm; for that reason it falls away in the state of rafʿ as a sign of the pause, in His saying, Most High: wa-al-layli idhā yasri “and by the night when it passes” [89:4]. It takes naṣb when you bring the governor of naṣb onto it, because of the lightness of naṣb; and it did not take naṣb in the like of lan yakhshā “he will not fear”, because the alif does not bear a vowel.

lessons.title: The command irmi, the nūns of emphasis, and rāmin
body: The command irmi, “throw!”, is from irmī: “the yāʾ was dropped as the sign of jazm”, as in lam yarmi. Irmū, “throw! (men)”, is from irmiyū: the yāʾ made quiescent, then dropped before the wāw. Irmī, “throw! (a woman)”, is from irmiyī: “the root yāʾ was made unvowelled, then dropped”; the ī that remains is the pronoun.

With the heavy nūn: irmiyanna, irmiyānni, irmunna, irminna, irmiyānni, irmīnānni; with the light: irmiyan, irmun, irmin. The root yāʾ comes back in irmiyanna, where the nūn has given it a vowel, and in the dual. In irmunna and irminna the root yāʾ is gone and the pronoun's ū and ī have dropped before the nūn, the ḍamma and the kasra being enough to show them, as in iḍribunna, iḍribinna (lesson 21). Lesson 61 gives the general rule.

The active participle is rāmin, from rāmiyun. In rafʿ and jarr the yāʾ was made quiescent, the ḍamma and kasra being heavy on it, and then dropped, meeting the quiescent nūn of the tanwīn: rāmin, “a thrower”, bi-rāmin. In naṣb it stays, “because of the lightness of naṣb”: rāmiyan.
Rāmūna is from rāmiyūna: the yāʾ made quiescent and dropped, “then the mīm was given a ḍamma, because the wāw calls for the ḍamma”.

Rāmin is the type of the defective noun (al-manqūṣ) of naḥw: a noun ending in a yāʾ after a kasra, which loses the yāʾ with tanwīn in rafʿ and jarr and keeps it in naṣb. Every active participle of a defective verb behaves the same way.

terms.en: the command of the defective: irmi, with the weak letter dropped
the root yāʾ, distinct from the yāʾ of the pronoun
the noun ending in yāʾ after kasra, as rāmin
the nūn of the indefinite ending, which meets the quiescent yāʾ

tasks.prompt: Analyse irmī, “throw! (a woman)”: which yāʾ remains?
tasks.answer: Its origin is irmiyī. The root yāʾ was made quiescent and dropped; the ī that remains is the pronoun of the woman addressed.

tasks.prompt: Why is the yāʾ dropped in rāmin but kept in rāmiyan?
tasks.answer: In rafʿ and jarr the ḍamma and kasra are heavy on the yāʾ, so it is made quiescent and then drops before the quiescent nūn of the tanwīn. In naṣb the fatḥa is light, so the yāʾ keeps it: rāmiyan.

tasks.prompt: Why does rāmūna have a ḍamma on the mīm?
tasks.answer: From rāmiyūna the yāʾ was made quiescent and dropped; the mīm, which had a kasra, takes a ḍamma because the wāw that follows calls for it.

text.original: الْأَمْرُ: ارْمِ إِلَخْ، أَصْلُهُ ارْمِي، فَحُذِفَتِ الْيَاءُ عَلَامَةً لِلْجَزْمِ، فَصَارَ ارْمِ. وَأَصْلُ ارْمُوا ارْمِيُوا، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْيَاءُ، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتْ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، وَأَصْلُ ارْمِي ارْمِيِي، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْيَاءُ الْأَصْلِيَّةُ، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتْ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ.
text.en: The command: irmi “throw!” and so on, whose origin is irmī: the yāʾ was dropped as the sign of jazm, and it became irmi. The origin of irmū “throw! (m. pl.)” is irmiyū: the yāʾ was made unvowelled, then dropped because two unvowelled letters came together. The origin of irmī “throw! (f.)” is irmiyī: the root yāʾ was made unvowelled, then dropped because two unvowelled letters came together.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ بِنُونِ التَّأْكِيدِ الْمُشَدَّدَةِ: ارْمِيَنَّ ارْمِيَانِّ ارْمُنَّ ارْمِنَّ ارْمِيَانِّ ارْمِينَانِّ، وَبِالْخَفِيفَةِ: ارْمِيَنْ ارْمُنْ ارْمِنْ.
text.en: With the doubled nūn of emphasis you say: irmiyanna irmiyānni irmunna irminna irmiyānni irmīnānni “do throw!” (to one man, two, men; to one woman, two, women), and with the light: irmiyan irmun irmin.

text.original: الْفَاعِلُ: رَامٍ إِلَخْ، أَصْلُهُ رَامِيٌ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْيَاءُ فِي حَالَةِ الرَّفْعِ وَالْجَرِّ ثُمَّ حُذِفَتِ الْيَاءُ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، وَلَا تُسَكَّنُ فِي حَالَةِ النَّصْبِ لِخِفَّةِ النَّصْبِ. وَأَصْلُ رَامُونَ رَامِيُونَ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الْيَاءُ، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتْ لِاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، ثُمَّ ضُمَّ الْمِيمُ لِاسْتِدْعَاءِ الْوَاوِ الضَّمَّةَ.
text.en: The fāʿil: rāmin “throwing” and so on, whose origin is rāmiyun: the yāʾ was made unvowelled in the states of rafʿ and jarr, then the yāʾ was dropped because two unvowelled letters came together; it is not made unvowelled in the state of naṣb, because of the lightness of naṣb. The origin of rāmūna “throwing (m. pl.)” is rāmiyūna: the yāʾ was made unvowelled, then dropped because two unvowelled letters came together; then the mīm was given a ḍamma, because the wāw calls for the ḍamma.

lessons.title: Rāmiyya and marmiyy; the place, the passive, and ghazā
body: Annex the participle to yourself, “my”. The dual is rāmiyāya, “my two throwers”, in rafʿ, and rāmiyayya in naṣb and jarr, the dual's -ay merged into the yāʾ of “my”. The plural is rāmiyya, “my throwers”, in every state. In rafʿ it comes from rāmūya: the wāw of the plural and the yāʾ of “my”, “two letters of one kind in weakness”, met and were merged, the wāw becoming a yāʾ; in naṣb and jarr, rāmīya merged the same way.

The passive participle is marmiyy, “thrown”, from marmūy: the same merging, the wāw of mafʿūl turned into a yāʾ and folded into the root yāʾ, with a kasra before it. This is the mahdiyy of lessons 12 and 40. Annexed to “my”, its dual is marmiyyāya in rafʿ and marmiyyayya “with four yāʾs” in naṣb and jarr, and its plural marmiyyiyya, “also with four yāʾs, in every state”.

The noun of place is marman: by rule it should be mafʿil, from yarmī, “except that they fled from a succession of kasras” (lesson 27). The instrument is mirman. The passive is rumiya, yurmā: rumiya is unchanged, its yāʾ having the light fatḥa; yurmā is from yurmayu, the yāʾ turned into an alif after the fatḥa, “as in rumiya”.

Last: “the rule of ghazā yaghzū is like that of ramā yarmī in every state”, with a wāw where ramā has a yāʾ: ghazā, ghazaw, yaghzū, ughzu, ghāzin. “Except that they change the wāw into a yāʾ in the like of aghzaytu, following yughzī”: in the augmented forms, where the future has a kasra before the weak letter, the wāw of ghazā becomes a yāʾ throughout.
So the four yāʾs of marmiyyayya are not a puzzle: the root yāʾ, the yāʾ from the wāw of mafʿūl merged into it, the yāʾ of the dual in naṣb, and the yāʾ of “my”, merged into it.

merging two weak letters, wāw and yāʾ, as of one kind
the passive participle of the defective: marmiyy
a run of kasras, which gives marman instead of marmin

tasks.prompt: Explain rāmiyya, “my throwers”, in the state of rafʿ.
tasks.answer: Rāmūna annexed to “my” loses its nūn: rāmūya. The wāw and the yāʾ, both weak letters, meet with the first quiescent; the wāw becomes a yāʾ and is merged, and the mīm takes a kasra: rāmiyya.

tasks.prompt: Derive marmiyy from marmūy, and name the four yāʾs of marmiyyayya.
tasks.answer: The quiescent wāw of mafʿūl before the root yāʾ becomes a yāʾ and is merged, with a kasra before it: marmiyy. In marmiyyayya: the yāʾ from the wāw of mafʿūl, the root yāʾ (these two merged), the yāʾ of the dual in naṣb and jarr, and the yāʾ of “my” (these two merged).

tasks.prompt: Why is the noun of place marman, not marmin?
tasks.answer: By the rule a future with kasra gives mafʿil, but the defective flees a run of kasras (the kasra of the ʿayn, the yāʾ and the ending), so it takes mafʿal: marman.

tasks.prompt: How does ghazā differ from ramā, by the book?
tasks.answer: In nothing but its wāw for the yāʾ, “in every state”; except that the augmented forms change the wāw into a yāʾ, as aghzaytu, following yughzī, whose kasra before the weak letter calls for a yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: “My two throwers”, in rafʿ, is…
quiz.explanation: In naṣb and jarr: rāmiyayya.

quiz.prompt: Rāmiyya, “my throwers”, is used…
quiz.explanation: From rāmūya in rafʿ, rāmīya in naṣb and jarr.

quiz.prompt: The origin of marmiyy is…
quiz.explanation: Mafʿūl of r-m-y, merged.

quiz.prompt: How many yāʾs has marmiyyayya?
quiz.explanation: “With four yāʾs.”

quiz.prompt: The noun of place from ramā is…
quiz.explanation: Fleeing a run of kasras.

quiz.prompt: Rumiya is not changed because…
options: its yāʾ has the light fatḥa
quiz.explanation: Yurmā, from yurmayu, is changed.

quiz.prompt: Aghzaytu has a yāʾ…
quiz.explanation: Otherwise ghazā is like ramā in every state.

text.original: وَإِذَا أَضَفْتَ التَّثْنِيَةَ إِلَى نَفْسِكَ فَقُلْتَ: رَامِيَايَ فِي حَالَةِ الرَّفْعِ، وَرَامِيَيَّ فِي حَالَةِ النَّصْبِ وَالْجَرِّ بِإِدْغَامِ عَلَامَتِهِمَا فِي يَاءِ الْإِضَافَةِ. وَإِذَا أَضَفْتَ الْجَمْعَ إِلَى نَفْسِكَ فَقُلْتَ: رَامِيَّ فِي جَمِيعِ الْأَحْوَالِ، وَأَصْلُهُ فِي حَالَةِ الرَّفْعِ رَامُويَ، فَأُدْغِمَ؛ لِأَنَّهُ اجْتَمَعَ الْحَرْفَانِ مِنْ جِنْسٍ وَاحِدٍ فِي الْعِلِّيَّةِ، كَمَا فِي رَامِيَّ.
text.en: When you annex the dual to yourself you say rāmiyāya “my two throwers” in the state of rafʿ, and rāmiyayya in the states of naṣb and jarr, by assimilating their sign into the yāʾ of annexation. When you annex the plural to yourself you say rāmiyya “my throwers” in every state; its origin in the state of rafʿ is rāmūya, and it was assimilated, because two letters of one kind in weakness came together, as in rāmiyya.

text.original: الْمَفْعُولُ: مَرْمِيٌّ إِلَخْ، أَصْلُهُ مَرْمُويٌ، فَأُدْغِمَ كَمَا فِي رَامِيَّ. وَإِذَا أَضَفْتَ التَّثْنِيَةَ إِلَى يَاءِ الْإِضَافَةِ فَقُلْتَ: مَرْمِيَّايَ فِي حَالَةِ الرَّفْعِ، وَفِي حَالَةِ النَّصْبِ وَالْجَرِّ: مَرْمِيَّيَّ بِأَرْبَعِ يَاءَاتٍ، وَإِذَا أَضَفْتَ الْجَمْعَ إِلَى يَاءِ الْإِضَافَةِ فَقُلْتَ: مَرْمِيِّيَّ أَيْضًا بِأَرْبَعِ يَاءَاتٍ فِي كُلِّ الْأَحْوَالِ.
text.en: The mafʿūl: marmiyyun “thrown” and so on, whose origin is marmūyun; it was assimilated as in rāmiyya. When you annex the dual to the yāʾ of annexation you say marmiyyāya in the state of rafʿ, and in the states of naṣb and jarr marmiyyayya, with four yāʾs; and when you annex the plural to the yāʾ of annexation you say marmiyyiyya, also with four yāʾs, in every state.

text.original: الْمَوْضِعُ: مَرْمًى، الْأَصْلُ فِيهِ أَنْ يُؤْتَى بِهِ عَلَى وَزْنِ مَفْعِلٍ، إِلَّا أَنَّهُمْ فَرُّوا عَنْ تَوَالِي الْكَسَرَاتِ. الْآلَةُ: مِرْمًى. الْمَجْهُولُ: رُمِيَ يُرْمَى إِلَخْ، وَلَمْ يُعَلَّ رُمِيَ لِخِفَّةِ الْفَتْحَةِ، وَأَصْلُ يُرْمَى يُرْمَيُ، فَقُلِبَتِ الْيَاءُ أَلِفًا كَمَا فِي رُمِيَ. وَحُكْمُ غَزَا يَغْزُو مِثْلُ رَمَى يَرْمِي فِي كُلِّ الْأَحْوَالِ، إِلَّا أَنَّهُمْ يُبْدِلُونَ الْوَاوَ يَاءً فِي نَحْوِ: أَغْزَيْتُ تَبَعًا لِيُغْزِي.
text.en: The place: marman; the rule for it is that it be brought on the measure mafʿil, except that they fled from a succession of kasras. The instrument: mirman. The passive: rumiya yurmā and so on; rumiya was not changed, because of the lightness of the fatḥa; the origin of yurmā is yurmayu: the yāʾ was changed into an alif, as in rumiya. The rule of ghazā yaghzū “to raid” is like that of ramā yarmī in every state, except that they change the wāw into a yāʾ in the like of aghzaytu, following yughzī.

lessons.title: The letters of substitution: the hamza
body: The yāʾ of aghzaytu stands for a wāw, and that leads the book to a list of all the letters that can stand for others: the letters of substitution (ibdāl), gathered in the phrase istanjadahu yawma ṣāla Zuṭṭun, “he called him to help on the day the Zuṭṭ attacked”. Fifteen entries follow, one for each letter, telling what it replaces and how.

Each case is marked “necessary and regular” (wujūban muṭṭaridan), “optional and regular” (jawāzan muṭṭaridan), or left unmarked; the book ends the list by saying that the unmarked ones “are allowed but not regular”: found in some words, not a rule to apply. Keep the three kinds apart, and you can use the list.

The hamza first. It stands, necessarily and regularly, for an alif, as in ṣaḥrāʾ, “desert”: its hamza was an alif, like the alif of sakrā, and became a hamza at the end of the word after an added alif. The proof: the plural is ṣaḥārā, with no hamza; had the hamza been original, it would show in the plural in some form. It stands, necessarily, for a wāw: awāṣil, “ties”, to avoid wāws at the start; qāʾil (lesson 51); kisāʾ, the wāw having taken several vowels. And for a yāʾ: bāʾiʿ, “seller”.

Optionally and regularly it stands for a wāw with ḍamma: ujūh for wujūh, “faces”, the ḍamma being heavy on the wāw. Unmarked, that is, allowed in some words: for another wāw, ishāḥ for wishāḥ, “sash”; for a yāʾ, adayhi for yadayhi, “his two hands”; for a hāʾ, māʾ, “water”, from māh, which is why the plural is miyāh; for an alif, as in the reading wa-lā al-ḍaʾllīna (1:7) for al-ḍāllīna; and for an ʿayn, ubāb for ʿubāb, “a surge”.
The list is long, but most of it explains words you already know: māʾ and miyāh, qāʾil, ṣaḥrāʾ. Read it as a key to such words, not as a set of rules to apply.

terms.en: substitution: one letter put in the place of another
necessary and regular: a rule
optional and regular: allowed wherever it fits
allowed but not regular: found in some words

examples.en: istanjadahu yawma ṣāla Zuṭṭun: the letters of substitution
ṣaḥrāʾ, ṣaḥārā: the hamza from an alif, not original
ujūh for wujūh: optional and regular
māʾ from māh: hence the plural miyāh
