tasks.prompt: What are the three kinds of substitution, and how does the book mark them?
tasks.answer: Necessary and regular (wujūban muṭṭaridan); optional and regular (jawāzan muṭṭaridan); and, for the cases left unmarked, allowed but not regular, found only in some words.

tasks.prompt: How does the book prove that the hamza of ṣaḥrāʾ was an alif?
tasks.answer: The plural is ṣaḥārā, with no hamza. Had the hamza been original, it would have been allowed in the plural in some form (as it is with khaṭīʾa); so it was an alif, like that of sakrā, turned into a hamza at the end after an added alif.

tasks.prompt: Why is the plural of māʾ miyāh?
tasks.answer: The hamza of māʾ stands for a hāʾ: the origin is māh. The plural brings back the root hāʾ: miyāh.

quiz.prompt: The letters of substitution are gathered in…
quiz.explanation: Fifteen letters.

quiz.prompt: Unmarked cases in the list are…
quiz.explanation: The book says so at the end of the list.

quiz.prompt: The hamza of ṣaḥrāʾ stands for…
quiz.explanation: Its plural ṣaḥārā shows no hamza.

quiz.prompt: Ujūh for wujūh is…
quiz.explanation: The ḍamma is heavy on the wāw.

quiz.prompt: The hamza of māʾ stands for…
quiz.explanation: Hence miyāh.

quiz.prompt: The hamza of bāʾiʿ stands for…
quiz.explanation: From b-y-ʿ, necessarily and regularly.

quiz.prompt: Awāṣil has a hamza at the start…
quiz.explanation: Necessary and regular.

text.original: مَعَ أَنَّ الْيَاءَ مِنْ حُرُوفِ الْإِبْدَالِ، وَحُرُوفُهَا: «اسْتَنْجَدَهُ يَوْمَ صَالَ زُطٌّ». الْهَمْزَةُ: أُبْدِلَتْ وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا مِنَ الْأَلِفِ فِي نَحْوِ: صَحْرَاءَ؛ لِأَنَّ هَمْزَتَهَا أَلِفٌ فِي الْأَصْلِ كَأَلِفِ سَكْرَى، ثُمَّ جُعِلَتْ هَمْزَةً لِوُقُوعِهَا طَرَفًا بَعْدَ أَلِفٍ زَائِدَةٍ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ لَا يَجُوزُ جَعْلُهَا هَمْزَةً فِي نَحْوِ: صَحَارَى، يَعْنِي: لَوْ كَانَتْ فِي الْأَصْلِ هَمْزَةً لَجَازَ صَحَارِئُ بِالْهَمْزَةِ فِي صُورَةٍ مَا، كَمَا يَجُوزُ فِي نَحْوِ: خَطِيئَةٍ.
text.en: [This,] besides the yāʾ being among the letters of substitution (ibdāl), whose letters are [gathered in] istanjadahu yawma ṣāla Zuṭṭun “he called him to help on the day the Zuṭṭ attacked”. The hamza: it is substituted, necessarily and regularly, for the alif in the like of ṣaḥrāʾa “desert”, because its hamza is an alif in the origin, like the alif of sakrā “drunk (f.)”; then it was made a hamza because it stands at the end after an added alif; for that reason it is not allowed to make it a hamza in the like of ṣaḥārā “deserts”; that is, if it were a hamza in the origin, ṣaḥāriʾu with the hamza would be allowed in some form, as it is allowed in the like of khaṭīʾatin “a sin”.

text.original: وَمِنَ الْوَاوِ وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا فِي نَحْوِ: أَوَاصِلَ فِرَارًا عَنِ اجْتِمَاعِ الْوَاوَاتِ، وَنَحْوِ: قَائِلٍ كَمَا مَرَّ، وَنَحْوِ: أَدْؤُرٍ لِثِقَلِ الضَّمَّةِ عَلَى الْوَاوِ، وَفِي نَحْوِ: كِسَاءٍ لِوُقُوعِ الْحَرَكَاتِ الْمُخْتَلِفَةِ عَلَى الْوَاوِ، وَمِنَ الْيَاءِ وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا، نَحْوُ: بَائِعٍ كَمَا مَرَّ.
text.en: And for the wāw, necessarily and regularly, in the like of awāṣila “ties”, fleeing from the coming together of wāws; the like of qāʾilin “saying”, as has passed; the like of adʾurin “houses”, because of the heaviness of the ḍamma on the wāw; and in the like of kisāʾin “a garment”, because different vowels fall on the wāw. And for the yāʾ, necessarily and regularly, as bāʾiʿin “selling”, as has passed.

text.original: وَجَوَازًا مُطَّرِدًا عَنِ الْوَاوِ الْمَضْمُومَةِ، نَحْوُ: أُجُوهٍ لِثِقَلِ الضَّمَّةِ عَلَى الْوَاوِ، وَمِنَ الْوَاوِ الْغَيْرِ الْمَضْمُومَةِ، نَحْوُ: إِشَاحٍ، وَأَحِّدْ أَحِّدْ فِي الْحَدِيثِ، وَمِنَ الْيَاءِ، نَحْوُ: قَطَعَ اللَّهُ أَدَيْهِ؛ لِثِقَلِ الْحَرَكَةِ عَلَى الْيَاءِ، وَمِنَ الْهَاءِ، نَحْوُ: مَاءٍ، أَصْلُهُ مَاهٌ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ يَجِيءُ جَمْعُهُ مِيَاهٌ، وَمِنَ الْأَلِفِ فِي نَحْوِ: هَيَّجَتْ شَوْقَ الْمُشْتَئِقِ، وَنَحْوِ قِرَاءَةِ مَنْ قَرَأَ: ﴿وَلَا الضَّأْلِّينَ﴾، وَمِنَ الْعَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: أُبَابٌ بَحْرٌ ضَاحِكٌ زَهُوقٌ؛ لِاتِّحَادِ مَخْرَجِهِمَا.
text.en: And optionally and regularly for the wāw with a ḍamma, as ujūhin “faces”, because of the heaviness of the ḍamma on the wāw; for the wāw without a ḍamma, as ishāḥin “a sash” and aḥḥid aḥḥid “make it one, make it one!” in the ḥadīth; for the yāʾ, as qaṭaʿa Allāhu adayhi “may God cut off his hands”, because of the heaviness of the vowel on the yāʾ; for the hāʾ, as māʾin “water”, whose origin is māhun, and for that reason its plural comes as miyāhun; for the alif, in the like of hayyajat shawqa al-mushtaʾiqi “she stirred the longing of the one who longs” and the like of the reading of those who read wa-lā al-ḍaʾllīna “nor those who go astray” [1:7]; and for the ʿayn, as ubābun baḥrun ḍāḥikun zahūqun “a surge, a sea laughing [with foam], rising high”, because their point of articulation is one.

lessons.title: Substitution: sīn, tāʾ, nūn, jīm, dāl and hāʾ
lessons.arabic: إِبْدَالُ السِّينِ وَالتَّاءِ وَالنُّونِ وَالْجِيمِ وَالدَّالِ وَالْهَاءِ
lessons.transliteration: ibdāl al-sīn wa-l-tāʾ wa-l-nūn wa-l-jīm wa-l-dāl wa-l-hāʾ
body: None of these entries is marked, so all are “allowed but not regular”, except where the book says otherwise. Each gives the reason: the two letters are near in their point of articulation, or share a quality, such as whispering or voice.

The sīn stands for a tāʾ in istakhadha, “he took”, which is ittakhadha for Sībawayh: the two are near in whispering. The tāʾ stands for a wāw in tujāh, “facing”, and ukht, “sister”, the points of articulation being near; for a yāʾ in thintān, “two (f.)”, from thinyān, and asnatū, “they suffered drought”, “so that the vowel does not fall on the yāʾ”; for a sīn in sitt, “six”, from sids, and in the rajaz line ʿAmru bnu Yarbūʿin shirāru al-nāti, “ʿAmr ibn Yarbūʿ, the worst of people”, al-nāt for al-nās; for a ṣād in luṣūt, “thieves”, for luṣūṣ; for a bāʾ in al-dhaʿālit, “rags”, for al-dhaʿālib.

The nūn stands for a wāw in ṣanʿānī, “of Ṣanʿāʾ”, the nūn being near the weak letters, and for a lām in laʿanna, “perhaps”, for laʿalla. The jīm stands for a doubled yāʾ, Abū ʿAlijj for Abū ʿAlī, “so that different vowels do not fall on the yāʾ”, and, by analogy, for a single one, in the line lāhumma in kunta qabilta ḥajjatij, “O God, if You have accepted my pilgrimage”, ḥajjatij for ḥajjatī.

The dāl stands for a tāʾ in fuzdu, “I won”, and ijdamaʿū, “they gathered”, for fuztu and ijtamaʿū. The hāʾ stands for a hamza in haraqtu, “I poured out”, for araqtu; for an alif in pause, ḥayyahalah and anah; and for a yāʾ in hādhihi amatu Allāhi, from hādhī: the hāʾ, like the weak letters, is a hidden, breathy sound.

Many of these are dialect forms or poetic licences. Their use for the student of a text is to recognise a familiar word behind an unfamiliar spelling: sitt, thintān and ukht are everyday words, and the rest are traces of the old dialects that the grammarians recorded.

terms.en: nearness in the point of articulation, a cause of substitution
whispering and voice, qualities shared by letters
hiddenness: what the hāʾ shares with the weak letters
a common metre of popular and didactic verse

examples.en: istakhadha, from ittakhadha (Sībawayh)
thintān from thinyān: the tāʾ for a yāʾ
Abū ʿAlijj for Abū ʿAlī: the jīm for a doubled yāʾ
fuzdu, ijdamaʿū: the dāl for a tāʾ

tasks.prompt: Give the origin of sitt and thintān and the letter substituted in each.
tasks.answer: Sitt is from sids: the sīn and the dāl became tāʾs (near in whispering and in articulation) and were merged. Thintān is from thinyān: the yāʾ became a tāʾ, so that the vowel does not fall on the yāʾ.

tasks.prompt: What does the jīm replace in Abū ʿAlijj and in ḥajjatij, and why?
tasks.answer: In Abū ʿAlijj it replaces the doubled yāʾ of ʿAlī, so that different vowels do not fall on the yāʾ. In ḥajjatij it replaces the single yāʾ of “my”, by analogy with the doubled.

tasks.prompt: Why can the hāʾ stand for the yāʾ in hādhihi?
tasks.answer: Because the hāʾ is akin to the weak letters in hiddenness (a faint, breathy sound), so it can take the place of the yāʾ of hādhī.

quiz.prompt: Haraqtu stands for…
quiz.explanation: The hāʾ for a hamza.

text.original: السِّينُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ التَّاءِ، نَحْوُ: اسْتَخَذَ، أَصْلُهُ اتَّخَذَ عِنْدَ سِيبَوَيْهِ؛ لِقُرْبِهِمَا فِي الْمَهْمُوسَةِ. التَّاءُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ الْوَاوِ، نَحْوُ: تُجَاهٍ وَأُخْتٍ؛ لِقُرْبِ مَخْرَجِهِمَا، وَمِنَ الْيَاءِ، نَحْوُ: ثِنْتَانِ، أَصْلُهُ ثِنْيَانِ، وَأَسْنَتُوا حَتَّى لَا يَقَعَ الْحَرَكَةُ عَلَى الْيَاءِ، وَمِنَ السِّينِ، نَحْوُ: سِتٍّ، أَصْلُهُ سِدْسٌ، وَنَحْوُ: عَمْرُو بْنُ يَرْبُوعٍ شِرَارُ النَّاتِ، وَمِنَ الصَّادِ، نَحْوُ: لُصُوتٍ؛ لِقُرْبِهِنَّ فِي الْمَهْمُوسَةِ، وَمِنَ الْبَاءِ، نَحْوُ: الذَّعَالِتِ.
text.en: The sīn: it is substituted for the tāʾ, as istakhadha “he took”, whose origin is ittakhadha according to Sībawayh, because the two are near each other in the whispering. The tāʾ: it is substituted for the wāw, as tujāhin “facing” and ukhtin “sister”, because their points of articulation are near; for the yāʾ, as thintāni “two (f.)”, whose origin is thinyāni, and asnatū “they suffered a year of drought”, so that the vowel does not fall on the yāʾ; for the sīn, as sittin “six”, whose origin is sidsun, and as ʿAmru bnu Yarbūʿin shirāru al-nāti “ʿAmr ibn Yarbūʿ, the worst of people”; for the ṣād, as luṣūtin “thieves”, because they are near each other in the whispering; and for the bāʾ, as al-dhaʿāliti “the rags”.

text.original: النُّونُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ الْوَاوِ فِي نَحْوِ: صَنْعَانِيٍّ لِقُرْبِ النُّونِ مِنْ حُرُوفِ الْعِلَّةِ، وَمِنَ اللَّامِ، نَحْوُ: لَعَنَّ؛ لِقُرْبِهِمَا فِي الْمَجْهُورِيَّةِ. الْجِيمُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ الْيَاءِ الْمُشَدَّدَةِ، نَحْوُ: أَبُو عَلِجٍّ؛ حَتَّى لَا يَقَعَ الْحَرَكَاتُ الْمُخْتَلِفَةُ عَلَى الْيَاءِ، وَمِنْ غَيْرِ الْمُشَدَّدَةِ حَمْلًا عَلَى الْمُشَدَّدَةِ، نَحْوُ: لَاهُمَّ إِنْ كُنْتَ قَبِلْتَ حَجَّتِجْ * فَلَا يَزَالُ شَاحِجٌ يَأْتِيكَ بِجْ.
text.en: The nūn: it is substituted for the wāw in the like of ṣanʿāniyyin “of Ṣanʿāʾ”, because the nūn is near the letters of weakness; and for the lām, as laʿanna “perhaps”, because the two are near each other in the voicing. The jīm: it is substituted for the doubled yāʾ, as Abū ʿAlijjin [for Abū ʿAlī], so that different vowels do not fall on the yāʾ; and for the undoubled [yāʾ], by analogy with the doubled, as lāhumma in kunta qabilta ḥajjatij / fa-lā yazālu shāḥijun yaʾtīka bij “O God, if You have accepted my pilgrimage, then a braying [mount] will not cease to bring me to You”.

text.original: الدَّالُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ التَّاءِ، نَحْوُ: فُزْدُ، وَاجْدَمَعُوا؛ لِقُرْبِ مَخْرَجِهِمَا. الْهَاءُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ الْهَمْزَةِ، نَحْوُ: هَرَقْتُ، وَمِنَ الْأَلِفِ، نَحْوُ: حَيَّهَلَهْ وَأَنَهْ، وَمِنَ الْيَاءِ فِي: هَذِهِ أَمَةُ اللَّهِ؛ لِمُنَاسَبَتِهَا بِحُرُوفِ الْعِلَّةِ فِي الْخَفَاءِ، وَمِنْ ثَمَّةَ لَا تَمْتَنِعُ الْإِمَالَةُ فِي مِثْلِ: يَضْرِبُهَا، وَتَمْتَنِعُ فِي: كِلْتَ عِنَبَا.
text.en: The dāl: it is substituted for the tāʾ, as fuzdu “I won” and ijdamaʿū “they gathered”, because their points of articulation are near. The hāʾ: it is substituted for the hamza, as haraqtu “I poured out”; for the alif, as ḥayyahalah “come on!” and anah “I”; and for the yāʾ, in hādhihi amatu Allāhi “this is the handmaid of God”, because it is akin to the letters of weakness in being hidden; for that reason the imāla is not prevented in the like of yaḍribuhā “he hits her”, and it is prevented in kilta ʿinabā “you measured grapes”.

lessons.title: Substitution: yāʾ, wāw, mīm, ṣād, alif, lām, zāy and ṭāʾ
body: The hāʾ ends its entry with one regular rule: it stands, necessarily, for the tāʾ marbūṭa in pause, Ṭalḥah, ẓulmah, “to distinguish it from the tāʾ that is in the verb” (ḍarabat, which keeps its t). The yāʾ stands, necessarily and regularly, for an alif in mufaytīḥ, “a little key”, the diminutive of miftāḥ; for a wāw after a kasra in mīqāt, “appointed time”; optionally for a hamza in dhīb, “wolf”; and for one of two like letters in taqaḍḍī al-bāzī (lesson 28). Unmarked, it stands for a nūn (anāsiyy, dīnār), an ʿayn (ḍafādī for ḍafādiʿ, “frogs”), a bāʾ (al-thaʿālī, “the foxes”), a sīn (al-sādī, “the sixth”) and a thāʾ (al-thālī, “the third”), the kasra before them calling for it.

The wāw stands, necessarily, for an alif in ḍawārib, the plural of ḍāriba; for a yāʾ after a ḍamma in mūqin, “certain”; and optionally for a hamza in lūm. The mīm stands for a wāw in fam, “mouth”, for a lām in the ḥadīth said in the dialect of Ḥimyar, laysa mina am-birri am-ṣiyāmu fī am-safari, “fasting on a journey is not of righteousness”, for a nūn in ʿambar and al-banām, and for a bāʾ in rātiman for rātiban.

The ṣād stands for a sīn in aṣbagha, “he made ample”. The alif stands, necessarily, for the wāw and the yāʾ in qāla and bāʿa, and optionally for a hamza in rās. The lām stands for a nūn in uṣaylāl, “late afternoon”, and for a ḍād in ilṭajaʿa, “he lay on his side”. The zāy stands for a sīn in yazdulu, and for a ṣād in Ḥātim's saying hākadhā fazdī anah, “this is how I bleed [a camel]”.

The ṭāʾ, last, stands “necessarily and regularly” for the tāʾ of iftaʿala after the covered letters, iṣṭabara (lesson 33), and unmarked in faḥaṣṭu, “I searched”. Then the closing note: “the places among the forms mentioned that were not qualified are allowed but not regular”.

What to carry away: the regular substitutions are few and you have met them all as rules of iʿlāl and idghām: alif for wāw and yāʾ (qāla), yāʾ for wāw after kasra (mīqāt), wāw for yāʾ after ḍamma (mūqin), hamza in qāʾil and ṣaḥrāʾ, ṭāʾ in iṣṭabara, hāʾ in pause. The rest is a record of dialects.

terms.en: the hāʾ said for the tāʾ marbūṭa in pause
the diminutive, as mufaytīḥ
the dialect of Ḥimyar, with am- for the article
regular substitution, as against the merely allowed

examples.en: Ṭalḥah, ẓulmah: the hāʾ for the tāʾ in pause
mīqāt, mūqin: yāʾ for wāw after kasra, wāw for yāʾ after ḍamma

examples.arabic: لَيْسَ مِنَ امْبِرِّ امْصِيَامُ فِي امْسَفَرِ
examples.en: the mīm for the lām of the article, in the dialect of Ḥimyar

tasks.prompt: Why is the tāʾ marbūṭa said as hāʾ in pause, by the book's reason?
tasks.answer: To distinguish it from the tāʾ of the verb, as in ḍarabat, which keeps its t in pause.

tasks.prompt: Give the two necessary substitutions between wāw and yāʾ, with the book's examples.
tasks.answer: The yāʾ for a wāw after a kasra: mīqāt, from w-q-t. The wāw for a yāʾ after a ḍamma: mūqin, from y-q-n.

tasks.prompt: Sort these substitutions into “necessary” and “allowed”: the alif of qāla, the mīm of fam, the ṭāʾ of iṣṭabara, the zāy of yazdulu.
tasks.answer: Necessary: the alif of qāla (for wāw) and the ṭāʾ of iṣṭabara (for the tāʾ of iftaʿala). Allowed, not regular: the mīm of fam (for wāw) and the zāy of yazdulu (for sīn).

quiz.prompt: Ṭalḥah in pause has a hāʾ…
options: to tell it from the tāʾ of the verb
quiz.explanation: Necessary and regular.

quiz.prompt: Mufaytīḥ has a yāʾ for…
quiz.explanation: In the diminutive.

quiz.prompt: Mīqāt has a yāʾ for…
quiz.explanation: From w-q-t.

quiz.prompt: Mūqin has a wāw for…
quiz.explanation: From y-q-n.

quiz.prompt: In am-ṣiyām the mīm stands for…
quiz.explanation: The dialect of Ḥimyar.

quiz.prompt: The alif of qāla and bāʿa is a substitution that is…
quiz.explanation: For the wāw and the yāʾ.

text.original: وَمِنَ التَّاءِ وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا فِي نَحْوِ: طَلْحَهْ وَظُلْمَهْ لِلْفَرْقِ بَيْنَهَا وَبَيْنَ التَّاءِ الَّتِي فِي الْفِعْلِ. الْيَاءُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ الْأَلِفِ وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا، نَحْوُ: مُفَيْتِيحٍ، وَمِنَ الْوَاوِ وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا، نَحْوُ: مِيقَاتٍ لِكَسْرَةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، وَمِنَ الْهَمْزَةِ جَوَازًا مُطَّرِدًا، نَحْوُ: ذِيبٍ، وَمِنْ أَحَدِ حَرْفَيِ التَّضْعِيفِ، نَحْوُ: تَقَضِّي الْبَازِي كَمَا مَرَّ.
text.en: And for the tāʾ, necessarily and regularly, in the like of Ṭalḥah “Ṭalḥa” and ẓulmah “darkness”, to distinguish it from the tāʾ that is in the verb. The yāʾ: it is substituted for the alif, necessarily and regularly, as mufaytīḥin “a little key”; for the wāw, necessarily and regularly, as mīqātin “an appointed time”, because of the kasra before it; for the hamza, optionally and regularly, as dhībin “wolf”; and for one of the two letters of doubling, as taqaḍḍī al-bāzī “the swooping of the falcon”, as has passed.

text.original: وَمِنَ النُّونِ، نَحْوُ: أَنَاسِيَّ وَدِينَارٍ؛ لِقُرْبِ الْيَاءِ مِنَ النُّونِ، وَمِنَ الْعَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: ضَفَادِي لِثِقَلِ الْعَيْنِ وَكَسْرَةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، وَمِنَ التَّاءِ، نَحْوُ: وَأَيْتُ، أَصْلُهُ وَاوٌ، وَمِنَ الْبَاءِ، نَحْوُ: الثَّعَالِي، وَمِنَ السِّينِ، نَحْوُ: السَّادِي، وَمِنَ الثَّاءِ، نَحْوُ: الثَّالِي، لِكَسْرَةِ مَا قَبْلَهُنَّ.
text.en: And for the nūn, as anāsiyya “people” and dīnārin “dinar”, because the yāʾ is near the nūn; for the ʿayn, as ḍafādī “frogs”, because of the heaviness of the ʿayn and the kasra before it; for the tāʾ, as waʾaytu, whose origin is wāwun; for the bāʾ, as al-thaʿālī “the foxes”; for the sīn, as al-sādī “the sixth”; and for the thāʾ, as al-thālī “the third”; because of the kasra before them.

text.original: الْوَاوُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ الْأَلِفِ وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا، نَحْوُ: ضَوَارِبَ؛ لِقُرْبِهِمَا فِي الْعِلِّيَّةِ وَاجْتِمَاعِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، وَمِنَ الْيَاءِ وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا، نَحْوُ: مُوقِنٍ لِضَمَّةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، وَمِنَ الْهَمْزَةِ جَوَازًا مُطَّرِدًا، نَحْوُ: لُومٍ كَمَا مَرَّ.
text.en: The wāw: it is substituted for the alif, necessarily and regularly, as ḍawāriba “women who hit”, because the two are near each other in being weak and because two unvowelled letters come together; for the yāʾ, necessarily and regularly, as mūqinin “certain”, because of the ḍamma before it; and for the hamza, optionally and regularly, as lūmin “meanness”, as has passed.

text.original: الْمِيمُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ الْوَاوِ، نَحْوُ: فَمٍ؛ لِاتِّحَادِ مَخْرَجِهِمَا، وَمِنَ اللَّامِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ: «لَيْسَ مِنَ امْبِرِّ امْصِيَامُ فِي امْسَفَرِ»؛ لِقُرْبِهِمَا فِي الْمَجْهُورِيَّةِ، وَمِنَ النُّونِ السَّاكِنَةِ، نَحْوُ: عَمْبَرٍ، وَمِنَ الْمُتَحَرِّكَةِ، نَحْوُ: وَكَفِّكِ الْمُخَضَّبِ الْبَنَامِ؛ لِقُرْبِهِمَا فِي الْمَجْهُورِيَّةِ، وَمِنَ الْبَاءِ، نَحْوُ: مَا زِلْتُ رَاتِمًا؛ لِاتِّحَادِ مَخْرَجِهِمَا.
text.en: The mīm: it is substituted for the wāw, as famin “mouth”, because their point of articulation is one; for the lām, as in his saying, peace be upon him: laysa mina am-birri am-ṣiyāmu fī am-safari “fasting on a journey is not of righteousness”, because the two are near each other in the voicing; for the unvowelled nūn, as ʿambarin “ambergris”; and for the vowelled one, as wa-kaffiki al-mukhaḍḍabi al-banāmi “and your hand with the dyed fingertips”, because they are near each other in the voicing; and for the bāʾ, as mā ziltu rātiman “I kept standing firm”, because their point of articulation is one.

text.original: الصَّادُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ السِّينِ، نَحْوُ: أَصْبَغَ؛ لِقُرْبِ مَخْرَجِهِمَا. الْأَلِفُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنْ أُخْتَيْهَا وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا، نَحْوُ: قَالَ وَبَاعَ، وَمِنَ الْهَمْزَةِ جَوَازًا مُطَّرِدًا، نَحْوُ: رَاسٍ كَمَا مَرَّ. اللَّامُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ النُّونِ، نَحْوُ: أُصَيْلَالٍ، وَمِنَ الضَّادِ، نَحْوُ: الْطَجَعَ؛ لِاتِّحَادِهِنَّ فِي الْمَجْهُورِيَّةِ.
text.en: The ṣād: it is substituted for the sīn, as aṣbagha “he made ample”, because their points of articulation are near. The alif: it is substituted for its two sisters, necessarily and regularly, as qāla “he said” and bāʿa “he sold”; and for the hamza, optionally and regularly, as rāsin “head”, as has passed. The lām: it is substituted for the nūn, as uṣaylālin “late afternoon”; and for the ḍād, as ilṭajaʿa “he lay on his side”; because they are one in the voicing.

text.original: الزَّاءُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ السِّينِ، نَحْوُ: يَزْدُلُ، وَمِنَ الصَّادِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِ حَاتِمٍ: هَكَذَا فَزْدِي أَنَهْ. الطَّاءُ: أُبْدِلَتْ مِنَ التَّاءِ وُجُوبًا مُطَّرِدًا فِي افْتَعَلَ، نَحْوُ: اصْطَبَرَ، وَفِي فَحَصْطُ؛ لِقُرْبِ مَخْرَجِهِمَا. وَالْمَوْضِعُ الَّذِي لَمْ يُقَيَّدْ مِنَ الصُّوَرِ الْمَذْكُورَةِ يَكُونُ جَائِزًا غَيْرَ مُطَّرِدٍ.
text.en: The zāy: it is substituted for the sīn, as yazdulu “he lets down”, and for the ṣād, as in the saying of Ḥātim: hākadhā fazdī anah “this is how I bleed [a camel]”. The ṭāʾ: it is substituted for the tāʾ, necessarily and regularly, in iftaʿala, as iṣṭabara “he was patient”, and in faḥaṣṭu “I searched”, because their points of articulation are near. The places among the forms mentioned that were not qualified are allowed [but] not regular.

lessons.title: The lafīf: waqā and ṭawā, and the nūns of emphasis
body: The seventh chapter takes the verb with two weak letters, the lafīf, “wrapped”, “because the two letters of weakness are wrapped together in it”. It is of two kinds. The separated (mafrūq), weak in fāʾ and lām, as waqā yaqī, “to guard”: “the rule of their fāʾ is like the rule of waʿada yaʿidu, and the rule of their lām like the rule of ramā yarmī”. The fāʾ drops in the future as in yaʿidu; the lām behaves as in yarmī.

So the command of waqā is a single letter, qi, “guard!”: the wāw dropped as in ʿid, the yāʾ as in irmi. Its persons are qi, qiyā, qū, qī, qiyā, qīna; with the heavy nūn qiyanna, qiyānni, qunna, qinna, qiyānni, qīnānni; with the light qiyan, qun, qin. The doer is wāqin, the one done to mawqiyy, the place mawqan, the instrument mīqan, and the passive wuqiya, yūqā.

The joined (maqrūn), weak in ʿayn and lām, as ṭawā yaṭwī, “to fold”: “their rule is like the rule of the defective, and their ʿayn is not changed”, for the reason of lesson 46: two changes would meet. Its command is iṭwi, iṭwiyā, iṭwū, iṭwī, iṭwiyā, iṭwīna; with the heavy nūn iṭwiyanna, iṭwiyānni, iṭwunna, iṭwinna, iṭwiyānni, iṭwīnānni. Rawiya yarwā, “to drink one's fill”, makes irwayanna, irwayānni, irwawunna, irwayinna, irwayānni, irwaynānni.

Then the book gathers the rule for the nūns of emphasis in the defective and the lafīf: look at the weak letter before the nūn. If it is a root letter, dropped in the singular command, it comes back, “because its dropping was for the sukūn, and that has gone”, and it takes a fatḥa: iṭwiyanna, ughzuwanna, irwayanna. If it is a pronoun (the wāw of the men, the yāʾ of the woman), look at the letter before it: after a fatḥa the pronoun stays and takes a vowel, irwawunna, irwayinna, as in wa-lā tansawu al-faḍla baynakum, “and do not forget generosity between you” (2:237); after any other vowel it drops, iṭwunna, iṭwinna, as in ughzū al-qawma, “raid the people!”.
With that one rule every command with a nūn in chapters six and seven can be made: irmiyanna and irmunna, rayanna and rawunna, qiyanna and qunna.

terms.en: the verb with two weak root letters
the separated lafīf: weak in fāʾ and lām, waqā
the joined lafīf: weak in ʿayn and lām, ṭawā
bringing back the dropped root letter before the nūn

tasks.prompt: Why is the command of waqā a single letter?
tasks.answer: Its fāʾ (wāw) drops as in ʿid, the mithāl's command, and its lām (yāʾ) drops for the jazm, as in irmi; only the qāf with its kasra remains.

tasks.prompt: Why does the wāw of ṭawā never change?
tasks.answer: Its lām is already changed (into an alif, or dropped); changing the ʿayn too would bring two changes into one word, which the language avoids (Ibn Jinnī's condition).

tasks.prompt: Apply the rule of the nūns: make the commands with the heavy nūn of ṭawā for one man and for men, and explain.
tasks.answer: For one man the root yāʾ, dropped in iṭwi, comes back with a fatḥa: iṭwiyanna. For men the weak letter is the wāw of the pronoun after a ḍamma, so it drops before the nūn: iṭwunna.

tasks.prompt: Why irwawunna for men, but iṭwunna?
tasks.answer: In both the wāw is the pronoun. In irwawunna the letter before it has a fatḥa, so the wāw stays and takes a ḍamma (as tansawu); in iṭwunna the letter before it does not have a fatḥa, so the wāw drops.

quiz.prompt: The separated lafīf is weak in…
quiz.explanation: Waqā: w-q-y.

quiz.prompt: The fāʾ of waqā behaves like that of…
quiz.explanation: It drops in the future: yaqī.

quiz.prompt: The command of waqā to one man is…
quiz.explanation: A single letter.

quiz.prompt: The joined lafīf is like…
quiz.explanation: Ṭawā yaṭwī, like ramā yarmī.

quiz.prompt: Before the nūn of emphasis, a dropped root letter…
quiz.explanation: Its dropping was for the sukūn, now gone.

quiz.prompt: A pronoun wāw after a ḍamma, before the nūn…
quiz.explanation: Iṭwunna, as ughzū al-qawma.

quiz.prompt: Wa-lā tansawu al-faḍla shows the pronoun…
options: kept with a vowel after a fatḥa
quiz.explanation: The model for irwawunna.

text.original: يُقَالُ لَهُ: لَفِيفٌ؛ لِلَفِّ حَرْفَيِ الْعِلَّةِ فِيهِ. وَهُوَ عَلَى ضَرْبَيْنِ: مَفْرُوقٍ وَمَقْرُونٍ. الْمَفْرُوقُ مِثْلُ: وَقَى يَقِي، حُكْمُ فَائِهِمَا كَحُكْمِ وَعَدَ يَعِدُ، وَحُكْمُ لَامِهِمَا كَحُكْمِ رَمَى يَرْمِي، وَكَذَلِكَ حُكْمُ أَخَوَاتِهِمَا. الْأَمْرُ: قِ قِيَا قُوا قِي قِيَا قِينَ، وَبِنُونِ التَّأْكِيدِ: قِيَنَّ قِيَانِّ قُنَّ قِنَّ قِيَانِّ قِينَانِّ، وَبِالْخَفِيفَةِ: قِيَنْ قُنْ قِنْ. الْفَاعِلُ: وَاقٍ، وَالْمَفْعُولُ: مَوْقِيٌّ، وَالْمَوْضِعُ: مَوْقًى، وَالْآلَةُ: مِيقًى، الْمَجْهُولُ: وُقِيَ يُوقَى إِلَخْ.
text.en: It is called lafīf “wrapped”, because the two letters of weakness are wrapped together in it. It is of two kinds: separated (mafrūq) and joined (maqrūn). The separated is like waqā yaqī “to guard”: the rule of their fāʾ is like the rule of waʿada yaʿidu, and the rule of their lām like the rule of ramā yarmī; and such too is the rule of their sisters. The command: qi qiyā qū qī qiyā qīna “guard!” (to one man, two, men; to one woman, two, women); with the nūn of emphasis: qiyanna qiyānni qunna qinna qiyānni qīnānni; and with the light: qiyan qun qin. The fāʿil: wāqin; the mafʿūl: mawqiyyun; the place: mawqan; the instrument: mīqan; the passive: wuqiya yūqā and so on.

text.original: الْمَقْرُونُ، نَحْوُ: طَوَى يَطْوِي إِلَخْ، وَحُكْمُهُمَا كَحُكْمِ النَّاقِصِ، وَلَا يُعَلُّ عَيْنُهُمَا لِمَا مَرَّ فِي بَابِ الْأَجْوَفِ. الْأَمْرُ: اطْوِ اطْوِيَا اطْوُوا اطْوِي اطْوِيَا اطْوِينَ، وَبِنُونِ التَّأْكِيدِ: اطْوِيَنَّ اطْوِيَانِّ اطْوُنَّ اطْوِنَّ اطْوِيَانِّ اطْوِينَانِّ، وَبِالْخَفِيفَةِ: اطْوِيَنْ اطْوُنْ اطْوِنْ.
text.en: The joined, as ṭawā yaṭwī “to fold” and so on: their rule is like the rule of the defective, and their ʿayn is not changed, for what has passed in the chapter on the hollow. The command: iṭwi iṭwiyā iṭwū iṭwī iṭwiyā iṭwīna “fold!” (to one man, two, men; to one woman, two, women); with the nūn of emphasis: iṭwiyanna iṭwiyānni iṭwunna iṭwinna iṭwiyānni iṭwīnānni; and with the light: iṭwiyan iṭwun iṭwin.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ مِنْ رَوِيَ يَرْوَى: ارْوَيَنَّ ارْوَيَانِّ ارْوَوُنَّ ارْوَيِنَّ ارْوَيَانِّ ارْوَيْنَانِّ، وَبِالْخَفِيفَةِ: ارْوَيَنْ ارْوَوُنْ ارْوَيِنْ.
text.en: From rawiya yarwā “to quench one's thirst” you say: irwayanna irwayānni irwawunna irwayinna irwayānni irwaynānni “do drink your fill!”, and with the light: irwayan irwawun irwayin.

text.original: وَإِذَا أَرَدْتَ أَنْ تَعْرِفَ أَحْكَامَ نُونَيِ التَّأْكِيدِ فِي النَّاقِصِ وَاللَّفِيفِ، فَانْظُرْ إِلَى حَرْفِ الْعِلَّةِ: فَإِنْ كَانَتْ أَصْلِيَّةً مَحْذُوفَةً فِي الْوَاحِدِ تُرَدُّ؛ لِأَنَّ حَذْفَهَا كَانَ لِلسُّكُونِ، وَهُوَ انْعَدَمَ بِدُخُولِ النُّونِ، وَتُفْتَحُ لِخِفَّةِ الْفَتْحَةِ، نَحْوُ: اطْوِيَنَّ وَاغْزُوَنَّ وَارْوَيَنَّ، كَمَا فِي اطْوِيَا وَاغْزُوَا وَارْوَيَا. وَإِنْ كَانَتْ ضَمِيرًا نُظِرَ إِلَى مَا قَبْلَهَا: إِنْ كَانَ مَفْتُوحًا تُحَرَّكُ لِطُرُوِّ حَرَكَتِهَا وَخِفَّةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، نَحْوُ: ارْوَوُنَّ وَارْوَيِنَّ، كَمَا فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَلَا تَنْسَوُا الْفَضْلَ بَيْنَكُمْ﴾، وَإِنْ كَانَ غَيْرَ مَفْتُوحٍ يُحْذَفُ لِعَدَمِ الْخِفَّةِ فِيمَا قَبْلَهَا، نَحْوُ: اطْوُنَّ وَاطْوِنَّ، كَمَا فِي: اغْزُوا الْقَوْمَ، وَيَا امْرَأَةُ اغْزِي الْقَوْمَ.
text.en: When you want to know the rules of the two nūns of emphasis in the defective and the lafīf, look at the letter of weakness. If it is a root letter dropped in the singular, it is brought back, because its dropping was for the sukūn, and that has gone with the coming of the nūn; and it is given a fatḥa, because of the lightness of the fatḥa, as iṭwiyanna, ughzuwanna and irwayanna, as in iṭwiyā, ughzuwā and irwayā. If it is a pronoun, one looks at what is before it: if that has a fatḥa, it is given a vowel, because its vowel is accidental and what is before it is light, as irwawunna and irwayinna, as in His saying, Most High: wa-lā tansawu al-faḍla baynakum “and do not forget generosity between you” [2:237]; and if it has no fatḥa, it is dropped, because there is no lightness in what is before it, as iṭwunna and iṭwinna, as in ughzū al-qawma “raid the people!” and yā imraʾatu ughzī al-qawma “woman, raid the people!”.

lessons.title: Ṭāwin, rayyān and maṭwiyy: the book's last forms
body: The active participle of ṭawā is ṭāwin, “folding”, and “its wāw is not changed, as in ṭawā”: the wāw keeps its kasra, and only the yāʾ at the end falls, as in rāmin.

From al-riyy, “quenching”, come rayyān, rayyānān, riwāʾ, “quenched” (masculine singular, dual, plural), and rayyā, rayyayān, riwāʾ for the feminine. In riwāʾ the wāw is not made a yāʾ, as it is in siyāṭ (lesson 46), “so that two changes do not come together”: the wāw of the ʿayn would become a yāʾ, and the yāʾ of the lām has already become a hamza.

Two forms test everything learnt so far. The feminine dual in naṣb and jarr is rayyayayni, “like ʿaṭshayayni”. Annexed to “my” it is rayyayayya, as in raʾaytu rayyayayya, “I saw my two quenched ones”, “with five yāʾs”: the first changed from the wāw that is the ʿayn; the second the lām; the third changed from the alif of the feminine; the fourth the sign of naṣb; and the fifth the yāʾ of annexation.

The rest of ṭawā: the passive participle maṭwiyy, as marmiyy; the place maṭwan, as marman; the instrument miṭwan; the passive ṭuwiya, yuṭwā. “The rule of the lām of these things is like the rule of the defective”, and their ʿayn follows ṭawā: unchanged where two changes would meet, and unchanged even where they would not, “for following”, as ṭawayā and ṭāwiyāni.

Here the book ends. It began with the seven bābs and the nine things derived from every maṣdar, and it has now run each kind of root through all nine. A student who has followed it can take any root, sound or weak, set up its base forms on the patterns of ḍaraba, and reach the spoken form by the rules: the sukūn, the moving of the vowel, the change into alif, wāw or yāʾ, the dropping, and the merging.

terms.en: following: ṭawayā keeps its wāw after ṭawā
two changes in one word, which the language avoids
the alif of the feminine, as in rayyā
the yāʾ of “my”, the fifth yāʾ of rayyayayya

examples.en: ṭāwin: the wāw unchanged
rayyān, rayyānān, riwāʾ: “quenched”
raʾaytu rayyayayya: five yāʾs
ṭuwiya yuṭwā: the passive

tasks.prompt: Why is the wāw of riwāʾ not changed into a yāʾ, as in siyāṭ?
tasks.answer: Because the word already has one change, the yāʾ of the lām turned into a hamza; changing the wāw of the ʿayn into a yāʾ as well would bring two changes together.

tasks.prompt: Name the five yāʾs of rayyayayya.
tasks.answer: The first, changed from the wāw that is the ʿayn; the second, the lām; the third, changed from the alif of the feminine; the fourth, the sign of naṣb (of the dual); the fifth, the yāʾ of annexation, “my”.

tasks.prompt: Give the derived forms of ṭawā, each with its model in ramā.
tasks.answer: Ṭāwin like rāmin; maṭwiyy like marmiyy; maṭwan like marman; miṭwan like mirman; ṭuwiya yuṭwā like rumiya yurmā. The wāw of the ʿayn is never changed.

quiz.prompt: The active participle of ṭawā is…
quiz.explanation: Its wāw is not changed.

quiz.prompt: Rayyān means…
quiz.explanation: From al-riyy, quenching.

quiz.prompt: Why is riwāʾ not changed to riyāʾ?
quiz.explanation: The lām is already a hamza.

quiz.prompt: How many yāʾs has rayyayayya?
quiz.explanation: “With five yāʾs.”

quiz.prompt: The third yāʾ of rayyayayya comes from…
quiz.explanation: Rayyā ends in the alif of the feminine.

quiz.prompt: The passive participle of ṭawā is…
quiz.explanation: As marmiyy.

quiz.prompt: Ṭawayā keeps its wāw…
quiz.explanation: No two changes would meet in it, but it follows ṭawā.

text.original: الْفَاعِلُ: طَاوٍ، وَلَا يُعَلُّ وَاوُهُ كَمَا فِي طَوَى. وَتَقُولُ مِنَ الرِّيِّ: رَيَّانُ رَيَّانَانِ رِوَاءٌ، رَيَّا رَيَّيَانِ رِوَاءٌ أَيْضًا، وَلَا يُجْعَلُ وَاوُهُمَا يَاءً كَمَا فِي سِيَاطٍ حَتَّى لَا يَجْتَمِعَ الْإِعْلَالَانِ: قَلْبُ الْوَاوِ الَّتِي هِيَ عَيْنٌ يَاءً، وَقَلْبُ الْيَاءِ الَّتِي هِيَ لَامٌ هَمْزَةً.
text.en: The fāʿil: ṭāwin “folding”; its wāw is not changed, as in ṭawā. From al-riyyi “quenching” you say: rayyānu rayyānāni riwāʾun “quenched” (m. sg., du., pl.) and rayyā rayyayāni riwāʾun (f. sg., du., pl.) as well; and their wāw is not made a yāʾ as in siyāṭin, so that two changes do not come together: changing the wāw that is the ʿayn into a yāʾ, and changing the yāʾ that is the lām into a hamza.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي تَثْنِيَةِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ فِي حَالَةِ النَّصْبِ وَالْخَفْضِ: رَيَّيَيْنِ مِثْلُ عَطْشَيَيْنِ، وَإِذَا أَضَفْتَهُ إِلَى يَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ قُلْتَ: رَأَيْتُ رَيَّيَيَّ بِخَمْسِ يَاءَاتٍ: الْأُولَى مُنْقَلِبَةٌ عَنِ الْوَاوِ الَّتِي هِيَ عَيْنُ الْفِعْلِ، وَالثَّانِيَةُ لَامُ الْفِعْلِ، وَالثَّالِثَةُ مُنْقَلِبَةٌ عَنْ أَلِفِ التَّأْنِيثِ، وَالرَّابِعَةُ عَلَامَةُ النَّصْبِ، وَالْخَامِسَةُ يَاءُ الْإِضَافَةِ.
text.en: In the dual of the feminine in the states of naṣb and khafḍ you say rayyayayni, like ʿaṭshayayni “thirsty (f. du.)”; and when you annex it to the yāʾ of the speaker you say raʾaytu rayyayayya “I saw my two quenched ones”, with five yāʾs: the first changed from the wāw that is the ʿayn of the verb, the second the lām of the verb, the third changed from the alif of the feminine, the fourth the sign of naṣb, and the fifth the yāʾ of annexation.

text.original: الْمَفْعُولُ: مَطْوِيٌّ، الْمَوْضِعُ: مَطْوًى، وَالْآلَةُ: مِطْوًى، الْمَجْهُولُ: طُوِيَ يُطْوَى إِلَى آخِرِهِمَا. وَحُكْمُ لَامِ هَذِهِ الْأَشْيَاءِ كَحُكْمِ النَّاقِصِ، وَحُكْمُ عَيْنِهِنَّ كَحُكْمِ طَوَى فِي الَّتِي يَجْتَمِعُ فِيهَا الْإِعْلَالَانِ بِتَقْدِيرِ إِعْلَالِهَا، وَفِي الَّتِي لَمْ يَجْتَمِعْ فِيهَا الْإِعْلَالَانِ يَكُونُ حُكْمُهَا أَيْضًا كَحُكْمِ طَوَى لِلْمُتَابَعَةِ، نَحْوُ: طَوَيَا وَطَاوِيَانِ.
text.en: The mafʿūl: maṭwiyyun “folded”; the place: maṭwan; the instrument: miṭwan; the passive: ṭuwiya yuṭwā to their end. The rule of the lām of these things is like the rule of the defective; and the rule of their ʿayn is like the rule of ṭawā in those in which the two changes would come together on the supposition of changing it; and in those in which the two changes do not come together its rule is also like the rule of ṭawā, for following, as ṭawayā “they two folded” and ṭāwiyāni “folding (du.)”.
